JOHN W. DRISKELL

JOHN W. DRISKELL

The mark made upon the Masonic Fraternity by the 120th Grand Master, John W. Driskell, will forever be indelible. He has touched the lives of
hundred s upon hundred s of Masons and their families. He has maintai ned
an open, friendly manner and truly been a Grand Master who is, above all,
available and approac hable and more than willing to listen.
Born in Barnha m, Texas on August 15, 1924, he was educate d in the
local public schools. As the storm clouds of war were gathering early in
1941, with dedication, loyalty and concern for his country, John joined the
U.S. Naval Air Corps at the age of 17. He served in the Pacific Theater of
the war in many posts and in many capacities. An especially moving experience for John as Grand Master was to view the plaque dedicated to those
members of the Masonic Fraterni ty lost at Pearl Harbor on December 7,
1941 and to place a lei upon the now still waters above the U.S.S. Arizona
Monum ent in their memory. He served with the U.S. Naval Air Corps until
1947. In 1948 he entered the U.S. Air Force and served until 1953. Again,
his concern for others entered into his work with the U.S. Air Force on his
assignment to the Air-Sea Search and Rescue Team.
In 1945, he was most fortuna te when the lovely Eleanor agreed to
become his bride as well as his best friend. They have been blessed with
two beautiful daughte rs, Janet and Pamela , who were both born in Honolulu, Hawaii while John was statione d at Hickam Field. Both girls were
active in Bethel No. 74 of the Interna tional Order of Job's Daught ers;
Janet served as Honore d Queen of that Bethel. John and Eleanor both
untiringly gave many years of devotio n to Job's Daughters and Bethel No.
74 in particular. John served as Bethel Guardia n Treasurer for eight years.
In recognition and apprecia tion of his efforts, he was made a "Memb er of
Honor" in that Btthel.
Following military service, the Driskell family settled in the Sacram ento
area. He worked at Aerojet Corpora tion for some time; then began a long
career at the University of Californ ia at Davis. He worked in the physical
plant departm ent and finally retired from there as the Senior Superintendent, Services Division of the Physical Plant Departm ent. His rapid rise to
that position was indicative of his innate ability to work well with people,
particularly as liaison between outside contrac tors, faculty members and
his own staff member s . The campus of the University of Califor nia at
Davis grew and prospered under his guidance.
While working at Aerojet in the early 1960's, John was impressed by several of the men with whom he worked - they were Masons. He petitioned
to receive the three degrees of Masonr y in Capital City Lodge No. 499 in
Sacram ento and was raised in 1962. Immedi ately thereaft er he became
active in the Lodge serving on many committees and was appoint ed to the
line of officers. He served with distinction as Worshipful Master in 1969.
He continued to be a vital force in his Lodge working on several committees from the negotiation to purchas e and then renovat ion of a church into
the present Capital City Masonic Temple.

Grand Master
October 16, 1985-0 ctober 15, 1986
iii

John became a member of the Sacramento Scottish Rite Bodies and
immediately became active serving on committees and participating as a
cast member of the Fourteenth Degree. He maintained much of the Scottish Rite Building for many years, including the heating and air conditioning systems. He is a member of the Scottish Rite Temple Board Association, even while serving as Grand Master. The Supreme Council of the
Scottish Rite recognized John's accomplishments and decorated him a
Knight Commander of the Court of Honor in 1983.
A member of Ben Ali Shrine Temple in Sacramento, he has served as
Ambassador for that Temple and also as Ambassador of Al Malaikah Temple in Los Angeles. He is a member of the Past Masters Unit of Ben Ali.
Membership in the Royal Order of Scotland, Sciots Tract Pyramid No. 11
and Life Membership in the Davis High 1Welve Club are held by John .
In addition to his work with Job's Daughters, he also served as an advisor to the Order of DeMolay. In appreciation and recognition of his
endeavors with the young men, he received the coveted Honorary Legion
of Honor Degree.
In 1974 he was appointed Senior Grand Deacon of the Grand Lodge of
California. In 1977 he was a member of the Junior Grand Warden Selection Committee. From 1977 through 1981 he was Inspector of the 219th
Masonic District. He was appointed to serve on the Commission to Study
the Organizational Structure of Grand Lodge in 1979-1980. In 1981 he
served on the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees and certainly has left his
mark on that Board with his expertise in the building field.
In 1982, his talents, abilities and dedication to the Masonic Fraternity
were recognized and he was elected Junior Grand Warden. He was subsequently elected to each successive office and finally elected Grand Master
on October 16, 1985.
John has a unique ability to bring out the best in people and to perceive
the true personality of those whom he meets . Using these talents, he chose
open and friendly men to serve as Grand Lodge Officers during his term as
Grand Master.
As Grand Master, John Driskell will always be remembered - from
every corner of California and Hawaii, from the largest to the smallest of
Lodges, and in every inch of the more than 91, 700 miles he traveled - as
an open, friendly, decisive, and positive leader who brought "Masonry, the
Last Frontier" into reality. Masonry has indeed been the better for the
service of John W. Driskell.

Devotional Message: "Living the Life We Profess"
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Members of the Grand Lodge:
Before I get into the main theme for this occasion, l would like to make
a couple of personal comments. First, I would like to express my appreciation to our Grand Master, John Driskell, for giving me the opportunity to
fill the shoes of "Grand Chaplain:• I hope that I have fulfilled his anticipation of my qualifications for this honor and prestige. He well knows that I
originally had a "hang-up" or two in accepting this office. I am an Episco-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

7

pal Clergyman and I had two problems. First, I was told that I could not
wear my clerical collar to official functions. That is the chief sign of my
Priesthood which I treasure most highly. Second, I was informed that I had
to be careful not to bring Christian theology into my official prayers as
Grand Chaplain. My loyalty to my Lord and my Priesthood is extremely
important in my life. I did some praying about this. I came up with this
resolution. Maybe God was saying to me, "Maury, these are all my children too . Show them the Way!" So, I resolved my dilemma by sensing that
God was asking me to broaden my Ministry and proclaim His Word in
broader concepts. This I have tried to do and again I say, "Thank you,
John:'
In arriving at the content for this "Devotional Message" or sermon, if
you will, I was given some copies of the messages that were given by some
past Grand Chaplains. Each one was an erudite description of the teachings and tenets of Masonry. Each one was quite aware and cognizant of the
aims and purposes of the Craft. I could not emulate their offerings and I
do not intend to try to come up to their excellent portrayal of "Free and
Accepted Masons:•
I am a "Pragmatist:' stemming from the fact that I was in business and
in the selling game prior to entering the Ministry at the age of forty. Let me
define the word: "Pragmatism is the doctrine that ideas have value only in
terms of their practical consequences and that results are the sole test of the
validity of the truths of one's belief!' I am reminded of a well known Gospel singer, Mahalia Jackson, who was so beautiful in her witness to her
belief. The song she made famous was titled, "I Want to Live the Life I
Sing About" - and she did. What follows is based on this premise. And
one more thougat: The job of the Preacher is not to comfort the afflicted BUT - to afflict the comfortable. So, let's see.
First , let me give you the basis for what is to follow. I attended a meeting
on China that was sponsored by "The University Women" and conducted
by a Professor from UCSB. He covered extremely well the economic, cultural and governmental changes that have occurred in the new regime following the disaster of Mao. It was interesting and enlightening. However,
some comments by a Chinese student following his talk was what electrified me. It was a shocker. At one time during her early life, when she was
ten, her parents were incarcerated by the Communist authorities for some
minor infraction of their rule. They were sentenced for two and one-half
years. So, here was a ten year old, a brother of seven, and a sister of five
left to fend for themselves. They were told in the Communist teaching that,
"THERE IS NO GOD. YOU'RE ON YOUR OWN!" And they literally
were for two and one-half years, scratching out a living from garbage pails
and whatever - "ON THEIR OWN:' They lived like animals.
However, lest we feel smug in our "Free, Democratic Society" of these
United States, let me quote you a piece written by Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn
in the September issue of The Reader's Digest. After confessing in his reading and writing - his own personal testimonies - of the cause of the ruinous
revolution in his Russia, he adds this , "If I were called upon to identify the

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

entire 20th Century, I would be unable to find anything more precise than
to reflect once again on how we have lost touch with our Creator. MEN
HAVE FORGOTTEN GOD'.'
Now, I would like to point out to you some ways in which I feel that this
can be applied to our time and space. God has literally been taken out of
our Public Schools. School properties can not even be used after school
hours for any kind of religious exercise. We have the stat~d fact that. there
is to be the separation of Church and State . Up to a pomt I su?scr~be to
that premise. However, I would submit that we have a c<:>nfus1on m the
word "Church" in that we immediately mentally substitute the word
"Denomination" and on that basis I would agree. However, too many contenders on this subject confuse this with "God" and h~rein we mus~ ag.ree
that State and God can not be separated. It is inherent m our Constitution
and Declaration of Independence that, "All men are created by God!' ~n
this context God is an avowed and acknowledged Presence and Power m
the conduct and operation both of our National and State Governments.
Masons have an inherent obligation in attempting to create within themselves and their neighbors that God is definitely a distinct ~art of our P.ublic School system. It is a tenet of our belief. The DeMolay ntual symbohzes
this when they place school books alongside of the Bible . But the unseen
hand of the State says, "NO WAY!" It is no wonder that Parochial Schools
of all varieties are growing by leaps and bounds. Parents see no oth~r alternative to impress upon their children's minds that God has a place m every
facet of their up-bringing.
There is another dangerous growth in our presence to remove God from
young minds as well as old. It is the rise of "Satanism" or Devil worship.
A recent account in the Los Angeles Times verifies this. It stated, "From
small towns like Sanford, Maine to Los Angeles the numbers are rising'. '
This is evidence of a disturbing element. An accused murderer exhibited
the "Sign of Satan" on his palm - a circle with crossed lines two points of
which symbolize the horns of the Devil. A part of the ritual describ~s the
"Waving of a human arm or bone through the air!' The author of this, an
Anton LeVey, adds, " I figured people would get the bone someplace other
than killing (e.g. grave robbing) but if they' re going to kill I hope they at
least get some deserving victim'.' How does that "grab you?" I repeat,
" When you take God out of our very lives we become like animals and act
like the same'.'
Another illustration that God is being pushed aside in our daily living is
the wide-spread use of "gutter language" - the four Jette~, perverse. language of the street. Recently, my wife and I, at the ~uggest1on of a fnen~ ,
viewed the picture, "Ferris Bueller's Day Ofr' , bastcally a comedy and m
its comedic portrayal - excellent. However, the "gutter language" that permeated the entire picture - which was geared to the teen-ager (PG the ad
stated) - was not only offensive, it was solely distasteful. I was later
informed by some friends that such language is not only in the teen-ager's
vocabulary, even some six year olds come home using what I call "gutter
language'.'

In my estimation, a truly God-minded person would abhor and never use
such foul and ignorant language. As an illustration, all too many of our
children are hearing the word " God" - but followed by a four letter word.
In the Christian Community this is called a "sin'.' But even to strictly Godfearing and God-minded people such a phrase is not only considered an
insult to God, it is actually a denial. Add to this the growing influence of
pornographic materials in all forms of communications - a frightening
addition to a people who revere and respect their Creator. I, and I hope
you as well, will agree with Solzhenitsyn that the evidence is there that ,
"Men Have Forgotten God'.'
That is the dark scene with which we are confronted. So, now the question comes before us, "What can we do about it?" And this is where my
"Pragmatism" takes over. We must encourage all Masons and their related
organizations to some kind of action. To allow its continuance is to deny
what we proclaim by word and by symbol. And it seems to me that "The
Order of Free and Accepted Masons" and our fellow organizations, are in
an unqualified position to " Live the Life we Profess:• First, Masonry is not
a "Religion" but it is "Religious" . We are without a Credo or particular,
peculiar symbolism portraying a specific religion. That puts Masonry in an
enviable position.
Our basic premise is our belief in a Universal God. We proclaim, "The
Great Architect" - "The Ruler of the Universe" - "The Source of Brotherhood" - "The Creator of all Creatures and Creation!' These symbolic
words can be attributed to the God of all Religions; e.g., the Christian God
- the Holy Trinity; the Jewish God - Yahweh; the Moslem God - Allah; the
American Indian - the Spirit of Life. Thus when we proclaim that God
must be recognized in public schools - as well as in every facet of our lives as our ritual portrays, we act as a mantle over all "Religions" and / o r
"Denominations!' We are simply saying, GOD IS AND GOD IS FOR
ALL! Period.
Now, if I may put it bluntly, we must "put our actions where our mouth
is!" We must prove that our rituals and our symbols are not just pretty,
sentimental and emotional parts of our proclamation . They are TRUE and
for REAL. Let me suggest something. The United States Supreme Court
begins every session with this proclamation: " GOD BLESS T HESE
UNITED STATES. GOD BLESS THIS COURT.' If this is constitutional
for our Supreme Court, I see no reason why it can not be used to begin
each day's session in our schools. With practically every school wired for
sound it would be a tremendous acclamation for a school principal to begin
each day with the words, "God bless these United States. God bless this
School! "
Only as we literally proclaim " God" in every facet of our living can we
then experience that Love and Brotherhood for all peoples of the earth.
Only then can we truly understand that "Bourne" to which we are all traveling along this pathway of Life . May God be proclaimed now, forever and
everywhere. It 's up to each and everyone of us to - "LIVE THE LIFE WE
PROFESS!'

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

EULOGY
LAURENCE E. DAYTON, P.G.M.
By Chester R. MacPhee, P.G.M.
We have come together today in Jove and appreciation to pay our last
respects to a Past Grand Master of this Jurisdiction, a great Californian,
beloved husband, father, and grandfather, Most Worshipful Laurence
Edward Dayton.
Larry Dayton was a man who added to the word honor. To those who
knew him best, he was Mr. Integrity. In his every assignment in life he was
highly respected - his advice and wise counsel always extensively sought.
Born November 28, 1900 in College View, Nebraska, he was brought to
California as a young child and lived in Sonoma County. He attended public schools in Sebastopol prior to graduating from the University of California at Berkeley.
He served as Chief Assistant District Attorney in Alameda County and
as an Assistant United States Attorney - always with great credit and honorable effort - he judged with candor - admonished with friendship - and
affirmed with justice.
As a family man his affection for his beloved wife "Mac:' his children
and grandchildren was as beautiful as was his exemplary character.
As a Mason, with constancy, he faithfully discharged his every Masonic
obligation - he was indeed a faithful counselor to this Grand Lodge.
As Grand Master, he was quiet, yet formidable, reserved, yet tenacious persistent, yet right minded.
Larry Dayton was raised in Live Oak Lodge No. 61 in Oakland on February 28, 1941, and served as Master in 1951. In 1952 he served as President of the East Bay Masters and Wardens Association and was the fourth
Master of Northern California Research Lodge .
Larry passed away quietly on February 1st, 1986 at 85 years of age.
Because he came among us, we are better men and better Masons . My
Brethren, we properly honor Larry Dayton by the exemplification of our
own personal course of conduct.

BORN
November 28, 1900
College View, Nebraska

LAURENCEE. DAYTON
Grand Master - 1966

DIED
February I, 1986
Petaluma, California

MEMORIAL TRIBUTE

OSWALD JON BONG LAU
By E. Arthur Haglund, P.G.M.
The Grand Lodge of California, and even more, the Masons of the
Aloha state of Hawaii have lost one of our most active and revered Grand
Lodge Officers, Worshipful Brother Oswald Jon Bong Lau .
Born in Honolulu, Hawaii on September 17, 1925, he is survived by his
beloved wife Jasmine , two daughters Stephanie and Barbara, along with
four grandchildren .
Our Brother was educated in the public schools of Honolulu and
attended the University of Hawaii. A veteran of World War II, he served
for twenty-two years in the U. S. Air Force with duty assignments throughout the Pacific. Following his retirement, he continued to serve his government as a civilian Communication Specialist for the U.S. Army.
A devoted father and son , Ozzie was also active in the Episcopal
Church , serving as a Vestry member and Lay-reader. For thirteen years he
served the United States Department of Justice, Immigration & Naturalization Service as a member and chairman of the Citizenship and Constitution
Observance Day Committee.
Brother Lau was raised to the sublime degree of Master Mason on April
4, 1967, in Schofield Lodge No. 443 . In 1973 he served as Master and was a
member of the Schofield Temple Association from 1972 to 1978. He was
also a plural member of King Solomon's Seaport Lodge No. 260 in San
Francisco, and Angeles Mesa Lodge No. 625 in Garden Grove.
Very active ii! many Masonic affiliated organizations, Brother Ozzie was
a 33rd Degree Inspector General Honorary in the Scottish Rite and had
been named Chairman, Inspector General's Advisory conference in 1985.
A member of the York Rite, Red Cross of Constantine, Royal Order of
Scotland, Aloha Shrine Temple, the Ali Shan Oasis Shrine Club of Taiwan,
Order of Eastern Star, Order of the White Shrine of Jerulsalem, and four
Square and Compass Clubs on Oahu . He served as a member, Advisory
Board, Leilehua Assembly No. 3, International Order of the Rainbow for
Girls from 1980 until his death and was honored with the Grand Cross of
Color. He also served on the Advisory Executive Committee for the International Supreme Council, Order of DeMolay and received the Legion of
Honor honorary.
Recognizing his outstanding Masonic and personal abilities, he was
appointed Inspector of the 385th Masonic District in 1974, having previously served on the Grand Lodge Youth Committee. It was my honor to
appoint him Assistant Grand Lecturer for the newly formed Division VII
and I was most pleased to formally install him in that office in the presence
of his family and Brother Masons of the Aloha State in Honolulu in January 1984.
We all remember the prayer at initiation given for each one of us.
"Vouchsafe Thine aid, Almighty Father of the Universe, to this, our

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

present convention, and grant that this candidate for Freemasonry may
dedicate and devote his life to Thy service, and become a true and faithful
Brother among us. Endue him with a competency of Thy Divine Wisdom,
that by the influence of the pure principles of Freemasonry, he may the better be enabled to display the beauties of holiness, to the honor of Thy Holy
Name'.'
No Mason was more exemplary, more dedicated and devoted to His service than Brother Oswald J. B. Lau. No man became a more true and faithful Brother among us than did Brother Oswald J. B. Lau. He said his
hobby was people; no man perfected his hobby better than he did. He was
one of Hawaii's best, and he will be sorely missed by this Grand Lodge.

He embraced Masonry with total commitment and gave to his Brothers
all that he had. In the 12 years of his Masonic life he was Master of his
Lodge, served as President of the Temple Association , Head Officer's
Coach, and, at his death, was serving Grand Lodge as Junior Grand Steward. At the same time, he stood beside Pat as Worthy Patron of their Eastern Star Chapter.
When the lives of Vic and Pat collided in 1973, it probably could have
been recorded as 8.5 on the Richter Scale. When they had a problem, they
stood toe to toe and slugged it out verbally with each other, and then stood
side by side and took on the world.
He loved the Navy, his job, Masonry, Pat - and fishing; not necessaril y in
that order.
He was the only man I knew who stood seven feet tall in a five foot
frame. I affectionately called him "The Little Giant'.' He was a fighter and
he loved a challenge. This was the one fight he couldn't win, but he went
down swinging, and he gave it all he had . He expected all of us to do the
same. Everyone who knew him could tell of some way that he affected
their life, but one thing was always there - he could always make you
laugh; either with him or at him, it didn't matter. You always knew when
Vic was around .
H~ was always surprised when honors came to him, as though somehow,
he didn't understand why. But he accepted everything that life dealt to him,
the good and the bad, and kept right on going.
In conclusion, let me share with you a poem, written by a dear friend
and colleague, Worshipful Jack Forseth, which expresses how many of us
felt about Vic. This, I dedicate to his memory.

Victor D. Dryden was born in Stockton, Kansas, on April 12, 1933, and
he died on July 5, 1986. In the short 53 years that he lived, he changed the
world for a lot of people.
Vic's profession was a weatherman. He furnished information to ships at
sea so that they could reach their home ports safely. Vic always maintained
that, as a "weather guesser,• he was the only guy around who had a license
to lie.
He gave 25 years of his life to the Navy, and served his country with the
same zeal and intensity that he put into everything he did. When he retired
from the Navy in 1977, he was a LCDR, having risen through the ranks.
He served on several ships, spending six and one-half years out of the 25
on sea duty. He held degrees in Mathematics, Meteorology and Oceanography.

ADRIAN C. WEST
By Kermit A. Jacobson, P.G.M.
"It is the Lord who goes before you. He will be with you. He will not
fail you or forsake you. Do not fear or be dismayed:' Deuteronomy 31 :8
"God is love and he that dwelleth in love dwelleth in God, and God in

These beautiful passages were well known to Adrian C. West, and now
bring comfort and strength and peace to our hearts.
Very early in life Adrian made friends with the Bible and throughout his
life expressed his firm belief in the Fatherhood of God, the Brotherhood of
Man and the immortality of the soul.
Adrian C. West was born on February 4, 1922, in San Jose, California.
He attended the public schools and graduated from San Jose State College
as a Petroleum Engineer. He was a brilliant student and his scholastic abilities were further recognized as he pursued graduate studies at Harvard
University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. From these outstanding academic institutions, he received honors .
Enlisting in the Navy, he served his country with distinction from 19431946 and retired at the end of World War II with the rank of Lieutenant.
Professionally, Adrian was selected by the Standard Oil Company to
join their staff of engineers. His brilliance and dedication to his work were
again recognized when he was singled out from his engineering group to
become Assistant to the General Tax counsel and provide tax services to
employees scatttered around the world. He retired June 1, 1984, after 37
years with Standard Oil.
As a Mason - He was raised to Master Mason on September 24, 1970, in
East Bay Lodge No. 489, and became its Master in 1975. He continued as
Master through 1976 and assisted East Bay Lodge No. 489 to consolidate
with Alamo Lodge No. 122.
Adrian was active in the Oakland Scottish Rite Bodies, serving in the
important office of Venerable Master of the Lodge of Perfection. He was
elected to be coroneted a 33rd Degree Mason, with the conferral to take
place on December 14, 1985, but three weeks before this honor could be
conferred upon him, he went to his reward. He was one most deserving of
this high honor. He was a member of Aahmes Temple of Shrine Masonry.
His services were in demand by our Grand Lodge, serving as a member

MEMORIAL TRIBUTE

JAMES C. MYERS
by Glenn D. Woody
My Brethren,. it is our great privilege to come together today and
acknowledge the beauty that came into our lives because we were touched
by the person and talent of Jim Myers.
And truly we were all touched. No one who was ever in the presence of
Jim's music could help but be inspired, uplifted and touched in a very special way by its beauty.
He was born October 24, 1924, in Anaheim, California. While still
young he moved with his family to Cincinnati, Ohio, where he attended
school. After high school he entered the Army during World War II and
served as a Radio Operator in the Asian Theatre.
Following World War II he returned to Cincinnati and continued the
development of a music career by attending the College of Music in that
city.
At college he met Elna and, after his return to California in June, 1949,
Elna soon followed. They were married October 9, 1949. That marriage
was blessed with a son in September 1950.
Jim was raised to Master Mason on March 23, 1948 in Lafayette Lodge
No. 81 in Cincinnati, Ohio, and affiliated with Francis Drake Lodge No.
376, South San Francisco, California, November 3, 1961, serving as its
Master in 1974.
Our Brother was an active DeMolay in Cincinnati, Ohio, and was

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

awarded the Degree of Chevalier. As an adult he served on the Advisory
Council of the South San Francisco Chapter, and as District Supervisor,
and received the DeMolay Legion of Honor.
Brother Myers was an elementary school teacher and a music teacher. In
1984, after more than 20 years, he retired from his own picture framing
business in San Francisco.
Brother Jim was probably best known by this Grand Lodge for his
music. He was an organist most of his life, and, since his father was a minister, Jim was almost always a church organist. At the time of his death he
was organist for and a member of Holy Cross Lutheran Church in Pacifica. He was always ready to play for his many friends at installations and
for many Lodges at their degrees.
Brother Jim served this Grand Lodge as its Grand Organist for 5 consecutive years. He was first appointed by then Grand Master Vernon Gordon
in 1980, and was subsequently reappointed by Grand Masters Lemons,
West, Maynard and Haglund. He was affectionately dubbed " 1Winkle Fingers" by his several Grand Lodge families .
Our Brother entered into rest on September 14, 1986 with services,
including the Masonic Funeral Service, at the First United Methodist
Church in San Bruno on September 20, 1986. The tightly packed Chapel,
over half of which was filled with his many Masonic friends , and the stirring memorial tribute delivered by Dr. Arnold Compton, former Grand
Chaplain, are further testimony of the love and affection felt for Jim .

GRAND MASTER'S ACHIEVEMENT AWARD
The following 41 Lodges qualified as first time recipients and were presented with a handsome and suitably engraved plaque. To properly recognize the earning of this award, the Master or representative of each of these
Lodges was escorted into the Grand Lodge by the Grand Marshal and presented with the plaque by Grand Master Driskell . Following these presentations, the Brethren accorded these Lodges a standing ovation.

1987 TOURNAMENT OF ROSES PARADE FLOAT
"FREEMASONRY SUPPORTING THE CONSTITUTION"

By H. Douglas Lemons, P.G.M.
1987 marks the first year in its 137 year history that the Grand Lodge of
California has sponsored a Float in the annual Tournament of Roses
Parade in Pasadena.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

27

The principal purpose for the Grand Lodge Float is to call attention to
the American Constitution, and to point up the fact that 1987 is the Bicentennial of the signing of the Constitution, the greatest document of personal freedom ever penned by the hand of man, and a document which is
truly one of the wonders of the world!
The Float is designed to represent "Liberty, Peace and EqualitY.' Over
sixty-five feet in length, the Float is designed with three huge American
eagles in full night over the base of the Float. The first eagle with its wing
tips reaching a height of twenty-eight feet, has its talons resting upon a replica of the Liberty Bell, representing "Liberty'.' The second eagle carries in
its beak garlands of palm leaves, representing "Peace:• The third eagle with
talons resting upon the scroll of the Constitution represents "EqualitY.'
The base of red roses represents America's fertile lands, and the stars
springing for th from the base of red roses represents the fifty states of the
Union.
Six foreign national flags, three forward and three aft are symbolic of
the fact that the United States Constitution served as a model for all fifty
of our states, Canada, Mexico, five republics of Central America, nine
republics of South America, Australia, France, Belgium, Union of South
Africa and Switzerland. The six flags depicted on the Float are those of
Chile, France, Great Britain, Peru, the Philippines and Switzerland.
Riding upon the Float, and representing all Masons in California and
Hawaii will be one of the most prominent members of the Fraternity; the
Oscar winning star of stage, screen and television - star of the recent television series, "Airwolf;' an actor best known to many as Captain McHale of
the television series, "McHale's NavY,' Brother Ernest Borgnine, Master
Mason, Thirty-thjrd Degree Scottish Rite Mason and Shrine Mason.
The Grand Lodge Float will be decorated entirely by members of the
California Youth Groups, the International Order of DeMolay, the International Order of Job's Daughters, and the International Order of The Rainbow for Girls. Some three hundred of these young people will commence at
eight o'clock a.m. on the 26th of December, and will work every day from
eight a.m. to five o'clock p.m . through December 31st to complete this tremendous task.
This magnificent Float could very well win one or more prizes in the
Tournament of Roses Parade, but win or not, it will surely make every
Masons' heart beat with pride and joy as it makes its way down the parade
route in Colorado Boulevard on New Year's Day, 1987.
At 12:00 Noon Grand Lodge was called off with labor to be resumed at
1:30 P.M.

REPORT OF THE GRAND TREASURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
The accounting firm of Lindquist, Von Husen and Joyce has examined
our financial records, performed the required verification of assets and
commented on matters that need management attention. Their several
reports for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1986 have been pre-printed as
part of this Grand Treasurer's report, available for your questions and
comments.
Membership decline eased a bit, notwithstanding new low levels in the
number of initiates and the number of Master Masons raised.
1\vo years ago, in the fiscal year ended June 30, 1984, a record spending
level for the operation of this Grand Lodge was established at one million
sixty-one thousand dollars ($1,061,000.00).
At the present time, that operational cost exceeds the 1984 level by about
ten percent (10%); and your Finance Committee has already informed you
of an impending twenty-two percent (22%) increase in the per capita levy,
from S6. 30 to S7. 70, for the current year.
Your Grand Treasurer continues to direct closer attention to management
of our fiscal matters; you are urged to carefully review the Finance Committee report.
California and Hawaii Masons well deserve our thanks for their substantial generosity in support of the Statue of Liberty Restoration Drive, and
of more importance closer to home, their continuing contributions to the
Endowment .F und of our Masonic Homes. This support becomes increasingly important considering the higher level of operating costs upon the
completion of tne added facilities at Union City and Covina.
Thank you again for the opportunity to serve.
Respectfully submitted,
JOHN A. S1CKENBERGER, Grand Treasurer

Referred to the Committee on Distribution. The Committee on Distribution referred the entire report to the Committee on Finance.

COMPUTER UPGRADE

For several years our membership records as well as our accounting
records have been contained on our office computer. However it was found
necessary to upgrade the system due to obsolescense and limited capacity
caused by more requests for information at both the Grand Lodge and
constituent Lodge levels. At the Annual Communication in 1985 the
Finance Committee of Grand Lodge recommended a phased approach for
an upgrade of our computer system and included an amount of $28,000.00
for phase one of this upgrade. I am pleased to report that phase one has
now been completed within this budgeted amount and the system is serving
us well. One of the immediate benefits to be realized will be the ability to
add to our membership listings the addresses of our entire membership and
by use of our high speed printer we will print the address labels which are
affixed to the California Freemason Magazine for mailing purposes. Heretofore the printing of these labels has been accomplished by an outside
source and by printing our own labels we will realize substantial savings in

38

the total costs charged to the publication of the Freemason Magazine.
SUSPENSIONS N .P.D.
Early in the year, the Executive Committee determined that a letter of
concern should be sent to those members who were delinquent in their dues
payment to their respective Lodges. This letter was sent over the signature
of the Grand Master after we received from the Lodge Secretaries the
names and addresses of those who were liable for suspension. By actual
count 1461 letters were sent. Many responses, both in writing and over the
telephone were received and the comments expressed were truly amazing.
Undoubtedly the Grand Master will refer to this subject in his message to
Grand Lodge so I shall not elaborate. Suffice it to say that in many cases
the Lodges are not proceeding properly before actual suspension for nonpayment of dues occurs. This is bourne out by the comments received from
the members in response to the Grand Master's letter, and can be summed
up in two short phrases - "No one cared about me:' or "The only time I
ever hear from my Lodge is when they want money'.' My Brethren, what a
sad commentary on Masonry!
OFFICE PERSONNEL
Each year several changes occur in our Grand Lodge office personnel.
This past year was no exception.
On March 31, 1986, Assistant Grand Secretary Clare "Bud" Wilson
retired after serving in that capacity for five years. It was my pleasure to
appoint Brother H. Francis Lewis to fill that position and this appointment
met with the approval of the Grand Master as well as the members of the
Executive Committee. Brother Lewis has been a most valuable member of
our office staff since the beginning of 1978 and is well acquainted with the
policies and procedures practiced in our office. He has assumed the important duties of Assistant Grand Secretary and is fulfilling these duties in a
most creditable fashion.
With this appointment a vacancy occurred in our Membership department and after conducting interviews with several potential applicants we
were fortunate to engage the services of Brother Kenneth J . Brisbin, a
former Inspector and currently the Secretary of Naval Lodge No . 87. His
experience as a Lodge Secretary has enabled him to rapidly adapt to the
requirements of the Membership department. He is performing his functions in an exemplary fashion.
On Thanksgiving Day last, our office lost the services of Brother Adrian
C. West, the Director of Charitable Gifts. Brother West had been ill for
some months past and on the day following Thanksgiving we were
informed of his demise which had occurred the previous evening. Our
shock was tempered in the knowledge that he no longer would be subject to
the pain and suffering he had endured for some weeks prior to his demise.
He was truly an exemplary man and Mason and as such has been sorely
missed.

. ACTION BY GRAND LODGE
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has reviewed 135 Requests to the
Grand Master for his Dispensation or permission authorizing the petitioning Lodges to conduct a variety of activities not otherwise permitted by the
California Masonic Code.
By and large the Lodges are to be commended upon the care demonstrated in making their requests for these Dispensations. Nevertheless, we
again must point out that too much reliance is placed upon the office of
the Grand Secretary to call attention to procedural errors which could easily be prevented by reference to the Masonic Code and the careful reading
of the Section or Sections applicable to the particular Petition for Dispensation.
The Committee on Jurisprudence reviewed the Petitions on an ongoing
basis throughout the year which allowed Dispensations issued in error to be
corrected so as to conform to the California Masonic Code. The action of
the Grand Master in approving 130 Dispensations either originally or after
the Petitions were modified was found to be correct. There were two
instances, both involving reballoting upon rejected candidates, wherein the

PROCEEDING S OF THE

Dispensation was erroneously granted and the Grand Master has referred
to those matters in his Message to this Grand Lodge. In three other cases,
corrective action is being undertaken at this time.

TRIAL RECORD No. 2rn

In Trial Record No . 2231 a member of Tehama Lodge No. 3 was charged
with unmasonic conduct on the grounds that he presented a false claim
against the State Compensation Insurance Fund after having presented a
claim for the same loss to another insurance carrier.
The accused responded with a plea of not guilty. After a Masonic Trial
the Trial Commissioners were unanimous in their findings of guilty of
unmasonic conduct, and by divided vote set the penalty at suspension.
Your Committee on Trial Review believes that the acts of the accused
involve moral turpitude and are of sufficient severity that the penalty
should be raised from suspension to expulsion.
Your Committee therefore submits the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that in Trial Record No. 2231 the findings of guilty of
unmasonic conduct be affirmed, but that the penalty be raised to expulsion.
TRIAL RECORD No. 2232
In Trial Record No. 2232, a member of Hammonton Lodge No. 433 was
charged with unmasonic conduct based upon two (2) specifications:
First: that he was arrested and convicted of the felony of possessing
$50.00 worth of cocaine and was placed on probation.
Second: that upon testing for cocaine usage by the probation department
he was found to have violated his probation conditions by reason of a positive test result and was thereupon arrested and convicted of the crime of
probation violation.
The accused filed a plea of guilty to both specifications and the Trial
Master found him guilty of unmasonic conduct and fixed the penalty at
Reprimand in open Lodge.
Your Committee believes that while the recommendation of the Trial
Master for leniency might be sustainable for conviction of a mere possession charge, the violation of probation is a more serious instance of unmasonic conduct which warrants a more severe penalty.
Your Committee can sympathize with the great difficulty the accused
faced when he agreed to attempt to " kick the habit" of cocaine addiction
by accepting his probation for the possession offense. He did, however, so
agree. His subsequent usage of cocaine was not only a crime, that of probation violation, but was also a breach of his promise .
We wish the accused luck in his fight with the drug habit and sincerely
hope he is successful. His probation violation however, we believe, warrants a penalty of suspension.
We therefore submit the following Resolution:

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

G RAND LODGE OF CALIFOR NIA

RESOLVED, that the findings of the Trial Master in Trial Record No.
2232 be affirmed but the penalty be raised to suspension.

GOLDEN VETERANS' AWARDS
TRIAL RECORD No . 2236

This Trial Record involves a member of Hills Ferry Lodge No . 236 who
was charged with unmasonic conduct in that he had unlawful sexual intercourse with a 14 year old girl. The tr ial record reflects that the accused
pleaded no contest to a criminal complaint for sexual battery and was
placed on probation after serving time in jail. He also pleaded guilty to the
Masonic charges filed against him. The Trial Master found the accused
· guilty and fixed the penalty at reprimand .
Your Trial Review Committee concurs with the findings of the Trial Master. However, this Committee believes that an offense of this nature is such
a serious violation of our Masonic and moral law as to merit a greater penalty than reprimand . It therefore recommends that the penalty be increased
to that of expulsion .
TRIAL RECORD No. 2244

A member of Normal Heights Lodge No . 632, San Diego, California
and a dual member of Lebanon Lodge No. 104 in the Jurisdiction of Washington was charged with unmasonic conduct alleging that he did violate the
chastity of a Brother Master Mason's wife.
The accused entered a plea of not guilty and Trial was By Commission.
The Commissioners voted 4 to 3 to find the accused guilty on the Specification as charged.
Your Committee, after a review of the Trial testimony as recorded by a
reporter, is of the opinion that the evidence as submitted at the Trial was
not sufficient to support the Specification of unmasonic conduct.
All the evidence produced at the Trial was circumstantial evidence and
we do not question its validity. However, we find the evidence insufficient
to support the finding. Underlying our concern is the well-known fact that
these particular charges are easily brought and difficult to disprove.
Your Committee submits the following Resolution:
RESOLVED , that the finding and penalty in Trial Record No . 2244 be
reversed and a not guilty verdict entered.
Respectfully submitted,

The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California, a charitable
corporation organized under the laws of the State of Califor_nia, respectfully presents its ninety-fourth annual report on the Masonic Homes of
California for the fiscal year July l, 1985 through June 30, 1986.

MEETINGS
The Board of Trustees meets on a monthly basis at the Masonic Homes,
alternating between the North and the South. Meeting at the Homes provides a closer relationship and better understanding of the operations of
each Home.
This is a working Board dedicated to providing the facilities, staff and
environment essential to the security and happiness of our elderly at Union
City and to the health, education and development of our children at Covina.
Many hours are spent in Committee meetings on rehabilitation, long
range planning, scholarship grants, special projects, budget and finance.
Trustees and Administrators present special reports on operations of the
Homes, resulting in a broader understanding of these complex units and
improved guidance and management of the Homes .
Representatives from the Masonic Homes Endowment Board are invited
to attend the monthly Board meetings. This interchange of information is
invaluable in communicating our needs to the Brethren through this impo rtant Board charged with the responsibility of raising funds for our Homes.
You will note that the Administrators and members of the Board of
Trustees have been given the opportunity to participate in the preparation
of this Annual Report as follows:

UNION CITY AND COVINA EXPANSION
by Stanley L. Channon, Chairman Expansion Committee
On March 5, 1986, the Board of Trustees approved a major expansion
and improvement program for the care of our elderly Brethren, their
spouses and widows at Union City and Covina. The program includes the
construction at Union City of a much needed 120-bed Skilled Nursing
Facility, a centrally located chapel and Masonic Temple building at the
North end of the new Plaza to be developed between the Adams building
and the new Skilled Nursing Facility, the construction of a secondary road
for emergency access, the construction of parking areas for employees and
visitors and the construction of a new residence for the Administrator.
Relocating the Administrator's home will provide ground area for the construction of the new Chapel and Masonic Temple buildings at the head of
the new plaza which will be constructed in accordance with the Master Plan
developed for the Union City Home. At Covina, the first phase of an adult
apartment complex which will ultimately house up to 224 adult residents
with a community center and various other services will be constructed .
These projects were reported in our annual report of last year and were

UNION CITY STATISTICS
by J. Burton Brown, Administrator
This year has seen an increase in the average number of people living at
the Home from 378 to 393. The total of 393 is composed of 138 men and
255 women. This resulted in the monthly averages of 135 men and 251
women. Included in this total are 45 couples.
Within the twelve months from last year's report, there were 34 Masons
admitted and 43 wives or widows admitted with the ave~age age of a~I new
residents being 81. 7 years. During the same period, the hves of 62 residents
came to an end. Twenty-nine men died at an average age of 85. 7 years,
after living at the Home for an average length of time of 3 years, 6 months.
The thirty-three women who passed away, had spent an average of 8 years,
2 months at the Home, and were deceased at an average age of_88.6 years.
T he overall averages indicate an age of 87 .2 and length of residency of 6
years.
A remarkable statistic that will undoubtedly never be equaled o~c.urred
in April when Rachel Browne expired at the age of 97 years after hvmg at
the Ho~e for more than 31 years. She came to "Decato" in Septemb~r
1954, and was always very appreciative and proud that her husband. W1l-

RESIDENTIAL CARE - 49 men and 86 women, with a
capacity of 142.
PERSONAL CARE - 36 men and 78 women with only 6
rooms unassigned. Capacity 124.
SKILLED NURSING FACILITY - 47 men and 85 women
are considered as Extended Care residents, plus an average of 21 temporary patients. Capacity 167.
Our newest addition to the Residential living section of the Home is
called The Acacias. These are apartments designed to accommodate 24
couples and represent another type of residential Care. Residents have their
own bedroom, living room, bathroom and kitchen, so they can be self-sufficient regardi ng meals if they desire. We do encourage residents in The
Acacias to participate in all of the Home's activities, and also to eat at least
one meal per day in the dining room. They also are included in all medical
and administrative operations of the Home, and any other service that we
offer. At the tim~ of this report, six couples should be living in The Acacias.
With the addition of these units the total capacity of the Home now
becomes 481. However, the situation of being "near capacity" still exists
for the same reason as was reported last year. The number of beds in the
Skilled Nursing Facility used temporarily by residents who retain their
rooms in the Residential or Personal Care sections, has increased this year,
while the number of rooms available for new residents has decreased. The
number on the Waiting List which consists mainly of single men or women
remains approximately the same each month. This is a result of the application process that is used by the Trustees. Evaluation of each applicant 's
needs is the basis for approval of those who are judged to have the most
viable reasons for entering the Home. As of August 1, there were 41 people
on the Waiting List, including 9 who were assigned rooms, and almost
ready to enter, and 2 couples who were able to move into The Acacias very
soon after their date of the Board of Trustees' approval.

UNION CITY OPERATIONS
by J. Burton Brown, Administrator
The daily operations of the Masonic Home for Adults described herein
differ from the Activities identified elsewhere, in that operations are asso-

ciated with buildings, equipment, employees, and their functions. In the
past year, several significant events occured that deserve notice.
The long awaited completion of The Acacias occured in November
which was immediately followed by inspection and approval for occupancy
by the Licensing section of the State's Department of Social Services. Consequently the first couples moved into these apartments in December, one
of which transferred their belongings from the main Residential building.
Currently, there are six units occupied. Six of the apartments will be held as
a Reserve Factor, which means approved new couples will be able to move
in very soon after their applications are approved, until 18 of them are
assigned . The Acacias add another dimension of services for those who
seek residency at the Home.
December also saw residents and employees rejoicing over the completion of the renovation of the South elevator in the administrative building.
The inconvenience of the four months to replace the old one was soon forgotten. It was returned to service on Christmas Eve Day; thereby fulfilling
the job foreman's promise to have it done by Christmas.
Significant within the ranks of personnel are these very important
events. On April 15th, Assistant Administrat or, Philip Nichols was raised
to the degree of Master Mason by Alameda Lodge No. 167 in Fremont .
His travels were witnessed by a bus load of residents and several members
of the Board of Trustees. His Lodge is one of the earliest supporters of the
Home, as members volunteered their skills and labor during the construction of the first buildings. They also conducted the funeral in 1907 of the
very first male resident, who entered the Home on March 18, 1899.
National acclaim was afforded our Chaplain, Reverend A. Philip Johnson,
Castro Valley Lodge No. 713 for his many years of ministry. This was presented to him at the Banff Hotel, Alberta, Canada, by the Fellowship of
Christian Assemblies conference which he and his wife Alyce attended.
Also important to the operations of our facility was the employmen t of
two key persons, both of them arriving in March. Estelle Donovan
assumed the responsibilities of Director of Nursing, and Lloyd Simmons
was hired as Supervisor of Maintenance. Both came to us with many years
of experience in their respective fields and the Home has benefitted by their
presence.
During the year, we were able to add to the employees' benefit program
by providing life insurance for them on an individual basis. In addition, we
successfully arranged for those employees who so desire to take advantage
of the wide range of services offered by a nationally recognized Credit
Union . Each year we continue to encourage all employees to feel more a
part of our Masonic Family by participating in an annual Christmas party
and family-style picnic.
As participation in "Older Americans Week" which occurred in May, an
Open House was offered to members of the community and providers of
our medical services. Invitations were accepted by several city dignitaries,
including the Mayor and members of the City Council, as well as some of
the staff from the police and fire departments . Visitations like these, plus

ANNUAL PERSONN EL REPORT
by Ronald A. Sherod, Chairman , Personnel Commitle e
This past Masonic year has brought the Administr ators closer to the
Board through various endeavors . Even though we expect our Administr ators to perform their responsibilities with a great deal of independe nce, we
choose to meet with them to review specific personnel related problems.
Through this method the members of the Board of Trustees are better
informed on current matters and the Adminstra tors are more confident of
their day to day decisions on personnel matters.
During this year, the Personnel Committe e has conducted their bi-annual
review of the Administr ators' recommen dations for modificati ons to all
wage ranges. It is the continuing plan to carefully review these with other
similar facilities to insure an acceptable salary level for every employee.
Recomme nded revisions were proposed and approved by our full Board
this past June.
The Personnel Committe e recommen ded to the Board of Trustees a
merit pool for this year's merit increases for deserving employees .
Approval for this merit pool was given and the Administr ators were authorized to grant individual annual increases, at their discretion, within specific guidelines as outlined and approved within the Homes Board annual

REAL ESTATE REPORT
by Chester R. MacPhee, Chairman Real Estate Committee
Once again the Real Estate Committe e of the Masonic Homes has successfully disposed of real estate which comes to the Homes from direct
gifts, grants to our Pooled Income Fund, Wills, and other bequests. This
year these total real estate sales amounted to more than one million dollars
at no cost to the Masonic Homes.
Trustees Chester R . MacPhee, P.G.M. , Hambleto n F. Leas, Jack R .
Vickers and Ralph M. Hinds make up the Committe e ably asssisted by
P.M. Lou Goldkind, Irene M. Harrigan and Grand Secretary
Robert A . Klinger.
Routine matters are handled by the Committe e, and are regularly
reported to the Trustees of the Masonic Homes. Matters requiring greater
considerat ion are first approved by the Trustees.

PUBLIC/TY
by Ver/ Lobb, Chairman Publicity Committee
The Publicity Committee of the Board of Trustees, during the past year,
has completed numerous articles and inserts for the California Freemason.
These articles and inserts support the Fraternity's great Masonic Charity "The Masonic Homes of California:•
To better guide the Publicity Committee a General Publicity Plan was
developed.
The objective is to keep us ever mindful of the value, benefit and need
for our Masonic Homes; to emphasize the importance for each Mason to
financially and personally support our great Masonic Charity, and to promote the good image of the Homes with the Craft and with the general
public. The scope of this effort is to: (I) Provide to the Masonic Homes
Endowment Board, articles , actual happenings and material that will
enhance and aid their efforts in telling the story and the need to support
our Homes. (2) Provide articles and phocos in the California Freemason
that will keep us informed of the progress of our construction projeccs. (3)
Provide information to Lodges, Homes Endowment Board members, and
others that can be used for programs, talks, handouts, etc. (4) Assist in
providing information that could lead to a new human interest type movie,
a video cassette, or audio slide presentation, that could be used like the
"Best Kept Secret:'
The specific Homes publicity articles and inserts that were completed
and published in the California Freemason and for other uses this past year
are listed below for your information.
I. "The Acacias Open at the Masonic Home:• by Stanley L. Channon.
2. "Masons Can Build Forever,' by Ver! B. Lobb.
3. "Masonic Homes for Adults Comes to Covina:• by Ronald A.
Sherod.
4. "The Expanding Role of Masonic Service!' by Leo B. Mark.
5. "Expansion of the Masonic Homes of California;• by Ver! B. Lobb
and Stanley L. Channon.
6. "Brotherly Love and Relief:' by John W. Driskell.
If we are properly informed we will do our share for our elderly at
Union City and our children at Covina.

The report this year seems to be repetitious of previous years because so
rnuch of the information and activities are traditions which bear repeating.
However, each year also has its unique events, and people worthy of special
recognition .
Immediately, certain residents should be highlighted for the important
milestones they have reached in their lives. Five couples observed wedding
anniversaries of sixty-three (63) or more years. We recognized the seventieth (70th) of Brother and Mrs. Allen S. Cherry, Mariposa Lodge No. 24;
66th, for the Albert Mattson's, John P. Jarman Lodge No. 669; Brother
and Mrs . Duke Dykes, Stanislaus Lodge No. 206 for their 64th; and
Brother and Mrs. Perry Goodall, Santa Rosa Lodge No . 57 for their 63rd .
The Nathan Wotman's, Lebanon Pacific Lodge No. 136, observed their
second anniversary at the Home, and their 65th overall, on June 19th,
which sadly was followed six days later by the death of Brother Wotman.
This year did not lack for romance as two couples took vows of marriage. Brother Dayrnond Agnew from Sequoia-St. Elmo Lodge No. 345, a
bachelor for 81 years, and after living here more than ten years , slowed
down enough for Edith Akers, sponsored by Atascadero Lodge No. 493 ,
to catch him and tie the knot on October 6, 1985.
The other wedding occurred on September l, 1985 and joined Brother
Mahlon "Mike" Turk of Magnolia Lodge No. 242 and Amelia "Amy "
Bowers from Friendship Lodge No. 210 as a happy couple, both of whom
happened to be jll5t over 90 years of age.
News regarding our Centenarian s was both good and bad . The oldest
resident, Nona Hambly, Park-Crocke tt Lodge No. 139 reached her 101st
birthday on the 4th o f July, 1985, but only survived a few months until her
death on November 10th. Brother Stanley Creelman, Calaveras Lodge No.
78, succeeded her as our eldest person when he reached 101 on January 7,
1986. That was followed on February 12th, with Leslie Woodworth being
honored on his 100th birthday. Last year he was given recognition for his
75 years as a Mason; he has now attained two of his life-long goals. A
fourth resident reached a very important milestone of 100 years. Mrs. Eda
Morris, from Mount Jackson Lodge No. 295 on August 1st, celebrated the
day through a party held in the Skilled Nursing Facility. A very unique
birthday was also celebrated although not because of the number of years.
1Wo residents, Brother Everett Bagby, Mariposa Lodge No. 24, and Winnie
Freyschlag, also Mariposa No. 24, celebrated their birthdays on August
14th (their second one at the Home), and both were 88 years old. What is
noteworthy is that they are the only set of twins to have resided at the
Home as far as our records disclose. Brother Bagby and his wife Rhesa
reside in the Adams Building; Mrs . Freyschlag lives in the South Wing, and
all are identified, as you see, with Mariposa Lodge No. 24.
1\vo of the men were honored by their Lodges as recipients of the Hiram

Inasmuch as I have mentioned residents and 1dent1f1ed their Lodges,
share the following informat ion as to its relevance to our total populatio n.
There are 107 Lodges with one resident at the Home and 94 Lodges who
have two or more residents here. This association means a great deal to the
men and women living at Union City; especially when there is close conta:t
maintained by correspondence and/ or visitations from members of their
Lodges.
.. .
This association is further enhanced by the many vis1tat1on
s to the Home
by Masonic-affiliated groups. A total of 97 such visitations were enjoyed
by all people so involved.
Visiting groups included :

Other traditional Masonic events took place with residents participating
both at and away from the Home. Many of the men and women experienced a first-time visit to the Shriners Hospital in San Francisco. Some of
the Brethren attended Grand Lodge for the first time as we continue the
tradition of providing transpor tation to and from the proceedings and
activities. We are extremely grateful to the Grand Lodge Officers and the
Grand Lodge Activities Committ ee for their generous assistance with
accomm~ations and services provided to the residents during that
important week m October. Also, we were once again proud and pleased to host
the many dignitaries and other guests at the Home on Grand Lodge Visitation Day. This year we welcomed twelve (12) bus loads, 73 cars, and over
600 "lunch-e aters". Our thanks to the Islam Shrine Band and Chanters
who entertained and to the many Brethren and ladies who brought donations of clothing and a variety of items.
Another Masonic tradition was highlighted by one-on-one participation
between adults and children during Public Schools Month . Through the
efforts of staff members , adoption of Hillview Crest Elementary School (a
local intermediate school) took place with tremendous success. Reciprocal
visits by the " Masonic Hilltopp ers" and the school's choral group, plus
individual visits between them and us, resulted in many letters being written back and forth. Some of the letters (giant size of 2 feet by 2 feet) from
classes as a group arrived, and were posted near the dining room so that all
residents could enjoy them. Another pleasurable visit by children bas
occurred each of the last two Summers. The bus belonging to the Masonic
Homes for Children arrived in August and unloaded a large group of
enthusiastic boys, girls, and exhausted staff members who were nearing the
end of their 8 to rn day jaunt through Northern California. Sharing lunch,
tours, and each other's company was the order of the day and thoroughly
enjoyed by everyone.
Entertainment of various types is abundan t each year, and during these
past twelve months, a variety of non- Masonic groups on 43 different occasi~ns provided dance, music and drama for the residents. The ages of
these
friends ranged from the youngest of school children to some oldsters who
well could fit in perfectly at the Home. Our own now-famous group of
entertainers, known as "The Hilltoppers" have reached a pinnacle that will
be hard to top. In November they accepted an invitation to present their
show to a large group of attendees at the annual meeting of the American
Association of Homes for the Aged (nationally known as AAHA). After
this sterling performance they were presented with a miniature replica of
an "Oscar" for an outstand ing volunteer group of Older Americans. As
additional recognition, they were guests at two excellent musical concerts
by Henry Mancini and The Lettermen. During the Hilltoppers trip, they
were housed at the Home in Covina and renewed friendships with the children and staff. In addition to this spectacular event, they made 17 appearances away from Union City and gave two performances at the Home.
Included in their travels were trips to various Lodges, senior centers, retirement homes, and several cities such as San Jose, San Carlos, Santa Rosa,

Facility. We are all deeply indebted to them.

TWo interesting and exciting projects have been developed within the last

ye~; both of w~ich will be continued in the future. They will not only benefit current res1d~nts of the Home, but have the opportunity to impact

upon our Fraternity a!1d the _elderly segment of the Nation's population in

Fac~hty at Union ~tty, and the residential units for adults at Covina. These

projects are explained elsewhere in the Trustees' report.
The other one is best described as our entry into a joint venture of
research. Under the concurrance of the Trustees, the staff of the Home
have. become associated_with a research group from Stanford University
Medical School; the University of California, San Francisco and the Veterans Administration Medical Center at Palo Alto. From ; grant by the
National Institute of Aging, studies are being conducted under an umbrella
~cronym kn?~n as GRECC, which represents Geriatric Research, Education, a~d Clinical Care. A Sleep Disorders study has been conducted at the
M~s?mc Home under unique conditions and the direction of Doctor
Wilham D~ment. and Doctor Donald Bliwise. It is the first time a Nursing
Home setting has been used as a source of observation. The preliminary
res~Its, ~ repo~ted by Dr. Bliwise during a recent seminar held at Stanford
Uruvers1ty Medical School, appeared to reveal extremely valuable data that
may hav: great value to other national researchers working in the same
field. T?1s and other projects that residents participate in are being conducted m a non-threatenin g, non-coercive manner and under conditions
that respect _the residents' righ ts and dignity. Our contribution to the
research pr~Jects may be rather minimal at this point, but with a portion of
ou~ s~afrs u~e and. the willing participation of some residents, we may be
ass1~tmg the mcreasmg number of older people to enjoy healthier and better hves.

im~oss1bl~.task to hst everyone. It is said that the "Masons take care of

It is with continued pleasure and commitmen t that th is report to the
Grand Lodge is made.
This past year there has been continued concentratio n on the quality of
the child care program. The Home is often asked to serve children who
have suffered emotionally over the loss of family, home, and/or family
members. This often takes its toll in how children relate in thei r world,
with their peers, in their schools, in their academic achievement , in their
self discipline, and in their homes.
The Masonic Home has identified, documented , and implemented a system of child care managemen t and discipline. Again there has been
improvemen t in the overall grade point average of the children in our care
who attend the public schools. There continues to be attention to Houseparent training, managemen t, supervision, and how this position relates to
the overall child care program. The Administrat ion of this Horne, through
direction of its Board of Trustees, will continue its evaluation of effective
methods of providing excellent parenting to its children.
Your Board of Trustees and its Admissions Committee, by direction to
its Administrat or, has been very active in assessing and monitoring the continuing needs of children admitted to this Home. Should circumstanc es
improve for the families of the children in our care, the ability of a child to
return to his or her family is assessed. The needs of the children who
develop and ultimately reach adulthood while in the care of this Home are
equally assessed: The scholarship program of this Masonic Home is a fine
example of such attention.
Rainbow Park, a beautiful park area of the Masonic Home partially
funded through the California Rainbow Assemblies, has been opened for
the weekend and overnight visitations of Assemblies and Masonic groups .
This will increase the visitations to this Home.
By and through your example of Masonic Charity the following children
have been served:

The current population of the Masonic Home for Children consists of 37
boys and 14 girls, for a total of 51. Our youngest child is 5 years of age and
the oldest is 18 . We'll have 13 elementary students, 17 intermediate students, and 21 high school students . Our students continue their educations
through the public schools in the Charter Oak Unified School District. The
Masonic Home remains vitally interested and involved in the public
schools. Your Administrator was elected as president of the Charter Oak
Unified School District Board of Education and, in this way, helps assure a
quality education of the children .
You are encouraged to study the annual report of our Trustees which will
provide more detailed information about the Covina operations. You are
also encouraged to visit the Masonic Home for Children in Covina as have
the following groups:

Addendum to Homes Trustees Report-KERMIT A . JACOBSON, P.G.M.,
President
From time to time we have prepared short histories or references to the
Masonic Homes . This material has now been incorporated into a complete
document of the History of our great Masonic charity. These Masonic
Ho!11es of <;alifornia were the dream of Masons since they first
arnved here m 1848. We are indebted to Brother Chester R. MacPhee,
P.G.M., who has gathered the data, and to Brothers Ralph H. Head,
Robert A. Klin~er and others for their assistance.
On behalf of the Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California we are
pleased to present to you an authentic 135 year history of the Masonic
Homes in California which will be in the publisher's hands by the end of
this year.
We of the Masonic Homes sincerely urge that the Masters of the Lodges
present such a history to each new Mason as he completes his third degree
and to those who affiliate from other Jurisdictions.
We also hope that each member would desire a copy of the document of
Masonic History for his personal library.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON DISTRIBUTION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Distribution has examined the exemplary Message of
our Grand Master and wishes to commend him on his dedication to the
Craft.
GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE

The Grand Master's Message contains four Recommendations and four
Decisions, and we recommend that the subject matter be referred to the
following Committees:
Recommendation Number One, relative to making Temple facilities
available for community and public service without charge, be referred to
the Committee on Jurisprudence, the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes and the Committee on Temple Properties.
Recommendation Number Two, relative to the elimination of the one
year waiting period prior to application to concordant or appendant
bodies, be referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence and the Committee
on Policy and General Purposes.
Recommendation Number Three, relative to a special study commission
to explore the Committee structure of this Grand Lodge, be referred to the
Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
Recommendaiton Number Four, relative to a study of the "Health" of
Freemasonry in California, be referred to the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes .
Decision Number One, relative to the Declaration of Election of Officers
as null and void where Code provisions were not followed be referred to
the Committee on Jurisprudence.
Decision Number 1Wo, relative to disallowing Masonic Youth Groups'
raffles, be referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, the Committee on
Policy and General Purposes and the Committee on Youth Orders.
Decision Number Three, relative to the use of the Masonic insignia and
words "Masonic" and/or "Mason" by groups referred to in his Decision
be referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence.
On page 13 of the Grand Master's Message, referrence is made to granting Dispensations to re-ballot on rejected applications and to allowing
advancement of such candidates . We recommend that these items be
referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence and the Committee on Policy
and General Purposes.

GRAND TREASURER'S REPORT

We recommend that this report be referred to the Committee on
Finance.

115

GRAND SECRETARY'S REPORT

We recommend that this report be referred to Committees as follow:
That portion relating to change of meeting place be referred to the Committee on Charters.
That portion relating to Consolidation of Lodges be referred to the
Committee on Charters.
That portion relating to the formation of new Lodges be referred to the
Committee on Charters and the Committee on By-Laws.
Exhibit "N' concerning dispensations issued, be referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence.
Exhibit "B" concerning Amendments to By-Laws be referred to the
Committee on By-Laws.
Exhibit "C" concerning Trial Records be referred to the Committee on
Trial Review.
GRAND LECTURER'S REPORT

We recommend that the part referring to the budget be referred to the
Committee on Finance.
MASONIC HOMES TRUSTEES' REPORT

We recommend that this well organized report of our Masonic philanthropy be referred in its entirety to the Committee on Finance.
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD

We recommend that this uplifting report reflecting the strength of our
charitable efforts' be referred in its entirety to the Committee on Finance.
Respectfully submitted ,
VERNE

LEROY G. CONNELLY. Chairman

REPORT OF TRUSTEES
CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
The Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple
hereby submits its 31st Annual Report.
At the close of the 1985 Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge,
the Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple held its

l 16

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDING S OF THE

organization meeting as required by the California Masonic Code, nominating and electing the following officers for the ensuing year:
STANLEY M . CAZNEAUX.
ROBERTO . WEST, PGM,
JOHN A. SICKENBERGER.
ROBERT A. KLINGER,

President
Vice President
Treasurer
Secretory

The California Masonic Memorial Temple serves as a patriotic monument and memorial, commemoratin g the members of the Armed Forces of
the United States and the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of the State of California, who gave their lives in battle
during World War I and World War II. Our Temple is open to the public
and attracts visitors from all over the world.
The inscription in our lobby over the entrance to the Auditorium states:
"California Freemasons honoring their heroic dead erect this Temple
dedicated to Freemasonry, Virtue and Universal Benevolence - that
the cause of Freedom for which they died shall ever be therein the
sacred trust of their Brethren and Freemasons yet unborn~'
With this charge in mind, it continues to be the policy of the Trustees
and of all the employees of the Temple to maintain this building to the
highest possible standards. The Board of Trustees would like to express its
appreciation for an excellent job done by Worshipful Loren Stritenberger,
our Executive Vice President and General Manager of the Temple. Under
his direction the daily maintenance is not only supervised but the entire
rental and operation of the Auditorium and Exhibit Halls is achieved.
In October of 1984 your Board of Trustees voted to assume the responsibility for the operation and budget funding of the Library and Museum
located on the second floor of our Temple. The Board of Trustees is totally
committed to improving the operation of the Library and Museum and has
authorized an operation budget of $26,000 for the fiscal year July I, 1986
through June 30, 1987. The Board would like to thank the chairman of the
Grand Lodge Library and Museum Comittee, C. John Bellman, Jr., and
his fine staff for an excellent job in 1985-1986.
Although the maintenance of our Temple requires a continued expenditure of monies, your Trustees are pleased to report that we are still able this
year to donate $80,000 to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund, in
accordance with our By-Laws.
The Trustees are pleased to announce the continuation of our policy of
providing free parking to our delegates during the official transactions of
Grand Lodge at the Annual Communicatio n. In addition, we have also
provided decorative plants and additional seating in our Temple lobby during Grand Lodge Week.
The Board of Trustees would like to express our appreciation for the
continued good counsel of our Grand Treasurer and our Grand Secretary.
Their expertise and advice to this Board of Trustees has led to another sue-

117

cessful year. Your Trustees have endeavored to discharge their duties, to the
best of their abilities, so that this beautiful monument will continue to
serve the needs of our great Fraternity of Masons in the States of California and Hawaii.
Respectfully submitted,
STANLEY M . CAZNEAUX, President
JACK R. LEVITT

REPORT OF THE CALIFORN IA I<,REEMASO N
PUBLICATI ON BOARD
To the Most Worshipful Grarrd Lodge, F & A. M. of California:
A Board comprised of the Grand Master, Grand Secretary, such advisors
as may be desirable, and an Editor-in-Chief , appointed by the Grand Master, administer the quarterly editing and distribution of the California Freemason, the official publication of the Grand Lodge of California.
Members of California and Hawaii Lodges, the Grand Lodges of other
Jurisdictions, and paid subscribers have received nearly 20 million copies
of the magazine .during its 34-year history. Publications of American and
foreign Grand Lodges, from time to time, quote from its pages .
Keeping the members of California and Hawaii Lodges fully informed is
the primary purpose of the California Freemason. Thus articles in the magazine cover the full range of activities of Grand Lodge, the Masonic Homes
of California, U.S. Constitution Observances, California Masonic Foundation, Public Schools Week and constituent Lodge's events including
Hiram Awards, Fifty Year pins, Widows Nights, Laymen's Nights, and
many more. The paramount goal is to maintain the high principles of the
Fraternity.
A $2.00 subscription fee will bring two years (eight issues) of the California Freemason to friends and families of California Masons. A gift order is
an excellent way to spread the Good News about the ideals, practices and
principles of Freemasonry to the general public .
Respectfully submitted,
RALPH H . HEAD, Editor-in-Chie f
ROBERT A. KLINGER,
JOHN W. DRISKELL,
