REPORT OF THE SOJOURNERS COMMITTEE
To Jhe Mos/ Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on seeking out the many sojourners in California and
Hawaii is pleased to report some small gains.
At the last Annual Communica tion we provided a method to invite these
visiting Brothers to our Lodges and if one is a permanent resident of the
said locale invite him to affiliate with a California Lodge. We called this
the "Rusty Nail Degree:• Its only purpose was to acquaint the Brother, who
has not been in a Lodge for sometime, with the signs, etc. so he can gain
admission into a Lodge without fear of being rejected . The program was
made available on "G" Floor last year and those Lodge Senior Wardens
who did not pick up a copy were sent one soon after the Annual Communication.
Since then, we have , as a Committee, made contacts with Lodges in our
Local areas and offered our assistance and encouraged the Masters to
make an effort to seek out the Sojourners and solicit them as members of
their Lodges.
On May 30th, a letter was sent to all Lodges in this Grand Jurisdiction
asking for a report on the results of the Lodge's program to reach out to
those sojourners. There were only 39 Lodges chat responded and the results
were somewhat mixed. Those who used the suggest~d program did locate
sojourners and were able to get them to affiliate. We know that there are
other Lodges that have had some success but failed to report any activity.
Some ot :he members of this Committee have had the opportunity to speak
at Lodge meetings to explain the program and the importance of the Lodge
itself.
We also know that in such a short period of time it is most difficult to
motivate volunteers to take on a new project. However, we feel if we persevere and continue to meet with and talk to as many upcoming Masters as
possible, we will make some more gains.
It is our recommenda tion that the Grand Lodge Committee be organized
in the same manner as the AGL:s, in Divisions . We feel a member from
each Division would suffice as a Grand Lodge Committee. Then, each
Inspectoral District would have a strong, motivating Brother to provide the
push to get each Lodge to take off the blinders and try something new and
seek out those sojourners. We cannot wait for them to come to us. We must
go to them and invite them to attend our Lodge. The way to do this is
through one's own innovation and using what we have provided. We can
gain in membership, but it will take work, work, and work and then more
work.
We strongly urge every Master to call the Lodge officers together and
discuss a plan to seek out sojourners, then select a strong leader and put
your plan into operation. After you have followed through with your program, it is essential that you conduct a critique to determine your degree of
success and also your failures. The next time you propose to institute the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

119

program you will have a greater degree of success because you will be able
to overcome those areas that did not produce to the end success.
There is a great big world outside those Lodge doors, my Brothers, and
if you will take your Lodge beyond those doors and let the community
know we are alive and healthy you are sure to entertain some thought in
the minds of those who are not members.
Always remember, nothing ventured, nothing gained. Opportunity is
knocking at your door - so let it in.
Respectfully submitted,
FRANK B. STIMSON, Chairman

REPORT OF CALIFORNIA MASONIC FOUNDATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Trustees of the California Masonic Foundation report as follows:
The work of your Board is current and has been promptly and efficiently
dispatched. Your Trustees have worked diligently and effectively to achieve
the purposes of the Foundation and to make them known to the Brethren
of this Grand Jurisdiction and to encourage their support by contribution s
and donations.
During this reporting period we received contribution s and donations in
the amount of $29, 77 I. Appropriate acknowledgements were sent to the
contributors and donors and to the families of those persons in whose
memory many of the donations were made. Our income from investments
during this period was $114,816.
The investments, income and expenses of the Foundation are detailed in
the Grand Treasurer's report and will not be repeated here. Direct Trustee
expense for this period was 9. 7 percent of the total income.
The Foundation can expend no capital funds. All expenses, awards and
grants are paid out of the income or contribution s specifically designated
for that purpose. The Foundation has not received any funds from the
Grand Lodge by way of per capita tax or assessment. Its sole support
comes from contribution s and donations generously given by the Masons
and other persons.

PROCEED INGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFOR NIA

Grants for leadership training were made to Order of Rainbow for Girls;
Order of Job's Daughters ; Order of DeMolay, each in the amount of
$2,000. The three youth Orders in Hawaii were granted a total of $1,500.
During this period scholarshi p awards were granted in the total amount
of $91,000.
The Statue of Liberty Restoratio n Fund solicitatio n was completed
around June of this year. The total amount collected in this Grand Jurisdiction was in excess of $900,000. This amount was greater than what was
contribute d by all of the other Grand Jurisdictio ns combined! California
Masons are to be congratula ted for their generosity in contributi ng to this
national effort.
Plans are being formulated at this time to embark upon a publicity campaign that will inform everyone in this Grand Jurisdictio n of the existence
and mission of the California Masonic Foundatio n. Since the Foundatio n's
inception it has been considered as an entity that grants scholarshi ps to
deserving st udents only. However, the real mission and purpose of this
Foundatio n, as the Trustees now view it, is to promote Freemason ry in all
ways possible in this Grand Jurisdictio n! The granting of scholarshi ps
being just a vehicle to achieve that purpose. This Foundatio n has the greatest latitude of any Masonic entity in this Grand Jurisdictio n, having the
power to use any form of media advertising and to approach the general
public for support of its endeavors . The Foundatio n is mandated to engage
in "Cultural, Scientific and Education al" pursuits . Therefore the Trustees
have now broadened their scope and will in the future make sure that its
purpose and mission are accomplish ed . The support of our Brethren is earnestly solicited not only in the financial area but to assist us in promoting
Freemason ry to the fullest extent in this Grand Jurisdictio n. We hope that
by this time next year no one will ask, "What is the California Masonic
Foundatio n and what does it do?" Our first effort will be to publicize the
donations made by Brother Harry Walker Lister of Buena Park Lodge No.
347, which established scholarship awards in his name. We would be happy

REPOR T OF THE COMM ITTEE ON
MASON IC SERVI CE BUREA US
To the Most Worshipful Grand lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committ ee on Masonic Service Bureaus is pleased to submit its
Annual Report on the operation s and condition s of the seventeen Masonic
Service Bureaus for the year ending June 30, 1986. The Committ ee is in its
59th year.
The Right Worship ful Jack R. Levitt, Deputy Grand Master, was
appointe d liaison officer to the Committ ee and we appreciat e his support
and assistance during the year.
The Committ ee is keenly aware of its responsibility in directing the operation of the various Bureaus in a uniform manner. The Service Bureaus
assist sojourne rs, their widows and orphans; operate blood banks; arrange
and conduct funerals for deceased Masons; make investiga tions; assist in
processing applicati ons for the two Masonic Homes; visit the sick and promote fraternal relations with sojourne rs.
NEW COMMITT EE MEMBERS

We welcome Worshipful Merrill R. Shelley, a member of Ojai Lodge No.
663 and we also fraternall y greet Worshipful DeMay H. "Dee" White, a

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFO RNIA

123

member of Granada Hills Lodge No. 790 who serves as Committ ee Secretary. A continue d welcome is also extended to Worshipful A . Bruce Ivie, an
old member of the Committ ee, but who serves as Chairma n this year.
Bruce replaces Delmer W. May as Chairma n but Del will continue to
provide his valuable advice to the Committ ee. We also bid farewell to
William W. Widenha m who leaves this Committ ee to serve on the Widows
Committ ee.
NEW EXECUTIVE SECRETARIES

We are pleased to welcome Worshipf ul Robert J. MacDon ald who
assumed the duties of Executiv e Secretary of the Long Beach Bureau
replacing the late Worshipf ul William Atkins . Brother Atkins served many
years as Executive Secretary of that Bureau and his many friends will miss
his presence.
MEETINGS

The Committ ee held four meetings during the year. One was held during
Grand Lodge Week, which permitted members of the various Bureaus and
Lodge officers to contact the Committ ee and to receive help with the many
problems applicabl e to their areas.
A regional meeting was held in Oakland on February 1, 1986 with 42
members and guests of the Bureaus from Central Californ ia in attendan ce.
Former Chairma n Arthur R. Kirk was our honored guest at the afternoo n
session and our guest speaker was Very Worship ful Robert A. Klinger,
Grand Secretary.
A regional meeting was held in Los Angeles on April 5, 1986 with 34
members and guests attending . Chairma n Ivie was pleased to introduc e
Delmer W. Mai, past Chairma n and current advisor, and John Allen
Crosby, Executive Secretary Emeritus of the Los Angeles Bureau . We were
again pleased and honored to have Very Worship ful Robert A . Klinger,
Grand Secretary, as our guest speaker.
On Wednesday, June 11, 1986, the Committ ee met in Pasaden a for
reviewing the proposed budgets of the seventeen Masonic Service Bureaus
in Californ ia. The Committ ee also reviewed its own budget for the
Masonic year 1986-1987. The Pasadena Scottish Rite provided the facility
for our meeting and William Van Houten, Executiv e Secretary of the Pasadena Bureau, was our most gracious host.
After each of the above meetings, a short meeting of the Committ ee was
held to discuss items of immedia te import.
WORKSHOPS

The Chairma n was appointe d a member of the Grand Lodge Masonic
Leadersh ip and Worksho p Committ ee and he participa ted in all nine workshops held througho ut the State. Lloyd Smith, Executive Secretary of the
Los Angeles Bureau, was also on this Committee. All other members of
our Committ ee as well as Delmer W. May also participa ted in presentat ions
at these importan t worksho ps. We thank the Los Angeles Bureau which

124

PROCEE DINGS OF THE

furnished all written material on Masonic Service Bureaus for our use in
the workshop s.
The purpose of our participa tion in the above worksho ps was to communicate what Masonic Service Bureaus are and what they do. In this regard,
at the direction of the Chairma n, Dee White, Secretary of our Committ ee,
wrote an article on Masonic Service Bureaus, their purposes and functions .
This was submitte d to Ralph Head, Editor, for publicati on in the California Freemason.
CONSOLIDATIONS

The Richmon d Bureau was discontin ued and its Lodges absorbed by the
East Bay Bureau.
TAXES

All Bureaus filed the required informat ion with the Internal Revenue
Service on Form 990 and with the State Franchis e Tax Board on either
Form 199 or l 99B. The Los Angeles Bureau uses forms other than the 990
and 199. All Bureaus required to file tax returns did so and filed them on
time.
BUS H MASON IC RELIEF FUND

The Trustees of the Bush Masonic Relief Fund provide the operating
funds for the Bureaus located in the greater Los Angeles area. The contributions from this fund amount to more than 63 percent of the total budget
for the seventeen Bureaus . The Masters, officers and members of the various Lodges join with the members of the Committ ee in expressing appreciation to Ralph H. Head and the other Trustees of the Bush Fund for their
generous contribu tion for operation s in the greater Los Angeles area.
BLOOD BANKS

Several of our Bureaus operate blood banks for the benefit of Californi a
Masons and their families as well as for sojourne rs. 1208 units of blood
were donated during the year and 1209 units were released to provide this
importan t life support to our members , their families and to sojourne rs.
We complim ent the Bureaus and our members for supportin g this worthwhile activity.
UNIFORM COMPACT S

CONCLUS IONS

Wor~h1pful John W. Driskell, and his Grand Lodge office staff for their

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON TRAVEL ALLOWANCES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Travel Allowances submits the following report covering the 137th Annual Communica tion of Grand Lodge.
Those entitled to Travel Allowances are the Master, or in his absence, the
ranking Warden, or in the absence of the Master and Wardens, the duly
elected representative in accordance with Section 1148, California Masonic

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

13 1

Code. However, no payment shall be allowed for the officers or representatives of any Lodge, the dues of which have not been paid in full, or which
shall be reported by the Grand Secretary as having been delinquent in the
transmission of certificates of the election and installation of officers of
their respective Lodges. Past Grand Masters, not on committees, will be
reimbursed as provided in Section 1150, California Masonic Code. In
accordance with Section 1148a, California Masonic Code, when a Master
and Warden from the same Lodge are present at an Annual Communica tion, and one of said officers serves on a Grand Lodge Committee entitled
to travel and expense reimburseme nt, he shall be reimbursed under Section
1150, California Masonic Code. The other officer shall receive reimbursement under Section l 148, California Masonic Code, as the officer representing his Lodge on the floor of Grand Lodge.
Mileage from the various points within the State of California to San
Francisco has been taken from the published records of the California
State Automobile Association. Mileage from points in the State of Hawaii
to San Francisco, has been taken from the published reports of air lines in
accordance with Section 1148, California Masonic Code. No compensatio n
is allowed to members representing Lodges in San Francisco and the immediate 30 mile vicinity. Compensati on of members from the State of California has been computed on the basis of eleven (11) cents per mile, the rate
fixed by the Committee on Finance. Compensati on of members from the
state of Hawaii has been computed on the basis of published class of fare
next below first class round trip air rate of regularly scheduled major air
lines, from Honolul u to San Francisco, plus inte r-island air fare to Honolulu when necessary.
The payroll hiJ.s been checked with the registration records as submitted
to us by the Committee on Credentials, and the amounts required to meet
the travel allowances costs for the 1986 Annual Communication are as follows:
Past Grand Masters (Not on Committees) ....... ... ..... . .... $185.24
Representati ves of Lodges . ..... . . .. ... ... . ......•.. .. . . .$3 5,471.70
Total ...... . ........... .... .... ...... . ...... ... .... .$35,656.94
Checks will be ready for distribution at the registration desk on "G"
Floor on Wednesday morning immediately following the election of the
Junior Grand Warden in accordance and as noted in the program for the
137th Annual Communica tion . Brethren, if you are the Master or Warden
representing your Lodge, or the duly elected representative of yo ur Lodge,
the Committee on Travel Allowances urgently requests you to pick up your
check . You must present a properly validated credential.
Arrangemen ts have been made so that those who may wish to cash their
checks, can do so at the Fairmont Hotel Branch of the First Interstate
Bank located at California and Mason Streets. Its entrance is on California
Street. Your Grand Lodge credentials will serve as suitable identificatio n .
The members of the Travel Allowances Committee wish to express their
sincere appreciation to members of the Grand Lodge office staff for their

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

cooperation throughout the year in assembling, preparing and computing
the detail necessary for the functioning of this Committee.
Respectfully submitted,

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE
My Brethren:
It is the duty of the Grand Master to present at each Annual Communication a "'.'r!t~en message, therein setting forth all his official acts during the
year, exhibiting the general condition of Masonry within the Jurisdiction
and recommending such legislation as he may deem necessary or expedien~
for the welfare of the Craft. Accordingly, I am pleased to present to you
the following message:
How often have each of you been asked by a non-Mason, "What is
Masonry?" The usual answers are: "It is a society of builders and a Fraternity of men who believe in Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth:' "It is an
organization that seeks to make good men better men:• "It is the oldest and
largest Fraternity in the world'.'
Do we truly understand Masonry? What is its purpose and why were certain symbols selected?
The pr~cti~~l objec~ of M_asonry is the intellectual and spiritual improveme~t of md1vi?ual_
s tn society. The whole world is but one republic, of
which each nation 1s a family and every individual a child. Masonry tends
to create a new people, which, composed of men of many nations and
tongues, are bound together by the bonds of science, morality and virtue.
It is neither a political party nor a religious sect. It embraces all parties
and all sects to form a vast world-wide fraternal association.
The "ancients" thought that universal humanity acted under the influence of two.opposing principles, the good and the evil. Masonry represents
the good prmc1ple and constantly wars against the evil one.
Masc:>nry is like Hercu~es, Osiris and Apollo in deadly and everlasting
feud with the demons of ignorance, brutality, baseness, falsehood, intolerance, s~~erstiti?n, tyranny, meanness and bigotry. When despotism and
superst1t_ion, twm powers of evil and darkness, reigned everywhere, invincible a?d immortal, Masonry developed the mysteries in order to avoid persecution. It created the allegory, the symbol and the emblem and transmitted its doctrines by the secret mode of initiation.
Masonry thrived in the simpler times before the advent of electronic distractions. With the increasing sophistication of television and other forms
of ~ntertainment, it became easier for us to neglect the philosophical obligattons that we owe to our inner soul. Yearly, our membership dwindles
and the average age of our members increases.
Nation-wide, we are an organization in decline. The chief obstacles to
Masonry's success are the apathy and faithlessness of its own children as
well as the indifference of the world. In the daily hurry of life and business, and the noise and confusion of politics, the quiet voice of Masonry is
often unheard and unheeded.
The fi~st lesson which one learns who engages in any great work of
reform, 1s that men are essentially careless lukewarm and indifferent to
everything that does not concern their ow~ personal and immediate welfare.

134

PROCEEDI NGS OF THE

Man who seeks possible reform with the cooperation of others should
remember that he cannot always inspire the multitude with his own determination. His vision may not be clearly communicated. Even those who
have associated themselves with him as co-workers can be slow to understand the significance of the need for progressive changes and are frequently given to criticism or to seek continuing comfort by remaining in
the past.
As a result, progress is often thwarted and the individual may lose his
earlier enthusiasm which is then replaced by discouragement and despair.
The man who strives to benefit and improve the world is like a swimmer
struggling against the rapid current in a rushing river. If he yields, he is
lost. If he persists and maintains his convictions, he may or may not attain
success.
It is a truism that many men resist change, even when the advantages of
change are readily apparent. Masons must not blind themselves to change,
nor should we rush into change without adequate and considered reasons
therefore.
It is not enough to say the society of Masons must modify its procedures
in order to exist.
It is not enough to say the downward spiral of membership, activities
and interest will soon stop or run its course.
What is necessary is for our leadership and our members to work for
improvement in our procedures. It is my considered judgment that more
information must be made available about what Masonry is, not only to
the public but also to our own members.
The Craft of Masonry, our Society of Builders, has nothing to hide. We
are holders of the greatest non-stop record of philanthrop y among any
body of men so organized. If for no other reason, that other men may
know and emulate our way for the betterment of all mankind, such emulation serves society.
Masons seek no publicity for their good acts, but as we serve silently, no
knowledge of such deeds is available for public consideratio n. In these
days of immediate transmission of activities the world over, the public
insists on the right to know.
While I offer no panacea for Freemasonry by urging a positive exchange
of our activities through the conveyance of information , nevertheless, it is
well to realize that almost all of the people other than our members and
their families know little about what Masonry is - what it believes in what it does for humanity and too often even some of our own members
do not know all that they should in this regard.
It may very well be that we do an injustice to the uninformed by keeping
them unenlightened about the subject.
Many knowledgeable Masons have indicated to me that we have among
our Masonic Fraternity in California and Hawaii the best brains of men
anywhere. If our fortunes continue to fall, it may be necessary to summon
these men to study our problems and offer recommendations.
Recently, I was told of a Brother in a Lodge who decided to clean the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

135

pedestal which supports the three lesser lights. Shortly after commencing
with this chore, he found that the gold color was coming off and that it
was nothing more than a coat of paint. After considerable work, he found
underneath a terribly tarnished brass surface. Painstakingsly, he removed
the tarnish and with careful polishing, created a most beautiful shining finish . Presently, the Lodge room was brightened by this seemingly new addition which was eye-catching in its splendor. None of the members could
remember when the pedestal had been painted. However, it was obvious
that many years ago the members of this Lodge had wearied of the chore
of shining the pedestal and had chosen instead, to cover the natural beauty
of the metal with a coat of metallic paint which could never shine.
The Craft is in a similar situation. After years of beauty, it has become a
chore to maintain its luster. All too often, it has become easier to cover its
true meanings with a surface application of adhering to the ritual without
exploring its true meanings of philosophy and inner improvement. As
when those Brothers tired of the repeated chore of fighting inevitable tarnish and chose the simple way out, we too, must look within ourselves and
see if we are not, in fact, covering the potential that we possess with a simple coat of apathy.
It is fitting that the three lesser lights enable us to observe the three great
lights of Masonry, the Holy Bible, the Square and Compass. Within the
Lodge, this material illumination has been restored to its original beauty.
Had the Brother been interrupted in his work of restoration, surrounded
by the scrapings of the false painted covering, he might have been accused
of damaging the significance of the pedestal. However, he finished and presented a completed project which spoke for itself.
PhilosophicaHy, the Craft is now in need of work. Apathy and ignorance
have, over the years, covered the secret of Masonry with simple explanations of what it stands for. Diligence and hard work are called for which
will restore the Craft by causing its members to "shine" as examples and
attract other men of quality to join our ranks. This work is necessary and,
as in the case of so many restorations , it cannot be allowed to be interrupted before it is completed.
As a society of men united, the Craft has produced material and philosophical works which are the admiration of every age.
As members of the Craft, let us reunite and produce new works which
will be the admiration of future ages.
YOUTH ORDERS

California and Hawaii Masons have good cause to be proud of the Youth
Orders we sponsor. The beautiful girls of Rainbow provide the color of the
rainbow itself. They bring great luster to Masons in this Jurisdiction. We
can be justifiably proud of the good works they do for all mankind.
Likewise, the lovely girls of Job's Daughters add to the total sum of love
and kindly consideration for others. We, in California Freemasonry owe
much to Job's Daughters. Each year the Grand Master urges the Masons in

this Jurisdiction to be more helpful to our Youth Orders. Instead of
acknowledging this need and doing something about it, most of our members do little or nothing. What about you? Where do you stand? What
have you done for these wonderful young people? Most of you, like many
other men of Masonry, agree that Masons should help, but only a handful
do! Most do nothing. Yet the need is great and it takes so little of our time.
I just wish I had the proper vocabulary to inculcate this great need into the
hearts and minds of the Masons in our Jurisdiction .
There is no suggestion here that we abdicate our family, or other activities! Each Mason could easily give a couple of nights a month to assist
young people. Not only is it a pleasure to do so, but we do God' s own
work as we help others, particularly young people.
Although I have not, as yet, mentioned DeMolay, everything I have said
here applies to these fine young men. For a Mason to give some time,
counsel and assist decent young men is an honor and an accomplishment of
note (even if no one but yourself knows about it).
You will find such minimal effort produces tremendous assistance to the
young man and also to yourself, so do it! You will never know about the
values you gain until you try.
I want to take a moment to call your attention to the two DeMolay
Foundations we have here in California Freemasonry. They deserve our
support. The Southern California DeMolay Foundation has developed
great momentum under the leadership of Tom Boles, Executive Officer,
Southern California DeMolay. The men working on behalf of that Foundation look forward to the time when the endowment funds will be sufficient
to take care of all expenses of DeMolay in Southern California.
The California DeMolay Foundation headquartered in Richmond, California has been successful in paying for most of the needs of the Northern
California DeMolay in providing sixteen DeMolay scholarships each year
while building an endowment for DeMolay.
These two Foundations need our help. If you are unable to give your
time and effort to these good causes, at least write out a check for what
you might spend out on the town for one night. Masons must make our
efforts and our substance count.
To THE CRAFT
Over the past years, we have become quite alarmed by the number of
suspensions for non-payment of dues. We went back and researched the
Proceedings of this Grand Lodge for the past five years and found that
suspensions for non-payment of dues were averaging 1567 per year over
that five year period. This year, we developed a plan whereby we requested
all Lodge Secretaries to submit the names of their members who were liable
for suspension for non-payment of dues to the Grand Secretary's office.
We then sent a personal letter over my signature to each of those members,
expressing our concern about their pending suspension. This letter went
out to over 1600 members and I am pleased to state that many of them

GRAND LODGE OF CAUFORNIA

137

replied, expressing their appreciation and gratitude for someone taking the
time to show concern about them as individuals.
The common thread running through all these responses that we
reviewed had one thing that stood out very clearly and that was why should
they remain as members when no one seemed to care whether or not they
retained their membership. This message has caused this Grand Master
great concern.
Permit me to share with you a few of the quotes from the letters that
were returned to the Grand Lodge office. " My father has been dead for
five years now. I think that dismisses him as a member'.' "My husband died
three years ago and I advised his Lodge:' "I find it hard to believe that
there has been no concern (letter or phone caJI) on the part of my Lodge
over the fact that I have not paid my dues!' "I have written to my Lodge
on two occasions, trying to explain my situation. Nothing has changed and
the fact that I have to keep writing about my problems is very humiliating
which makes me feel worse instead of better'.' "I wrote my Lodge fo ur
years ago that I was no longer able to be a member and wanted a withdrawal card. No one bothered to answer me!' "I am enclosing xerox copy
of my paid up 1985 dues. I am at a loss to understand how the Lodge made
such an error'.'
My Brethren, I could go on and on quoting from the responses we
received. Each response was xeroxed and a copy sent to the Secretary of
the respondent's Lodge so that the member's situation was made known to
his Lodge. I am pleased to report that many of those who would otherwise
have been suspended for non-payment of dues have now paid their dues
and thus have been retained as members of our Fraternity in good standing. Why? Because someone cared about them!
I would suggest that all Secretaries review their membership rolls and
that Masters work along with their Secretary and if in doubt, contact the
individuals involved well in advance of the time they might be in jeopardy
of being suspended for non-payment of dues.
There are two sections in the California Masonic Code which clearly outline the steps to be taken before a member is suspended for non-payment
of dues. Section 2814 relates to the Lodge Secretary sending registered letters to the members that are in jeopardy of losing their membership by suspension for non-payment of dues. The other which is my particular concern, is Section 2086 Article X, Sections 3 and 4 of the Uniform Code of
By-Laws. I would like to quote you these two Sections.
Section 3 - " A committee on delinquent members shall be appointed by
the Master at the Stated Meeting next succeeding his installation to personally, or otherwise, interview each delinquent member, ascertain the cause,
and to work closely with the Master and Officers in a continuing effort to
effect the retention of all members unable to pay, and deserving!'
Section 4 - "All reports of committees SHALL be made in writing:• No
member in this Jurisdiction should be suspended for non-payment of dues
unless some type of contact is made with that member personally. It is a
concern of this Grand Master and your Executive Committee that too

often these procedures as specified in the By-Laws are not being followed.
If they were, we would not be suspending or attempting to suspend members who are deceased, who had requested a dimit or who had actually paid
their dues and were not delinquent.
It is also of great concern to this Grand Master and to the Executive
Committee that too often a registered letter is sent to the last known
address of a Brother who may be in financial trouble or have health problems or otherwise and when no response is received from that registered letter because of personal embarrassment or pride, that we suspend that
member for non-payment of dues and consequently he loses all the rights
and privileges of this Fraternity after many, many years of devotion and
participation.
It is my sincere hope that in the future, all Lodges in this Jurisdiction,
through their Secretary and Master will follow to the letter the procedures
as specified in our California Masonic Code concerning delinquent dues
and stop this increasing spiral of suspensions of members who do not have
financial problems but do not pay their dues because they feel no one in
their Lodge cares whether or not they retain their membership. Responses
prove that they feel they are not needed as members and therefore they
allow themselves to be suspended for non-payment of dues. These are the
ones that we can save; these are the ones that we must show we care for,
that they are needed in our Lodges and that they can exhibit pride in being
a member of the greatest Fraternity in the world. To the others that have
financial problems and are embarrassed to share with their Lodge that this
problem exists and therefore would rather loose their membership than to
ask for assistance by way of remission of their dues, these are the ones that
are critical to us and we must see to it that they retain their membership.
We have to do our jobs better, we have to serve our members better, we
have to show our members that we truly care!
This year our losses were 4,692 members, a staggering amount. We could
cut our losses substantially if we would do our homework in our Lodges
and do the things that our Lodges were founded to do, namely caring for
their members. Let me explain some of the areas and some of the reasons
that I make this statement. Number one is that we lose 1,567 members by
way of suspension for non-payment of dues as an average each year. Number two, we lose on the average 600 Entered Apprentices each year by way
of forfeiture of fees. We have members who request a dimit and do not
affiliate with another Lodge. How many we are not sure, but we are
attacking this problem to see if we can find out by sending a letter to each
member who asks for a dimit to find out if he did indeed quit the Fraternity and if so, why he took this drastic action. I suspect from the responses
we have received from the letters we have sent out this year, that we will
find a great number of them quit the Fraternity because they felt no one
cared.
We can overcome some of our membership losses if we would continue
our candidates' coaching programs and show enthusiasm with and toward
our candidates who come to us seeking to become Masons. If we properly

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

139

coach them and inspire enthusiasm in our candidates, many who would
otherwise be lost to us would be retained . 600 Entered Apprentices each
year is far too many to lose, particularly when they come to us of their own
free will and accord seeking a Fraternal outlet in their lives. If we did our
homework correctly in our Lodges and retained the 1,567 now lost by way
of suspension for non-payment of dues and the 600 Entered Apprentices
who would become Master Masons, that would give us an additional 2,167
members reducing our losses by some 45 percent. If we were able to accomplish that, then we would be well under way toward establishing in this
Jurisdiction a growing and viable Fraternity of the future, but we must be
willing to give of ourselves to participate in our Lodge activities, to create
an atmosphere of true Brotherhood, and to show our neighbors, our
friends and our communities that we are indeed a caring, loving Fraternity.
It is so easy to be negative and claim that something cannot be done, but
my Brethren, let's proceed with things that can be done which might well
turn the negative to a positive. It is entirely up to you as Officers of your
respective Lodges as to how active your programs are and to how much
you relate to your community and your participation in activities. Grand
Lodge cannot solve the individual Lodge problems. Grand Lodge must
look to you to solve the problems in your Lodges and communities because
you are unique unto yourselves as is each Lodge in California and Hawaii.
Grand Lodge can only provide recommendations and programs that are
available to your Lodges. How you use them and how you benefit from
them is entirely up to the leadership in your own Lodge.

HAWAIIAN VISITATION

During April and May, we had the great pleasure and distinction of visiting the Lodges in the beautiful Islands of Hawaii. The friendliness and hospitality the Hawaiians displayed continue to be as warm and outgoing as
we found them on several occasions during our past visits .
While visiting on the Island of Oahu, we had the honor of opening
Grand Lodge and constituting King Kalakaua Daylight Lodge as a very
active and operating Lodge in Honolulu. This new Daylight Lodge will
serve the great number of Brethren and Sojourners in Hawaii who have not
been able to travel in the evenings, and it will give them an outlet for their
Masonic fellowship which they can enjoy. It is expected that this Lodge will
grow and prosper.
While in Honolulu, we were delighted to visit Koolau Lodge and assist in
conferring a Third Degree on one of that Lodge's candidates. It was truly a
beautiful evening, a typical example of Masonic fellowship.
After our visit and the official functions were completed on the Island of
Oahu, we visited the Islands of Maui, Hawaii and Kauai where we found
the same outgoing, traditional friendly and gracious hospitality that we
experienced on the Island of Oahu .
With all of the minor interruptions that we experienced while travelling
in the Islands , such as a Tsunami or tidalwave warning, which caused us to
evacuate our hotel and retire to high ground on the side of the mountain
on the coast of Kona for the evening, and missing a reception by Kona
Lodge, it was still a very delightful experience, and I can assure you that
the members of the Lodges in Hawaii will continue to prosper because of
their enthusiasm and proud traditions.

GOLDEN V ETERAN'S AWARDS

During the period September l, 1985 to September l, 1986 Grand Lodge
was pleased to present 692 Master Masons of this Jurisdiction with the coveted 50-Year Golden Veteran's Award. Since this program was instituted in
1928 and the first emblems were bestowed upon ten veteran Brothers at our
Masonic Home in Union City, 34,777 presentations have been made.
In addition to the 692 50-Year Golden Veterans' Awards which were presented, during the same period of time we presented seven 75-Year Awards,
six of them to California Masons and one as a courtesy to the Grand
Lodge of Illinois. Forty-five California 75-Year Awards have now taken
place since this program was first introduced and approved in 1955.
RECOMMENDATIONS AND DECISIONS

Recommendation No. 1 - Masonic Temples - Available for
Community Activities
It is apparent to this Grand Master that our Fraternity must become
more visible to the general public. In addition to our ceremonial events
which are open to the general public, news articles which have been prepared by our Public Information Committee, and other actions we have
taken during the past several years to enhance our image, there is another
avenue of approach which can only engender good public relations and a
positive image of our Craft. Accordingly, it is my Recommendation that
C.M.C. Section 2316 be amended to permit those Lodges that so desire, to
make their Temple facilities available for community and public activities
without any rental charges.
I fully realize that many Temples ha~e financial problems and offering
their facilities to community groups on a rental-free basis might not be in
accord with good " business " practices, but this must be weighed against
the favorable public image and the resultant publicity which would occur.

Recommendation No. 2 - Elimination of One Year Waiting Period
Prior to October of 1950, our law provided that a newly raised Master
Mason wait a period of six months before he might apply for membership
in a concorant or appendant body of Masonry. This requirement was
changed in 1950 to extend the six month waiting period to one of twelve
months, the theory being that it would require this period of time fo r
proper Masonic indoctrination of a newly raised Brother and as nearly as a
law can, to retain his interest in his Lodge.
Thirty-six years experience has proven that this theory is not valid and
this twelve month waiting period, or any waiting period for that matter,
merely delays the inevitable desire of the newly raised Master Mason fo r
membership in other Masonic bodies. It is therefore my Recommendation
that Section 2635 of our C.M.C. be amended to eliminate the one-year
waiting period requirement, but retaining the requirement of passing a satisfactory proficiency examination in the Candidate's Lecture of the Master
Mason Degree.

Recommendation No. 3 - Study of Grand Lodge Committee Structure
There are now forty Standing and Special Committees of this Grand
Lodge, in addition to five Boards, all charged with certain functions. Most
of these Committees perform in a creditable manner, however, some do
not. In certain cases misunderstandings exist and there have been instances
of overlap of duties. Needless to say, it is a monumental task which faces
an incoming Grand Master in the selection of the Committeemen to staff
all of these Boards and Committees. It may well be that there is no real
need for some of our Committees or that their functions might be incorporated into other Committees. AJso, the number of personnel of these Committees should be examined to see if they are properly staffed to perform
their respective functions. In addition, there does not seem to be an effective liaison between the Committee Chairman and the Grand Master and
the Executive Committee which can lead to confusion and misunderstandings. In view of this, it is my Recommendation that the incoming Grand
Master appoint a Special Study Commission to explore the entire Committee structure of this Grand Lodge and, if found necessary, to make appropriate recommendations to the Grand Master for his consideration or to
submit legislation on a timely basis to be considered at the next Annual
Communication of this Grand Lodge.

Recommendation No. 4 - Committee to Study and Report on the Health of
Freemasonry in California
I recommend that the incoming Grand Master appoint a committee to
develop the form and content of a Request for Proposal for a study and
report concerning the "Health" of Freemasonry in California.
The committee is to distribute the Request for Proposal to qualified consulting firms who will be asked to submit proposals which will include, but
not be limited to the scope of work, tasks to be performed, description of
the final product and statement of costs .
The committee is to review the Proposals and take whatever actions they
find necessary to select the consulting firm which demonstrates the best
qualifications to accomplish the goals and objectives as stated in the
Request for Proposal.
The committee's recommendation and the supporting information is to
be submitted to Grand Lodge at the next Annual Communication for
review and appropriate action.
Decision No. I - Declaring Lodge Elections Null and Void
Twice during the year, it was called to my attention by the Grand Secretary that Lodges had held illegal Elections of Officers. Surprise Valley
Lodge No. 235 was not able to hold an Election of Officers at its Annual
Meeting in November due to a lack of a quorum. The Lodge subsequently
wrote for a Dispensation to elect its Officers at its January 1986 Stated

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

143

Meeting, failing to state in its request that the Lodge took action_ to request
the Dispensation. In addition, the Seal of the Lodge was not afft~e~ to the
request. Our Grand Secretary advised the Lodge of these two om1ss1ons on
January 10, 1986. No response to this was received. On May 8, 1986, the
Lodge Secretary advised our Grand Secretary that since they had never
received a response to their request for the Dispensation, they "went ahead
and held the Election of Officers for 1986:' Upon being advised of this, I
declared the Election of Officers of Surprise Valley Lodge No. 235 to be
null and void and through our Grand Secretary ordered that Lodge to take
appropriate steps to request the requir.ed Dispensatio_n to hol~ an Election
of Officers. This was done, the required D1spensat10n was issued and a
proper Election of Officers was held.
.
The second instance of an illegal Election occurred by Lodge Mam No.
472 in that their duly elected Junior Warden failed to present himself for
Installation and had not been present at any Lodge meeting up to the time
of the Lodge's April Stated Meeting. At the April Stated Meeting, the Master declared the station vacant and proceeded to hold an election for the
station of Junior Warden without the required Dispensation. As in the
aforementioned case, I declared the election null and void and requested
the Lodge to then take the proper steps to secure a Dispensation to hold a
Special Election to fill the vacant Junior Warden's station. Subsequently
this was done, the election was accomplished and the station properly
filled.

Decision No. 2 - Holding of Raffles by Youth Groups
I was asked it: a Rainbow Assembly might conduct a raffle in order to
raise funds for their treasury. In view of Grand Master McCaw's Recommendation No. 3 in 1978, which provided for the elimination of the commercialism regulations of our Code as they pertain to our Youth Groups,
which Recommendation was adopted by Grand Lodge, I consulted with
our Jurisprudence Committee.
I was advised that under Sections 319-326 of the California Penal Code
and Sections 712-1229 of the Hawaiian Penal Code, raffles are illegal;
however, if tickets to a raffle were dispensed on a "donation" basis, there
would be no violation but that if a person did not wish to make a donation
they would have to be furnished a ticket to a raffle on a no-charge basis.
I concluded that this would be a subterfuge to circumvent the law and
certainly would not be in the best interests of our Youth Groups. Accordingly, it was my decision that raffles may not be conducted by any of the
Youth Groups located in California and Hawaii.

REJECTED APPLICANTS

During the year I granted two Dispensations to re-ballot on rejected
applicants in less than the required 12 month period. These were granted at
the request of two Lodges and seemed to me at the time to be in order. In
reviewing the Grand Master's Dispensations, the Jurisprudence Committee
has advised me that neither of these requests were of sufficient circumstances to warrant the granting of such Dispensations. Upon review of the
· facts in each instance I must now agree that no extraordinary facts were
revealed which should have occasioned these Dispensations being granted.
Since the time these Dispensations were granted, one last December and
one last March, the applicants were subsequently elected on the re-ballot,
and both have now received their Entered Apprentice Degree.
I do not believe any good purpose would be served in stopping the
advancement of these candidates since both were elected on the re-ballot,
which might well indicate that whoever was responsible in each case for
using the cube, did so in error or had a change of heart. Accordingly, I
have let the matter stand.
I would caution the Lodges, however, that unless a member approaches
the Master and admits his error in the use of the ballot box cube and wishes
to rectify his action or there are other extraordinary circumstances
involved , no Lodge should request of the Grand Master a Dispensation to
re-ballot on a rejected applicant in less than the required 12 month period.
Whatever the reason for a Brother using the ballot box to reject an appli-

C ONCLUSION

As I draw this message to a close, I stand before you humbled in heart
and mind, as all Grand Masters have done, who have stood in this position.
I must confess that words fail to allow me to express my deep appreciation to all of the people who have made this year what it has been for me
and, I hope, for this Grand Lodge. No person can spread himself thin
enough to effectively serve this Fraternity all by himself in a Jurisdiction as
great as California and Hawaii, and with that in mind I would like to
attempt to express my feelings to a few of those who have made this year
much, much easier for this Grand Master.
First, of course, to my wonderful Eleanor who has endured my short
temper at times, who has travelled with me and been my constant companion throughout this year, and , believe it or not, still remains my best friend
and travelling companion; to her my heart-felt thanks for allowing me to
take this journey and to share with me this four years of service to our
Grand Lodge. To her I will be eternally indebted .
To our Grand Secretary, Very Worshipful Bob Klinger, and his highly
expert staff; they have worked with me this year relieving me of many
details that have come before me and have been of great assistance in seeing that things run smoothly, my deep appreciation is offered. You and
your staff have made this year much easier.
To Tony Wordlpw, the Grand Marshal, and to his lovely lady Marilyn, I
extend my personal thanks for your unrestrained loyalty and service. This
past year you have served as my sounding block, my counselor and my
ever-present helper. You both have served this Grand Lodge in a tremendously outstanding way. To both of you for giving of yourselves this past
year, Eleanor and I will be forever grateful.
To the Grand Lodge Officers, the entire corps, you have been outstanding as representatives of the Lodges of this Jurisdiction. You have
responded eagerly when I have called on you at the last moment to serve
this Grand Master when I was unable to attend a function. You will always
have a special place in our hearts and thoughts. We shall ever remember
your kind patience and indulgence in listening to this Grand Master's corny
jokes over and over. I know that you share with me in a heart-felt thanks
for all of the courtesies that were extended to us this year in all of our travels throughout California and Hawaii. We have laughed together and
sometimes cried together especially when we learned of the loss of Oswald
J.B. Lau, Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division VII and Junior Grand Steward, Victor Dryden . For your year of dedication and devotion we shall be
ever grateful.
To our Grand Lodge committee members who have worked countless
hours, travelled great distances in the performance of their many functions

RECOMMENDATI ON No. I

MASONIC TEMPLES - AVAILABLE FOR COMMUNITY ACTIVITIES

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Recommendati on No. l of
the Most Worshipful Grand Master has been submitted, reports as follows:
The Grand Master has recommended, for purposes of public relations,
that constituent Lodges so desiring may permit the use, without rental
charge, of their Temple facilities for community and public activities.
To carry out the intent of the Grand Master's Recommendati on No. l,
your Committee on Jurisprudence submits the following legislation:
RESOLVED, that the second paragraph of Section 2316 of the California Masonic Code be amended by adding at the end thereof the words, "A
Lodge or Lodge controlled Temple Association, in its absolute discretion,
and subject to such regulations as it may impose, may permit use of its
facility, without rental charge, for community or public activities consistent
with the provisions of the California Masonic Code, provided, however,
that the user defray any separate expense resulting from such use~'
Since this Recommendati on amends an Ordinance, a five-sixths affirmative vote is required for approval.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of
the Recommendati on.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Master, in his Recommendati on No. 1, suggests that Section
2316 of the C.M.C. be modified to permit Lodges to provide their Temples
for community and public activities without any rental charge. The portion
of the Section that would be affected now reads as follows : "The Lodge
shall not use or permit the use of its funds or property or any part of them
for any other thing whatsoever except as hereinafter permitted. A Lodge or
Lodge controlled Temple Association shall not use any of its funds and
property to subsidize, directly or indirectly, any organization using or occupying its property, except Masonic oriented youth organizations. Charity
outside the Fraternity is not a lawful purpose for Lodge funds!'
This language was added to the Code, in 1957, on recommendatio n by
the Jurisprudence Committee as part of a report to give some degree of
authority to the then Committee on Lodge Finance. The words, "other
organizations:' as used in the report, referred strictly to Masonic related
organizations and no mention was made of public or community organizations. We recognize, however, that the law, as written, is all inclusive.

Anderson, in his message to Grand Lodge, spoke these words under the
heading of Masonry in Changing World: "My Brethren, we are gathered
here in the twilight hours of another Grand Lodge year, to renect on the

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
RECOMMENDATION No. 2

ELIMINATION OF ONE-YEAR WAITING PERIOD

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Recommendation No. 2 of
the Most Worshipful Grand Master has been submitted, reports as follows:
The Grand Master has recommended that the present law requiring that
a newly raised Master Mason wait a period of one year before application
for membership may be made in a concordant or appendant body of
Masonry be eliminated.
.
.
To carry out the intent of the Grand Master, your Committee on Junsprudence submits the following legislation:
.
.
RESOLVED, that Section 2635 of the Cahforma Masonic Code be
amended to read:
"A Mason who has received the Degrees of Masonry in a Lodge
of this Jurisdiction shall not apply for nor receive any Degree or
be initiated into any organization, other than another Lodge,
the prerequisite of membership wherein is that a pe~son be .a
Mason until he has given satisfactory evidence, by stnct examination 'in open Lodge, that he is proficient and qualified. in the
Candidate's Lecture of the Degree of Master Mason. This Section does not apply to organizations which do not confer
Degrees and do not have formal initiation ceremonies'.'
This amendment to our Ordinances requires a five-sixths vote for adoption.
·
f
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption o
the Recommendation.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Master recommends elimination of the one-year waiting period required of a newly raised Master Mas~n befo.r~ he may apply for
membership in prerequisite organizations, while retammg the requirement
that he pass a satisfactory examination in the Candidate's Lecture of the
Third Degree.
.
Similar recommendations have been made by other Grand Masters m the
recent past. Also, resolutions to this effect hav_e been presented to the
Grand Lodge numerous times in the past twenty-five years, and yo~r Committee on Policy and General Purposes has recomm~nded a vote 1~ favor
of deleting the waiting period. Each recommendation or resolut10n has
failed to receive a sufficient vote of the Grand Lodge to amend the present
law, although majority votes have occurred frequently.
..
In 1950 when our law was amended so as to require the one-year wa1tmg
period, it 'was thought by the Grand Lodge that this period of time _wou_ld
enhance the newly raised Master Mason's knowledge of ~aso~ry, its h.1story and law, and give him a better opportunity to acquaint himself with

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

151

all the members of his Lodge. Also it was hoped that he would find a place
for commitment and service in his Lodge before he was wafted away from
Craft Masonry by the inducements of other bodies dependent on Master
Masons for their membership.
Before we decide how we intend to vote on this Grand Master's recommendation, we should remember, my Brethren, that the one-year time limit
was initiated in 1950 at a time when membership in most of our Lodges
was in the post World War II period of hitting new highs in numbers of
members. Petitions were plentiful and the membership continued to grow.
The reasons behind the waiting period experiment were sound, and the
failure to accomplish the intended purpose should not be blamed on the
attempt. Perhaps one cause of failure was like that old saw: "You can lead
a horse to water, but you can't make him drink:' Newly raised Master
Masons are not to be equated with horses, of course, but the simile may be
apt.
Today, however, we find ourselves in a period of non-growth, and even
worse - a steady decline in membership. We know that this is a worrisome
problem to you who are the leaders of our Lodges and to the Grand
Lodge. We believe it is time, therefore, to encourage new Master Masons to
continue their interest in Masonry even though that interest might be in one
of the concordant bodies . The fact is that many of our members who are,
or have been, active in concordant bodies are, or have become, active in
Craft Masonry. Who is to say but that their interest and service in what we
call the Blue Lodge might well have been piqued by their activities in the
prerequisite organizations?
Therefore, we submit to you, my Brethren, that it is now time to admit
that the experiment .did not accomplish its intended purpose, and that we
should consider that the general welfare of Masonry may well be enhanced
by the elimination of that restrictive rule.
The time may come again when a waiting period will be desirable or even
necessary. If that should come about there is nothing to prevent the Grand
Lodge from reinstituting a waiting period. For 36 years it hasn't been of
any measurable benefit. Therefore, is it not time to see what meritorious
effect deleting the one-year waiting period might have on our new members? Bear in mind, approval of this recommendation eliminates only the
waiting period. The third degree proficiency requirement will be retained.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes respectfully recommends that you vote "Yes" to approve the Grand Master's Recommendation No. 2.
Failing the required five-sixths affirmative vote for adoption, but receiving a majority affirmative vote, the Grand Master's Recommendation No.
2 will be held over until the 1987 Annual Communication.

RECOMMENDATION NO . 3

APPLICATION OF C.M.C. SECTION 2050

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Recommendation No. 3. of
the Most Worshipful Grand Master has been submitted, reports as follows:
The Grand Master has recommended that the incoming Grand Master
appoint a Special Study Commission to explore the entire Committee struc.
ture of this Grand Lodge and, if found necessary, to make appropriate rec.
ommendations to the Grand Master for his consideration or for the sub.
mission of legislation on a timely basis to be considered at the next Annual
Communication of this Grand Lodge.
Your Committee finds that no legislation is required and that a majority
vote only is necessary for adoption.
To place this matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of
the Recommendation.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Master recommends that the incoming Grand Master appoint
a Special Study Commission to explore the entire committee structure of
the Grand Lodge and to make necessary recommendations to the Grand
Master and/ or submit proposed legislation to be considered at our next
Annual Communication.
The Grand Master notes that there are now forty Standing and Special
Committees of the Grand Lodge, in addition to five Boards of Trustees. He
also notes that, in his opinion, there is not an effective liaison between the
Committee Chairmen and the Grand Master.
In the past some Grand Masters assigned several committees to each of
the three Junior Officers to which they were to act as liaison to the Grand
Master. Your Committeee on Policy and General Purposes suggests that a
similar liaison structure within the Executive Committee might help to
alleviate the liaison problem.
However, the current Grand Master believes that special attention should
be directed to the number of committees and to the number of members on
each, it appearing to him that there is a possible overlap of duties. He
reports that some committees do not "perform in a creditable manner'.'
Operation of this Grand Lodge, as you know from reports of the Com·
mittee on Finance, is big business and entails the expenditure of large sums
of money. Most committees have budgeted their expenses, but if there is an
overlap in duties, some savings might accrue. We should recognize, also,
that some committees might be overstaffed and others understaffed. This
Grand Lodge is blessed with talented members who do great service to
Masonry. Your Grand Master and your Committee wish to see that this talent is used most judiciously, effectively and economically.
A study by an independent commission should be worthwhile and your
Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends approval of the
Grand Master's Recommendation Number 3.
Adopted.

DECISION No. 2

HOLDING OF RAFFLES BY YOUTH GROUPS

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Decision No. 2 of the Most
Worshipful Grand Master has been referred, reports as follows:
The Grand Master was requested to render a Decision as to whether a
Rainbow Assembly might conduct a raffle in order to raise funds in view
of Grand Master McCaw's Recommendation No. 3 in 1978 which provided
for the elimination of the Commercialism Regulations of the California
Masonic Code as they pertain to our Youth Groups and for the Youth
Groups to carry on their activities within the "bounds of propriety" as
required by C.M.C. Section 2071.
Grand Master Driskell had been advised by this Committee that
although under the California Penal Code and the Hawaiian Penal Code,
raffles, as lotteries, are illegal, the California Supreme Court had determined in a particular 1958 case that if tickets to a raffle were dispensed
without charge to the participant, it would not be a violation of the law.
The Grand Master correctly concluded under the facts then before him
that it would be a subterfuge to circumvent the law by distributing the tickets on either a gratuitous or donation basis. Accordingly, it was his Decision that raffles may not be conducted by any of the Youth Groups located
in California and Hawaii as such activities would not be within the
"bounds of propriety!'
Upon further research, it has been determined that in 1976, an Appellate
Court in California distinguished the facts upon which the Supreme Court

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

155

lllade its 1958 decision. In the former case no one was required to pay (or
make a donation) for a ticket. In the latter situation some, but not all, persons were required to make a donation or pay for a ticket.
The 1976 case makes clear that a lottery is illegal and in violation of California Penal Code Section 319 when any monies are paid or donated for
tickets.
In view of this holding, the Grand Master also wishes it clearly understood that not only are the Youth Orders forbidden to conduct a lottery,
but that Section 3314 of the California Masonic Code and Section V of the
Commercialism Regulations relating to Adult Orders likewise forbid all
organizations referred to in those Sections from conducting any such lottery.
Your Committee on Jurisprudence reports that this Decision of the
Grand Master is within his powers and is consistent with the facts and law
and does not require an amendment to the California Masonic Code. As a
result, a majority vote only is required to approve the Decision of the
Grand Master.
To bring the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the approval of
the Decision.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
A Rainbow Assembly asked if it might conduct a raffle to raise money.
In both California and Hawaii raffles are illegal. There is a method by
which the law can be circumvented, and some organizations use that
method.
The Grand Master decided that it would not be in the best interest of our
Youth Groups to use a subterfuge to violate the law.
We agree.
The policies and general purposes of the Grand Lodge are not always
expressly stated. We believe it can be expressly stated that among them are
honesty and obedience to the law. These should not distinguish us; they
should merely bring us to the same standards we expect all citizens to obey.
The example we desire to set for our youth will permit no subterfuge.
The Policy and General Purposes Committee recommends a "Yes" vote.
The Committee on Youth Orders:
The members of the Youth Orders Committee have been on the receiving
end of a great many inquiries regarding " Raffles" and such.
We are aware of and agree with the changes in the Masonic Code in
1976-1977 and 1977-1978 regarding commercialism and the more lenient
application to Youth Groups. This Decision, however, relates more to the
Section on Gambling than that of commercialism .
This issue seems clear and specific.
Your Youth Orders Committee believes that this Decision is correct and
we recommend your vote to uphold Grand Master's Decision No. 2.
Approved.

DECISION No. 3

USE OF MASON IC INSIGN IA AND WORDS "MASO NIC" AND/ OR
"MASO N"
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Commit tee on Jurispru dence, to which Decision No . 3 of the Most
Worshipful Grand Master has been referred , reports as follows:
Subsequent to rendering his Decision No. 3 as printed in the Grand Master's Message, the Grand Master has, after consulta tion with the Commit tees on Jurispru dence, Policy and General Purpose s, and Commercialism,
reconsidered and has determined to limit that Decision to apply only to a
specific request by High Twelve Interna tional to allow that organiz ation
within this Jurisdic tion to include the Square and Compas s in a uniform
plaque, rather than to be all encompassing as originally written.
The Grand Master has, therefore, authoriz ed this Commi ttee to report
that it is his Decision that High 1Welve Internat ional, an organiz ation consisting exclusively of Master Masons , be authoriz ed and licensed to include
the Square and Compas s in a uniform plaque to be placed at the entranc e
to its meeting places in Californ ia and Hawaii.
Your Commi ttee on Jurispru dence reports that this Decision of the
Grand Master is within his powers and is consiste nt with the facts and law
and does not require an amendm ent to the Californ ia Masonic Code. As a
result, a majorit y vote only is required to approve his Decision.
To bring the matter before the Grand Ldoge, we move the approva l of
the Decision.
The Commit tee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Master' s Decision No. 3 is now limited to a specific request
for a defined use.
Our Masonic name and insignia including the Square and Compas s are
registered with the Secretary of State. A court judgme nt against an abuser
perman ently enjoine d use of the words "Mason " or "Mason ic" or the
"Square and Compa ss" emblem . A ruling by Grand Master Clausen in
1955 confirmed these things and pointed out that unautho rized wearing of
our insignia is prohibit ed by Californ ia law.
The judicial decision, law and registra tion protect these things. But how
do we define what uses are proper?
Originally, the Grand Master attempt ed a definition with broad application to advise other Masonic bodies as well as the one which made the
inquiry.
However, this field is thorny and difficult to define on a broad basis.
We feel far more comfort able with the Decision in this modifie d form.
We believe that some uses are permissible, that the requested use is one
such and that the Grand Master' s Decision No . 3, as modifie d, should be
approve d.
We recomm end a "Yes" vote.
Approv ed.

PROCLAMATION

"4.ASONI C YOUTII ACTIVITIES MONlli
Today'a complex 9ociety offers unprecedented opportunities, challenges, pTeS9ures
and temptations to our youth. Con9equently, the re9ponsibility and need for adult
guidance is greater than ever before. Additionally, the rewards of working with
our youth are dramatically increased.
Hesonic Youth Orders -- Dellolay, Job's Daughters and Rainbow for l.iTls can significantly influence t he future direction of the lives of our young people. The ideal•
and leadership skills which they learn i n their respective Order, will be carried
with them to influence succeeding generations.
Brethren, the need for your individual participation in any or all of our Youth
Orders is cri tical. The very existence of Masonry is in jeopardy -- we need t o
help future generations understand and learn of our principles and tenets. The
time to begin is nov; the place to begin is working vith our Youth Orders. Tilese
young people need the benef it of sharing your experiences, ideals and friendsh ip .
n.ere is no better vay to spend a little of your time than by sharing yourself with
young people.
While it should be a regular and on-going part of the activities of each of our
constituent Lodges to plan, pro1110te and take pert in Fraternal re lat ions with
theae fine young people at every opportunity, I hereby proc laim the Month of March,
1986 a s
MASONIC Y01.TI1i ACTIVITIES MONTI!
in the Grand Jurisdiction of California and Hawaii and encourage each Lodge to make
special efforts to promote a closer relationship with the young people in their loe1l
Masoni c family, Further, 1 direct that such emphasis and effort not be confined
nierely to this official month, but should be made a part of the entire Masonic year
by including the members of the Masoni c Youth Orders in such activities as Public
Schools Observances , U.S. Constitution Observances, U.yman's Nights, llirain Awards,
Installations and any and all other public events . Further, I direct that this Proclamation should be read at the Mar ch Stated MeetinR of each Lodge and, where possible
published in the Lodge Trestleboard for the Month of Msrch.
Sincerely 6 Fraternally,

As America continues its journey into the third cen t ury of its even tful
l ife, we should never lose sight of the dominent r ole played by our Public
Schools in crea ting a na tion that i s preeminent among world power s .
Free public education -- available to every child in America -- has made
our Country great, and since our schools are determined that coming generations
shall be equally well educated, our PUBLIC SCHOOLS are truly the PILLARS or
AMER I CA ' S FUTURE •
I t has been said that no man is an island. The same is true of our
Public Schools. They are not a n isolated segment of soc iety; they are an integral
part o f our culture , a part that will determine the destiny of our beloved
Country. As such, our PUBUC SCHOOLS are the very foundation - PILLARS i f
you please -- OF AMERICA'S FUTURE.
'
In order for America to maintain its lofty s tatus among the nations of
the world , it is imperative that our t raditional system of free public e ducation
be supported, protec ted and preserved. It must not be allowed to fail; its
effectiveness must never be impai re d!
Titerefore, I cal l upon the Masons of California and Hawai i as well as a l l
citizens to join in supporting the greatest educational system ever devised -our free Public Schools. To this end, I do now Proclaim
PUBLI C SQIOOLS WEEK during APRIL 1966
n.roughout California and Hawaii, and I call upon all Masonic Lodges to arrange
with the school s in their a rea f or a mutually convenient week i n the Month of
April to be set aside for appropriate ceremonies and programs particularly aimed
at the concept of PUBLIC SQIOOLS -- PILLARS OF AKEllICA'S FUTURE,
Furthermore, I direct that no Lodge programs or meetings, other t han
Stated Meetings, be he l d during the designated week which might confli ct with
l oc a l Public Schools Ob servances ; and
That t his Proclamation be read by the Master or the Secretary at the April
Stated Meeting of all Lodges and, where feasible, thac it also be published in
Lodge Bulletins o~ dis tributed to each member •

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A . M . of California:
Another year has passed and in accordance with the requirements of the
California Masonic Code, I offer the following report.
CONFERENCES. COMMITTEE MEETINGS, SEMINARS

I have no intention of boring you with the details and dates of our
Annual Spring Conferences . I will only report that they were held in
accordance with the instructions of the Grand Lecturer and were most productive.
Committee meetings were held at each of the six conferences and on two
additional weekends.
Seminars are an important tool in the instruction of ritual to the masses.
A number of seminars were held throughout the Jurisdiction . All have
been well attended and accepted. If you haven't attended one of these I
would encourage you to do so.
LODGES

About twenty years ago, this Jurisdiction boasted a high of 711 Lodges
and a membership of almost 245,000. These peaks are noted in 1965 and
1966. 1986 records a reduction of almost 17 percent in the number of active
Lodges and a 33 percent loss of membership over this 20 year period. Our
assessable membership now stands at 169,000.
Is this reason for panic? No. Is it reason for major change? No. Is there
reason for concern? Perhaps. However, I think it is important to point out
that we didn't develop into the finest fraternal organization in the world
through continuous change and confusion. We got to be what we are and
where we are through fraternalism and brotherly love. Ritual and the good
rendition thereof. We need to get back to basics. Remember quality, not
quantity is the most important asset we possess. And regardless of what the
future holds, it can be our assurance of a future existence .
Nearly 500 Past Masters are serving in the 5 progressive seats of our
Lodges, Junior Deacon to Master excluding Treasurer and Secretary.
Approximately 100 vacancies exist in this 5 seat progression.
RITUAL

In 1983, at my recommendation, this Grand Lodge adopted the present
Funeral Certificate program and a new printing of the Funeral Service. I
point this out to you for two reasons. First, to let you know that the program of certification is improving as expected. And secondly, to remind the
Brethren that the new book is available in the supply room. Some may
believe that they do not need the new book because the wording has not
changed . However, I believe it is very important to all those who are doing
the service and learning it for the first time. It contains the Certification

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

175

program, funeral information, a checklist and ritual instructions for the
various types of ceremony that can be conducted . I urge you to at least
.
take a look at it.
While the ritual adopted by this Grand Lodge is used throughout this
Jurisdiction, with one exception, I have strong concerns that some of our
Lodges are doing a poor job of preparation and in the delivery of ~~r
degree and ritual work. I am not seeking perfection because I know this ts
an imposibility. What I am seeking is a sincere desire on the part of each
officer to do his very best. I don't think that that is really asking to~ much:
The ritual is the foundation upon which Masonry stands and without 1t
our Fraternity would be as an empty shell, devoid of its strength an?
beauty and entirely incapable of teaching to its followers the arts and sciences of the Craft. Perfection of the ritual and the proper rendition thereof
is a subject, worthy of much time and effort on the part of any Mason.
INSPECTORAL CORPS

Turnover in the lnspectoral Corps continues this year at 15 percent. T~is
coupled with a number of resignations timed to take place.~t year end wt~I
pose a difficult task and may be an area of concern. A?dit1onal responsibilities, with less guidance, continues to be added to their already overburdened shoulders. Each time I heap praise on them I know it is far short of
the pay they deserve for a job well done. My sincere thanks to each of them
for the efforts put forth on behalf of Masonry in this Jurisdiction.
BUDGET

Inflation throughout the country has cooled somewhat. However, costs
related to travel,' such as hotel, motel and meals, continue to escalate. Formal requests for a slightly increased budget have been submitted to the
Finance Committee for your consideration.
CONCLUSION

In conclusion, I wish to thank the Grand Lodge Officers, the Grand
Lodge office staff, and all the Brethren of this great Jurisdiction for assisting me and allowing me the opportunity of serving one more year. To those
great men of the Inspectoral Corps and those s~ven fine Assi~t~nt Grand
Lecturers, who serve this Grand Lodge in a multitude of capacities, what a
tremendous privilege it has been working with you , individually and collectively.
Respectfully submitted,
JoE HAMMOND, Grand Lecturer

I move the adoption of this report.
Report adopted .
