REPORT OF THE SPECIAL STUDY COMMITTEE
(C.M.C. Section 2048 and 2050)

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Special Study Committee was appointed by Grand Master John W.
Driskell in fulfillment of Grand Master Roy J. Henville's Recommendation
No. 5 at the 1985 Annual Communication that a special committee be
appointed to restudy Sections 2048 and 2050 of our Masonic Code for possible modifications and clarification. The two Sections have to do with
Meeting Place Limitations (Section 2048) and Serving of Liquor at Social
Functions (Section 2050) . Grand Master Henville also recommended that a
decision requested by a chapter of the National Sojourners be held in abeyance pending clarification and/ or modification of the two Code sections.
Your Committee believes that any difficulty or confusion in interpretation of Section 2048 lies with definition of the phrase "Masonic related
organization!' There is no basis for assuming that the term "Masonic
related" applies only to groups of women (it should be noted that the Eastern Star, the Order of the Amaranth, etc., include Master Masons as members). Any organization, the prerequisite of membership wherein is that a
person be a Master Mason, is "Masonic related" as per the dictionary definition of the word " related'.' One definition includes the phrase "the fact
or condition of being connected in some way, either objectively or in the
mind:' Obviously, the definition applies to the concordant and appendant
bodies of Masonry.
Section 2050 is titled "Serving of Liquor at Social Functions:• This Section permits a Masonic Lodge or any Masonic related group to hold meetings of a social nature in facilities other than those which they own or operate. The Section provides for both the use and serving of alcoholic
beverages at such meetings; and, further, the Section prohibits the serving
of liquor, wine or beer in a Masonic Temple or in any building or structure
owned or operated by a Masonic Lodge or Masonic related organization.
Clearly no group, including the Shrine and others, can serve liquor, wine or
beer in a building they own or operate.
In 1974, for the sole purpose of clarification of intent, by action of the
Grand Lodge, a distinction was made in Section 2050 (originally Section
324.2 of the former Code) between the phrase "used or served" and the
single word "used." This distinction is explained on pages 231-232 of the
1974 Proceedings under the title "Report on Construction of Section 324.2
of California Masonic Code'.' The distinction permits the use, but not the
serving, of alcoholic beverages by members of Masonic related groups
owning buildings in which separate club rooms are maintained and in
which members have individual lockers in which liquor for personal use
may be stored. This distinction adopted by Grand Lodge is merely footnoted at the end of Section 2050 of our current California Masonic Code.
Our Code should be complete in one book and not subject to referral to

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

177

other books which may not be readily available to the Mason using the
California Masonic Code.
In summary, your present Committee finds no contradiction in Sections
2048 and 2050.
However, this finding does not address the larger issue of what really
should be our law respecting the use and serving of alcoholic beverages. It
bas been over twenty years since a thorough review of this subject was conducted by a special Grand Lodge committee. As a result of recommendations by the Special Committee appointed following the 1964 Annual Communication our laws respecting liquor were modified at the 1966 Annual
Communication. The changes made were deemed to be both needed and
proper, and in line with the customs and practices of that time.
Your Committee believes it is again time for full review. There are many
devoted members of our Fraternity who sincerely believe that our present
law is overly restrictive and unrealistic. There are also many members of
equal sincerity and devotion to the Fraternity who believe that our present
Jaw is proper and that any liberalization would be detrimental. The issues
will not rest or be settled until there has been provided adequate opportunity for Masons in our Jurisdiction to express their feelings and beliefs concerning the liquor question.
Your Committee therefore recommends the appointment of a Special
Commission to conduct a thorough review of our liquor laws and also to
provide means whereby all Masons in the Jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge
may have an opportunity to express their feelings and beliefs with respect
to the liquor question . The Special Commission should make every effort
to ascertain the present thinking of Masons in California and Hawaii concerning the liquor· issue. Hearings at convenient times and places should be
held under rules established by the commission, and provision should be
made for the receipt of written comments and proposals under rules and
time constraints set by the commission. Following the conclusion of hearings and the closing date for receipt of written comments and proposals,
the commission should carefully review and consider all that has been
expressed and then make a determination as to the need of any change in
our law. If the commission concludes there should be a change or changes,
then it shall prepare proposed legislation to accomplish such change(s).
The proposed legislation should then be thoroughly circulated to the
Lodges well in advance of the Annual Communication at which a decision
would be made.
Your Committee urges that sufficient time be allowed for as thorough
and complete a study as possible. The study might well take two or even
three years, and those Brethren selected to serve on the special commission
should accept appointment with the full understanding that it may be a
time consuming task. In the judgment of yo ur present Committee that task
is necessary for the benefit of Freemasonry in California and Hawaii, and

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

178

we urge that it be embarked upon without delay.
Respectfully submitted,
THEODORE MERIAM, Chairman
W. BARRETT Ross
JOHN L. LOOMIS
JAMES W. McDONALD
LEO E. ANDERSON

E. ARTHUR HAGLUND, P .G.M . ,

(Consultant)
I move that the report of the Special Study Committee be adopted and
that the incoming Grand Master be directed to appoint a Special Commission as recommended in the report.
Adopted.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M . of California:
Your Lodge Resources Development Committee ~as been very bu_sy t~s

Jurisdiction, helping them to strengthen and improve their programs
through program suggestions and officer development. We have also be~n
developing a Lodge Leadership Handbook, which we hope to make avadable soon. In addition we have continued to administer the Grand Master's

The major function of the Lodge Resources Development Committee is
to assist Lodges in developing their resources. These resources can .range
from new Lodge Officers, program plans, advancement of candidates
through the degrees, to new members. Unfortunately, too many Lodges are
not willing to put forth the effort to achieve the resu!ts that they wa?t.
Each of us must establish the goals that we want to achieve and then stnve
to make them happen. Your Lodge Resources Development Committ~ is
available to help you to set those goals and then to help you accomplish
them . We are not here to take over any of your tasks or functions, but to
help you develop your resources. so that you can perform ~ho,se . tasks an~
functions yourselves. It takes a httle effort and work, but 1sn t it worth it
to see your Lodge prosper because of the efforts that yo~ _have put forth.
There are no overnight solutions, but results can be positive. How about
you? Wouldn't you and your Lodge benefit from some help from our
Committee? We're only a short telephone call away.
This is the third year for the Grand Master's Achievement Award. This
year we have 150 Lodges that participated in the program ..Ap~roximately
30 percent of them are qualifying for the Award for the third time. Sadly,
some Lodges have dropped by the wayside and did not apply this year and

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

179

too many Lodges haven't made application for their Award. To qualify for
the Award requires that a Lodge establish a well rounded program for its
members and officers. The Grand Master's Achievement Award program
consists of four basic areas: Lodge Officer Development, Programs,
Masonic Responsibility, and Social Responsibility. Receipt of the Award
indicates that a Lodge is healthy and has developed a program that contributes to its members and community. Unfortunately, less than 25 percent of
the Lodges in this Jurisdiction have applied for and are qualified to receive
the award at the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge in October.
If you want to see your Lodge grow and prosper, pattern your programs
and functions so that you can meet the Grand Master's Achievement
Award requirements.
The award itself is not the important part of the program. What is
important is that the Lodge establishes a strong, well rounded program for
its members; one that involves the individual members in their own Lodge
activities.
If your Lodge is having trouble obtaining Lodge Officers, new members,

turn around, attendance will improve and Officers and new members will
be easier to find.

REPORT OF THE INVESTMENT COMMITTE E
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Investment Committee has the responsibility of reporting annually
to Grand Lodge on the condition of the various funds of Grand Lodge and
those of its entities.
During the year quarterly meetings are held by the Committee with its
investment counselors. At each meeting an independent analytical firm
reviews the performance of the primary funds as compared with similar
funds, i.e., endowment, non-profit and trust funds, in the United States.
The primary concern of the Committee is the preservation of the principal of the various funds together with the highest rate of return commensurate with safety and good investment practice. Three funds, Masonic
Homes Endowment Fund, Masonic Homes General Fund and the Hugo
M. Lorber Union City Home Fund constitute 95 percent of the total investments.
Among other funds supervised by the Committee are the General Fund
of Grand Lodge, the funds of California Masonic Memorial Temple, California Masonic Foundation and Amaranth, Pooled Income and thirteen
restricted-use funds of the Masonic Homes.
The market value of the total portfolio on June 30, 1986, was
$188,548,000 compared to $148,789,770 a year earlier, an increase of 26.7
percent. The 1985-1986 cash yield from the total invested funds was 7 .3
percent.
Fixed income securities including government and corporate bonds composed 64 percent of the total portfolio. The remainder consisted of common stocks and cash equivalents.
The Pooled Income Fund is of particular importance to the Masonic
Homes. On June 30, 1986, the Fund had a market value of $2,615,701.
The cash yield was 9.9 percent. The Pooled Income Fund gives Masons and
others in California and Hawaii the opportunity to create a lifetime income
for themselves and for one-time designated beneficiaries. Certain tax
advantages accrue to the contributor. Eventually, the Masonic Homes
becomes the final beneficiary.
The rewarding accumulation of assets in the various funds of Grand
Lodge has been the result of the efforts of Masons and their friends . The
operations of the Masonic Homes at Union City and Covina are almost
entirely financed through the income from Endowment and General Fund
investments . Other revenues furnish support for the charitable activities
and educational grants of the Grand Lodge of California.
The fund investments rank among the highest in quality because the
Investment Committee exercises the utmost prudence and care in their

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

181

management.. The cash yield and total return have been satisfactory in light
of the Commntee's conservative investment policy.
Respectfully submitted,
RALPH H. HEAD, Chairman
EDWARD H. SIEMS, P.G.M.
JACK F. BOWLEY
B. ROBERT MALOUF
DAVID K. LESH
HENRY H.P. WILKINS

REPORT OF COMMIT IEE ON TEMPLE PROPERTIES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Temple Properties is pleased to submit the Annual
Report of its activities for the 1985-1986 Grand Lodge Year.
In addition to the usual number of requests for approval of proposals
and contracts which exceeded the $5,000 limit on expenditures set by the
C.M.C ., Section 1208, 1985 Supplement , this Committee has been kept
busy studying and explaining the Uniform Code of By-Laws for Masonic
Temple Associations, as mandated by the passage of Resolution 85-12 at
the October 1985 Communica tion of our Grand Lodge. (This Committee is
always happy to respond to such requests from Temple Association s, in
person, when possible, or by mail or telephone.)
The above mentioned By-Laws have been modified somewhat, the modifications having been suggested by a special study committee working with
Brother R. Stephen Doan, who drew up the original Uniform Set, and by
members of the Temple Properties Committee.
In its constitution ally prescribed duties, that of monitoring the expenditures of funds in excess of $5,000, and reviewing leases whose terms are in
excess of three years, this Committee has noted with concern that many

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

183

contracts and leases between Temple Associations and contractors or prospective tenants have been sent to us for review and approval without giving this Committee sufficient time to study and approve or disapprove
those proposed contracts or leases. At times we have even received requests
for approval of such documents after they have been signed and implementation of them has begun. This practice can lead to grave consequences for
those Temple Associations indulging in such procedures.
A minimum of two weeks after receiving a request for review is necessary for a reply. Four weeks minimum is necessary if the contract or lease
must be reviewed by the Executive Committee. A clause in the contract or
)ease st~ting that the approval of the Grand Lodge Committee on Temple
Properties and/ or the Grand Lodge Executive Committee is required. This
wiJI very often avoid future problems.
This Committee, and its Chairman especially, is most grateful to our
Most Worshipful Grand Master, John W. Driskell, for the great interest he
has continued to show in our work, and the sage advice and suggestions he
bas given when problems arose; to the Deputy Grand Master, Jack R.
Levitt, to Leo B. Mark, Senior Grand Warden, and to Stanley L. Channon, Junior Grand Warden, for the constant support they have given us.
A special note of thanks is due to our Grand Secretary, Robert A.
Klinger, and Assistant Grand Secretary, H. Francis Lewis, whose office
doors were never closed to us when advice and counsel were needed .
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF THE COMMI1TEE ON COMMERCIALISM
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
During the Masonic year, the Committee on Commercialism has
reviewed two public fund raising matters and one Shrine Temple's football
game financial statement.
The Grand Chapter of Royal Arch Masons requested permission to hold
a golf tournament to raise money for their charities. In order for a golf
tournament such as this to be put on, several Sections of the C.M.C. would
have to be amended. Section 2070k would have to be amended to permit
the public to be solicited, to participate in and to attend. Also Regulation
III in the Appendix to the C.M.C. regarding solicitation of merchandise
gifts of money, or prizes require amendments. Once the amendments wer~
made, a host of fund raising schemes would arise that would tear the fabric
of the Fraternity. Hence, we recommended this event not be held.
A gum vending company requested our Lodges be solicited to provide
names of corporate leaders to promote the sale of gum. The Commercialism Committee's opinion is that this is an unauthorized use of Masonic rosters for commercial purposes.
We reviewed the Al Malaikah Shrine Temple's football funds financial
statement and found it to be within the guidelines as set forth in the
C.M .C . .
Respectfully submitted,
SHERWOOD C. KINGSLEY, Chairman

everyone's attention. This handsome booth, staffed by knowledgeable

formats and guidelines for setting up local Lodge observances were distributed to all Senior Wardens.
Grand Master John W. Driskell, the Deputy Grand Master, as well as the
Senior and Junior Grand Wardens, and also the Grand Secretary, Robert
A. Klinger, and his staff have been of tremendous assistance to this Committee.
This year again as in 1985 with the Grand Master's permission, I
appointed Maurice R. Crosby as Vice Chairman. Due to the size of the
State, this appointment has greatly improved the efficiency of the Committee. We now have Southern and Northern representation.
This past year we have had a booth at all of the Leadership workshops
to promote our program, and also to furnish qualified speakers at all nine
workshops. Chairman Happel met twice with the California Commission
appointed by the Governor to help formulate plans for the Bicentennial
Observance of the U.S. Constitution to be held in 1987.
An active year was punctuated by two Committee meetings which were
held - one in Salinas and one in Pasadena, where we discussed and
exchanged ideas on different programs throughout the State, and to set up
a booth at all the workshops, with the idea that the Lodges would start
early to plan their programs. Grand Master John W. Driskell proclaimed
the month of September as Constitution Observance Month.
Constitution Observance programs again enjoyed increased attendance
this year, as there were a number of very fine programs held throughout
the State. Nevada.City had a large parade; in the Los Angeles area eighteen
Lodges sponsored for the tenth year a program to honor a great American
from the local area; San Diego sponsored a Citizen's Day where immigrants received their citizenship; twenty-four Lodges in the San Gabriel
Valley had a fine program; there were picnics, family nights and special
programs held with featured speakers such as judges, military generals,
State senators, assemblymen, county sheriffs, and city police chiefs. Mayors of many cities issued proclamations supporting the furtherance of Constitution Observance. Scottish Rite Valleys and the Shrine supported and
gave us special assistance which was greatly appreciated.
We acknowledge with gratitude the generous assistance rendered by the
Grand Lodge officers and the Grand Lodge office staff.

Again the Library and Museum Committee has the pleasure of submitting the following report for the year July 1, 1985 through June 30, 1986.
At the outset it must be remembered that the Library and Museum is not
only a keeper of artifacts and memorabilia of Freemasonry, but also has in
its keeping the philosophic and esoteric aspects of Freemasonry as represented by many books and symbols found in our Library.
We of the Committee, along with our volunteers, are continuing to carry
out the policies and procedures devised earlier. In June 1986 we received

a full time secretary-technician. We feel this is a step forward in making
our Library run as a business. The Chairman prepares the annual budget,
approves all expenditures and supervises the Library staff. Our volunteers
do an outstanding job in public relations . As a result we received, for the
second year, a donation from a British visitor.

Roumania, Sweden, Scotland and Turkey.

IMPLEMENTATION OF
MULTIPLE MEMBERS - SUSPENSION OR EXPULSION
(85-14)
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which "Carry-Over" Resolution
No. 85-14 has been referred, reports as follows:
The proponent of this Resolution seeks to provide that suspension or
expulsion in another Grand Jurisdiction of a Mason who holds dual membership in this Jurisdiction shall cause his suspension or expulsion in all
Lodges in this Jurisdiction in which he holds dual membership.
Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand

II

190

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Secretary to the constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of
the proponent.
Since this Resolution is a carry-over, a two-thirds affirmative vote is
required for adoption and no further motion for adoption is necessary.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponent of this Resolution seeks to provide that suspension or
expulsion in another Grand Jurisdiction of a Mason who holds dual membership in this Jurisdiction, shall cause his suspension or expulsion in all
Lodges in this Jurisdiction, in which he holds dual membership.
It is the policy of the Grand Lodge of California to recognize the authority of Grand Ldoges in certain other jurisdictions and to expect a reciprocal
policy of those Grand Lodges.
A Master Mason who holds dual membership in a Lodge of this Jurisdiction and a Lodge in another jurisdiction should be aware that he exposes
himself to the laws, rules and regulations of both jurisdictions.
Section 2032 of the C.M.C. restricts any member of this Jurisdiction
from holding Masonic intercourse with any other Mason who has been suspended or expelled.
This Resolution covers the suspension or expulsion of a member in two
categories, non-payment of dues, and other causes.
In the matter of non-payment of dues, Section 2402 of the California
Masonic Code provides that, "Suspension by a Lodge in the Jurisdiction
of this Grand Lodge for non-payment of dues of a multiple member shall
immediately and of itself, suspend his membership in all Lodges in this
Jurisdiction, and the Secretary of any Lodge suspending such a member
shall immediately notify the Grand Secretary and also every other Lodge in
which the multiple member holds membership:' Provision is also made for
notice of reinstatement, if such should occur, and for a sixty day prior
Notice of Intention to Suspend during which period such other Lodge may
contact the member in an effort to avoid such suspension.
Section 2402 does not provide for automatic suspension of a member of
a Lodge in this Jurisdiction if he is suspended for non-payment of dues in
another Grand Jurisdiction. The proponent intends to correct this by adding the following paragraph to Section 2402, Paragraph 6:
"Suspension by a Lodge in any other Grand Jurisdiction for nonpayment of dues shall forthwith suspend his membership in all
Lodges in this Jurisdiction but shall be handled in the same manner as provided above in this Section for members suspended by a
Lodge in this Jurisdiction by giving sixty days notice, and provided
further, that the restoration of such a member shall be in the same
manner as provided in this Code'.'
To deal with suspension or expulsion of a multiple member for other
than non-payment of dues, the proponent proposes to amend Section 2402,
Paragraph 10, to read as follows:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

191

"Suspension or expulsion by a Lodge in the Jurisdiction of this or
any other Grand Lodge, for other than non-payment of dues, of a
multiple member shall fo rwith suspend or expel his membership in
all Lodges in this Jurisdiction, ... "
The amended paragraph goes on to provide that proper notice be given
of such suspension or expulsion as well as in the case of restoration of
membership.
As presently written, Paragraph 10 provides that if a multiple member is
suspended or expelled by a Lodge in another Jurisdiction and notice
thereof is received by a Lodge in this Jurisdiction, the Master of such
Lodge shall cause such action to be taken by that Lodge or charges are to
be preferred against such multiple members as the facts shall require under
the Jaws of the Grand Lodge of California .
Adoption of this Resolution would eliminate the necessity for action by
a Lodge in this Jurisdiction other than the automatic suspension or expulsion of the member in accordance with the action taken by a Lodge in
another Jurisdiciton.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a " Yes"
vote.
Adopted.

LE PROGRES DE L'OCEANIE LODGE NO. 371 DEPARTURE FROM UNIFORM RITUAL
(85-19)
The Commiltee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which this " Carry-Over" Resolution No. 85-19 has been referred, submits the following special report :
At the Annual Communicaiton in I985, this Resolutio n received a
majority but less than the five-sixths vote required to amend Section 2688
of the California Masonic Code. As a result, pursuant to the provisio ns of
Section 4004, the Resolution was carried over to this year and may be
adopted in the event that a two-thirds favorable vote is received.
Under ordinary circumstances, your Committee on Jurisprudence does
not render a special report on carry-over legislation, for the matter would
have been properly before you in the preceding year. In this instance, ho wever, there a re special circumstances which mandate this special report.
You will recall that the proponents of this legislation seek to have certain
ritual of Le Progres de I.:Oceanie Lodge No. 371 approved as an exception
to Section 2688 of the California Masonic Code which requires that each
Degree conferred and all lectures in this Jurisdiction be in conformity with
the Ritual now or hereafter taught by the Grand Lecturer and recognized
by the Grand Lodge. T he fact is that this Grand Lodge in 1916 gave that
permission but seemingly due to some "confusion in the Temple" the
record of that permission in our Code has been lost along the way.

192

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The Proceedings of the Grand Lodge of California at its Annual Communication of 1916 reflect on page 156, the Report of the Committee on
Jurisprudence as follows:
"The Grand Master in his Address has submitted certain correspondence between the Grand Lecturer and the Inspector of the
64th Masonic District at Honolulu relative to a portion of the
Third Degree work as given by Oceanic Lodge No. 371 (now Le
Progres de L'Oceanie Lodge No. 371) at Honolulu. It appears that
a certain portion of that work, namely, the so-called "French"
work in the second section, differs in certain respects from our
regular ritual. This particular work, as we understand it, has been
followed in that Lodge ever since its institution, its original Charter having been granted over 65 years ago. The departures from
our prescribed ritualistic work, as we understand the matter, in no
way affects the substantial principles and teachings thought to be
inculcated by our Ritual. They are of the same character as the
departures that have at all times been tacitly allowed to our
French-speaking Lodges in San Francisco and Los Angeles. At the
same time we cannot question the view of the Grand Master that
these departures are violations of (former) Section 121 of our Constitution. However, we cannot feel that it is the disposition of the
Grand Lodge to actually prohibit the uniform practice in these
Lodges, a practice which has been acquiesced in and practically
approved during the whole history of this Grand Lodge. We do
think, however, that if the practice is to continue it should not be
in violation of our written Law. This Fraternity cannot with
decency or dignity occupy such a position.
"We would therefore recommend that Section 121 (now Section
2688) of the Constitution be amended by adding thereto a proviso
reading as follows:
' Provided, however, anything in this Section to the contrary notwithstanding, that the Lodges in this Jurisdiction whose long
established ritualistic work is in part a departure from the uniform
ritual of this Jurisdiction, may continue to perform such work as
the same is now being performed insofar as the same may not be
disapproved by the Grand Master and the Grand Lecturer. "
Se~tion 121 of the Constitution was thereupon amended as above by
unammous vote.
The then Section 121 became Section 247 of the old Ross Digest and the
language adopted in 1916 was continued as it was into Sections 554 of the
1956 Code.
Our research further discloses that from 1916 until the present C.M.C.
was adopted in 1975 by this Grand Lodge, a note was appended to the Section now in question designating Parfait Union No. 17, Vallee de France
No. 329 and Lodge le Progres de l'Oceanie No. 371 to be excepted Lodges.
This note confirmed that those Lodges were specifically allowed by this

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

193

Grand Lodge to confer Degrees and give lectures not necessarily in strict
conformity with the ritual taught by the Grand Lecturer.
For reasons unknown, Le Progres de L'Oceanie Lodge No . 371 was
dropped by the Code Commission in 1975 when it incorporated the language of this Section into a new Section numbered 2688. There is no legislative history for this omission. There is no reported action by the Grand
Lodge or decision of the Grand Master and Grand Lecturer disapproving
the ritual and it is reasonable to presume that the omission was in error.
Nevertheless, this Committee is charged by Section 1204 of the C.M.C.
to report to this Grand Lodge on the legal effect of proposed amendments.
That obligation has long been determined to require us to inform you of all
relevant facts necessary for you to vote intelligently. Consequently, we further report to you that we have reviewed 1959 correspondence between
then Grand Master, Phil N. Myers and Le Progres de I..:Oceanie Lodge No.
371 and find that both Grand Master Myers and Grand Master Leo E.
Anderson in 1958 concurred with then Grand Lecturer Elbert W. Davis in
disapproving portions of Le Progres' ritual. Both Grand Masters, according to the correspondence, entered into a conciliatory agreement with the
Lodge whereby certain parts of the non-conforming ritual were approved
while directing all other portions to conform to the ritual of the Grand
Lodge of California.
Le Progress at that time had a Resolution before the Grand Lodge seeking to have all of its non-conforming ritual approved such as it does now.
Concerning that, Grand Master Myers, in his letter of August 13, 1959 to
Le Progres Lodge said: "If the Lodge therefore, wishes to withdraw the
Resolution, this will mean merely conforming from now on to what was
agreed upon las1 year, and will enable the Inspector to certify your Officers. If, on the other hand, you do not wish to withdraw the Resolution
and desire the question to be decided on the floor of Grand Lodge, it must
be with the understanding that if the Resolution fails of adoption by the
necessary five-sixths vote the present Grand Master will withdraw all
approval for the second section of the third degree as now conferred in
your Lodge and thus properly leave the matter entirely to the discretion of
the incoming Grand Master and the Grand Lecturer without tying their
hands in any waY,'
The record reflects that although the Resolution was withdrawn, the
Lodge has failed or refused to conform to the direction of Grand Masters
Myers and Anderson.
Le Progres de I..:Oceanie Lodge No . 37 I by its Resolution now before
you is in the same position as it was in 1959 when Grand Master Myers
gave his warning. If this Grand Lodge does not by its two-thirds favorable
vote approve the ritual which was disapproved by Grand Masters Anderson and Myers and Grand Lecturer Davis and now by Grand Lecturer
Hammond, the approval or disapproval of its entire non-conforming ritual
shall be determined by subsequent Grand Masters and Grand Lecturers
acting together pursuant to Section 2688 of the California Masonic Code.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 85-19 is before you again for a number of reasons, not
the least of which was your response last year to an eloquent and emotional
appeal from the proponent of the Resolution. There is little doubt that in a
few minutes you will receive a similar appeal, and this is good, because that
is what makes our system work so well. It is the responsibility of this Commiteee, however, to persuade you to separate emotion from fact and view
the subject matter on its merit alone.
Despite the pronounciation of "Le Progres de l!Oceanie;• the Lodge
does not operate in the French language, but is an English-speaking-only
Lodge. No foreign languages are used. Thus, the proponent of the Resolution is asking that one English-speaking Lodge in this Jurisdiction be permitted to use a ritual in the Third Degree that is different from that now
taught by the Grand Lecturer to all of the other (some 600) English-speaking Lodges in the Jurisdiction.
Some of the supporting language to the Resolution is tenuous and misleading, if not erroneous. It is implied that this Grand Lodge has given
tacit approval for this variance in the ritual since 1905. On the contrary,
this Committee has written evidence that such permission was revoked in
1957-1958 and again in 1984. The correspondence confirming the revocation indicates that permission to continue using its variance in ritual
depended upon Lodge No. 371 complying with the restrictions contained
within the approval statement. Failing to comply, Lodge No. 371 nullified
the conditional approval. The power to revoke any implied use of variances in our ritual is granted to the Grand Master and Grand Lecturer as
stated in Section 2688 C.M.C ..
The Resolution is improvident in that it would create an ambiguity in
Section 2688 of the C.M.C .. Section 2688 states in part, "The officers of
an excepted Lodge, working in a foreign language under dispensation from
this Grand Lodge, may confer a degree or degrees in such foreign language
upon the candidate of another Lodge in such latter Lodge, when invited,
provided the candidate speaks, reads and understands such foreign language:' There are only three excepted Lodges listed in the C.M.C., but the
Resolution proposes to include the name and number of Lodge Le Progres
de l!Oceanie No. 371 among those exceptions. This would suggest to
future readers of the Code that Lodge No. 371 was a foreign-speaking
Lodge. It has been reported that Lodge No. 371 was deleted from the
excepted Lodges noted in Section 2688, by the Code Revision Commission,
in 1975. No other evidence appearing, we assume that the Commission
experiences the same revelation as have our members during the course of
study of this Resolution, to wit: That Lodge Le Progres de VOceanie is
NOT a foreign speaking Lodge, as is provided for in the Section. You see,
my Brethren, there is no comparison between Lodge Le Progres de
l!Oceanie and the excepted Lodges noted in Section 2688, and no comparisons should be drawn by this Grand Lodge.
The proponent speaks of their "cherished work" as a tradition of their

Lodge that has become a permanent possession of the Lodge. So, too, are
the traditions of this Grand Lodge a part of a rich and proud heritage, and
to be a part of it we must accept its "burdens and responsibilities as well as
its benefits and privileges:' The ritual of Freemasonry is a part of the Body
of Masonry and cannot, in any form whatever, be construed as the permanent possession of an individual Lodge.
It is doubtful that the proponent of the Resolution, or any member of
Lodge No. 371, can certify with any degree of certainty that their proposed
ritual has remained unchanged for the last 145 years, or even the last
twenty years for that matter. The integrity of the established ritual of this
Jurisdiction has been guarded, over the years, by a strict process of certification . How can we, as a Jurisdiction, vouch for the work of Lodge No.
371 if we have no one to teach the teacher?
Finally, my Brethren, you should put aside the geographic characteristics
of the area surrounding Lodge Le Progres de l!Oceanie. You should be as
subjective or objective in your deliberations as you would with a Lodge in
Torrance, in Grass Valley, or a Lodge contiguous to the service area of your
own Lodge. In recent years several ritualistic proposals have been presented to you. Some you have accepted, while others you have rejected;
however, in each instance the proposed ritual was either presented to or
exemplified for you. Can you adopt a ritual that you have never seen and
assume it to be the standard of this Grand Lodge?
Regardless of the arguments given in favor of Lodge No. 371 continuing
its ritualistic variance, it is the opinion of your Committee on Policy and
General Purposes that the Resolution does not conform to the policy of
this Grand Lodge.
We, therefore, \lrge a "No" vote on Carry-Over Resolution No. 85-19.
Not Adopted.

QUARTERLY GRAND LODGE COMMUNICATIONS
(86-3)
The proponents of this Resolution seek to add Section 151 to the California Masonic Code to provide for Grand Lodge to convene quarterly
each year in varying areas of the State.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the Grand Lodge is moving away from the concept of the
intimate involvement of the membership at the local level and Quarterly
Grand Lodge Communications in appropriate areas would bring Grand
Lodge closer to local Lodges and the general membership; and
WHEREAS, the Annual Communication meets to elect a Grand Master
Deputy Grand Master and Wardens; hear reports of the Committees of
Grand Lodge; and vote on Resolutions, all of which action necessitates the
delegation by the membership of its powers to the Master and Wardens
who represent the Lodge at such Annual Communications; and
WHEREAS, Grand Lodge could be linked to the general membership
through Quarterly Communications held in different areas so as to involve
as many Brethren as possible; and
WHEREAS, throughout California many initiates pass through the
degrees and, through lack of involvement, they then never return; and
WHEREAS, the success of any organization results largely from the
involvement of its members who must have a part both in setting the goals
for the organization and in the work necessary to attain those goals; and
WHEREAS, the greater the involvement by members at all levels, the
more successful the organization will become, and the strength of our
Grand Lodge is but the combined strength of its more that 600 Lodges;
and
WHEREAS, if it is our aim to keep Freemasonry strong, then our leaders must be able to tap the strength of the general membership to attain
this goal through Quarterly Communications of our Grand Lodge; and

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

199

WHEREAS, if Freemasonry is allowed to exist in two parts - a
"THEY" in the Grand Lodge who make all the decisions and a "WE" in
local Lodge rooms who do not venture beyond their confines - then the
real power of FREEMASONRY cannot be tapped or directed aright
because only when the Brethren become involved in the Masonic wo rk in
their Districts and Divisions and in the Quarterly Communications can we
achieve that strength needed for our Fraternity to survive and flourish; and
WHEREAS, these Quarterly Communications will serve to bring
together the diversity of talents needed - public relations, training,
finance, entertainment - to name the main ones; and
WHEREAS, the Brethren would bring more than themselves to meetings, bearing the special knowledge of their technical expertise translated
for application in or to the Masonic environment and thus the opportunity
for more Masons to be involved in ongoing affairs should help enthuse the
membership into working to attain the local determined objectives; and
WHEREAS, one session of each Quarterly Communication (two or
three hours) can be set aside for all current Lodge Masters and Wardens to
meet under the guidance of one or two Grand Lodge Officers to discuss
ideas - to talk about what was done in one Lodge and what others were
doing in their Lodges and thus Masters could obtain ideas which could
improve their Lodges and Wardens could plan their year ahead.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 151 be added to
the California Masonic Code to read as follows:
"Section 151. QUARTERLY COMMUNICATIONS. In addition to the
Annual Communications herein otherwise provided for, the Grand
Lodge ·shall hold Quarterly Communications in January, April and July
of each year in appropriate locations, consecutively, in the northern,
central and southern sections of California for the purpose of discussion
and the dissemination of information only. No other business shall be
conducted . The dates and locations of said Communications shall be
determined each year by majority vote taken at the next preceding
Annual or Special Communication . The provisions of this Code providing for a quorum shall not be applicable to Quarterly Communications'.'

"Section 158. BRETHREN WHO MAY ATTEND. Any Master Mason

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence to which Resolution No. 86-3 has
been referred, reports as follows:
. The pro~one~ts of the .~esolution seek to add Section 151 to the California Mas~mc. Cod~ requmng the .Grand Lodge to convene in Quarterly
Commumcauons m January, Apnl, and July of each year in addition to
the Annual Communication presently scheduled in October. The proponents further seek to amend Section 158 in order to authorize the attendance at the Quarterly Communications by Master Masons other than members of . thi.s Grand Lodge, as allowed for Annual or Special
Commumcat10ns.
Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand
Secretary to the constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of
the proponents.
As t~is Resol~tion .seeks to. amen~ the Constitution of the Grand Lodge,
a five-sixths affnmat1ve vote 1s required for adoption.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of
the Resolution.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 86-3 proposes to add Section 151 to the California
Masonic Code to provide for Grand Lodge to convene quarterly each year
in varying areas of the state. In addition to our Annual Communication in
October, additional Communications would be held in January, April and
July of each year alternating between the northern, central and southern
sections of California. The apparent purpose of these additional meetings
would be greater membership accessibility to the Grand Lodge by holding
Grand Lodge sessions throughout the state. It is suggested that a portion of
these quarterly communications be devoted to Masonic education.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes that there are
at present ample opportunities for the membership to attend Grand Lodge
Communications. Generally, there is a ceremonial communication of the
Grand Lodge each time a cornerstone is laid, a Lodge mortgage is burned,
a Lodge Hall is dedicated or a Masonic Lodge is instituted or constituted.
With few exceptions, the Grand Lodge is opened in the same form as it was
here Monday morning. In the 1984-1985 Masonic year, there were nineteen
such Ceremonial Communications, nine held in the northern portion of the
state, three held in the central portion of the state and seven held in the
southern portion of the state. These ceremonial communications give the
Brethren ample opportunities to attend a Grand Lodge session.
With respect to Masonic education, the Grand Lodge at present has a
fine Masonic education program for the Officers and members of the constituent Lodges conducted by the Masonic Leadership Workshop Committee. This Committee conducts about a dozen all-day workshops each year,
located throughout the state. At these workshops, numerous interesting
programs on Masonic education, Masonic law, Fraternal relations and

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

201

other important items of interest to a Master Mason are discussed in depth.
y0 ur committee does not believe that Quarterly Communications of the
Grand Lodge could improve upon this fine program presently being conducted by the Masonic Leadership Workshop Committee .
Although the cost has not been computed, based upon the present
expenses of the Grand Lodge Annual Communication, and expenses
incurred in connection with ceremonial communications, these additional
three quarterly communications could add as much as fifty cents a year to
the per capita tax. Your Committee does not believe that this additional
burden on the constituent Lodges is justified by what at best would be only
a modest increase in the visibility of the Grand Lodge or in the dissemination of Masonic education.
The proponents of the Resolution seek to foster membership enthusiasm, a goal which we applaud. We note that Section 152 of our Code
already gives the Grand Master the right to call special Grand Lodge Communications at any time or place in his sole and absolute discretion. To
accomplish the proponents' intent, perhaps a Grand Lodge Special Communication could be held in conjunction with a Masonic Leadership Workshop with only a modest increase in cost. We would encourage the Grand
Lodge Elective Line to review this possibility. However, we do not believe
that quarterly Communications should be mandated in addition to our
existing programs. Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes therefore recommends a "No" vote.

The Committee on Finance:
The Grand Lo<;tge Committee on Finance believes that the increased
costs for renting adequate space and travel costs for the Grand Lodge Officers and attendant paraphernalia for the three quarterly Communications
will be an additional burden on the per capita tax assessed to the constituent Lodges, at a time when we are recommending fiscal restraint in the
areas of Grand Lodge Officer travel and Grand Lodge Communication
expenses. As an example, if the cost were no more than $30,000 for each
additional Communication, the annual per capita tax would increase by
$.55. The costs of the quarterly Communications would not materially
reduce the cost of holding the Annual Communication in San Francisco in
October.
We recommend a "No" vote.
Not Adopted.

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence and Policy and General Purposes.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence to which Resolution 86-4 has been
submitted, reports as follows:
The proponents of the Resolution seek to stimulate the Secretaries of the
respective Lodges to attend the balance of the Annual Communication
after the conclusion of the Secretaries' session by giving one vote to each
Secretary. It is the hope of the proponents that this vote will stimulate their
desire to stay and participate.
To achieve the• proposed change, four Code sections will need to be
amended including those specifying the members of Grand Lodge: who the
representatives of the constituent Lodges are; who may vote at Grand
Lodge; and the section on cumulative voting.
Secretaries who are Past Masters and elect to vote the Secretary's vote
may not cast the vote afforded to Past Masters of the Lodge.
Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand
Secretary to the constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of
the proponents.
This Resolution seeks to amend the Constitution and a five-sixths
affirmative vote for adoption is required.
To place the matter before Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.
TIJe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to provide that the Secretary of
each Lodge shall have a vote in Grand Lodge, the same as is presently provided in the California Masonic Code for the Master and the Senior and
Junior Wardens of each Lodge.
However, no compelling reason is advanced as to why Secretaries of

204

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Lodges now should have a vote in Grand Lodge. Secretaries are not
required to attend Grand Lodge; although, like any Master Mason who is a
member of a constituent Lodge in this Jurisdiction, they may attend the
Annual or a Special Communication of Grand Lodge.
If a vote in Grand Lodge should be granted to each Lodge Secretary,
then why not, also, to each Lodge Treasurer, who ranks above the Secretary in the order of protocol. We believe that a Lodge is presently sufficiently well represented with voting privileges in Grand Lodge by the Master and Wardens having that right, together with all of the Lodge's Past
Masters having the same right as a single unit.
The proposed Resolution would make Secretaries members of Grand
Lodge when they have not been required to be proficient in our ritual. The
Secretary is elected for a different purpose than the Master and Wardens of
a Lodge. A Lodge Secretary is not required to have been the Master of a
Masonic Lodge, and often the Secretary is not a Past Master. Also, the
average Lodge Secretary serves in office for several years. Many Lodge
Secretaries serve as such for a great many years . Secretaries of Lodges do
meet together periodically, and many carry out their duties in an exemplary
manner.
However, we do not believe that it is advantageous to Freemasonry to
make them members of Grand Lodge and give them a vote therein solely
because of their Office as Secretary.
This proposed Resolution would amend the Constitution and therefore
requires a five-sixths affirmative vote for passage.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, therefore, recommends a "No" vote on this Resolution.
Not Adopted.

Referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes and Foundation Board.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:

Yo~r Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Resolution 86-6 has been
submitted, reports as follows:
. The proponents of the Resolution seek to limit the number of consecut~ve three year ter!11s to which a Trustee of the California Masonic Foundation may be appornted.
Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand
Secretary to the Constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of
the proponents.
. This Resolution seeks to amend an Ordinance and a five-sixths affirmative vote for adoption is required.
To pl~ce the matter before Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The ~alifornia Masonic Code provides for the Trustees of the California
Masonic Foundation to be fifteen in number and appointed by the Grand

207

Master (except for the Deputy Grand Master) to terms of three years
(C.M.C. 1602). This Resolution seeks to limit the service as a Trustee by
any one individual to three consecutive terms, or nine years.
We believe no one would argue the fact that in any organization or
capacity there must be some balance between experience and new ideas, or
with the fact that there comes a time in any service when the incumbent has
outserved his maximum contribution.
We all know of instances in which probably even the incumbent realized
he had served beyond his maximum usefulness, but pride and ego made his
replacement difficult without creating hard feelings and/ or controversy. It
would seem a firm limit on such service would give both the Grand Master
and the incumbent a face-saving way of making needed changes.
The Code and practice of this Grand Lodge has long recognized these
facts. The California Masonic Code allows ten years as the maximum tenure for Committee Chairman (C.M.C. 1201). There is an informal understanding that Inspectors shall serve no more than ten years . Trustees of the
Masonic Homes of California are limited in their service to three consecutive three-year terms (C.M.C. 1302).
The Special Commission to study the "Organization and Structure of the
Grand Lodge" recommended in 1980 that the service on any Committee or
Board in our Grand Lodge be limited to nine consecutive years. The Resolution resulting from that recommendation eventually failed to pass Grand
Lodge due to the strong objection of the Ritual Committee, which felt such
a limitation placed on the tenure of Inspectors would make it difficult to
keep Inspectoral posts filled with qualified, competent people in outlying,
sparsely populated areas. However, no such feelings or objections were
expressed regardipg such a limitation on service in other appointments . It
was the recommendation of this Committee then that the Resolution
should be adopted.
We believe this Resolution provides for that reasonable balance between
experience and new ideas and would serve to place service as Trustee of the
California Masonic Foundation under the same limitation as the limitation
on the service as Trustee of the California Masonic Homes, the other similar organization in the structure of our Grand Lodge.
It is interesting to note this Resolution is proposed by an individual who
has personal experience within the organization effected. He is the current
President of the Trustees. He presumably offers this limiting Resolution,
not from a position of inexperience, but rather from one of experience in
service as a Trustee.
Your Comittee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes"
vote.

The California Masonic Foundalion Board of Trustees:
Your Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Foundation concur in
the recommendation of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes
and recommends a "Yes" vote.
Adopted.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

209

of the California Masonic Code which presently reads, "The Flag of our
Country shall be displayed at all meetings of Lodges and carried on all ceremonial occasions except at funerals:• be amended by inserting the words
"and honored by the Pledge of Allegiance:• This portion of Section 2060 of
the C.M.C. would then read as follows:
"The Flag of our Country shall be displayed, and honored by the Pledge
of Allegiance, at all meetings of Lodges and carried in all ceremonial
occasions except at funerals~·
The substance of this Resolution has been presented in various forms
through the years. Your Committee is very cognizant and proud of our
Masonic heritage and believes that every effort should be made to so honor
our Flag at all of our meetings. We do not, however, see the need for this
legislation.
We display our Flag at all meetings and it is formally presented at the
Annual Election of Officers, or at any other meeting the Master so desires.
There is also nothing in our Code which prevents the Master of a Lodge
from asking the Brethren to join in the Pledge of Allegiance at any meeting, and your Committee, indeed, encourages such action.
However, we also feel that without compelling reasons, the Grand Lodge
should not force Lodges to do those things they are permitted to do of
their own volition.
With this in mind your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

The Ritual Committee heartily concurs with the patriotic intent of this
Resolution. Aside 'rrom the specified meetings when the Pledge is required,
the Master may, at his option, call for the Pledge at any meeting.
All Masons are, or should be, patriotic. It is an honor for a citizen to
pledge to his flag and should be done voluntarily. Our Country does not
require its citizens to salute or pledge to the flag. Likewise, we feel, to legislate patriotism is inappropriate and should not be mandatory.
The Committee on Ritual recommends a "No" vote.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

WHEREAS, C.M.C. 2104 provides that Lodges consolidating can bear
the name and number of one of the Lodges composing the consolidation
or the consolidated Lodge may retain the name of one Lodge and the num:
ber of another; and
WHEREAS, the Grand Lodge has ratified the Grand Masters' approvals
of consolidated Lodges with combined, hyphenated and new names for
many years as evidenced by the Grand Lodge Roster; and
WHEREAS, the approvals of consolidated Lodges with combined,
hyphenated and new names, are not presently provided for in the California Masonic Code.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the third paragraph of
Section 2104 be amended to read:
"The Lodge thus formed may bear the name and number of one of the
Lodges composing it, in which event it may retain the Charter and Seal
of that Lodge. However, it may bear the name of one and the number of
another of such Lodges; or it may bear a combination of the names of
the Lodges and the number of one of the Lodges; or it may bear an
entirely new name and the number of one of the Lodges; in which event
it shaII then receive a new Charter without charge, or it may have an
endorsement of the authorization of such consolidation by the Grand
Lodge made upon the Charter of one of the component Lodges. In the
event that the name or number of the Lodge is changed, the Lodge shall
obtain a new Seal:'

The proponent of the Resolution seeks the approval for greater flexibility in the selection of the name of a Lodge formed by the consolidation of
Lodges. Specifically, such a Lodge would be able to select a name that was
a combination of the names (hyphenated or non-hyphenated) of the consolidating Lodges or it might select a new name, not related to any of the
consolidating Lodges.
Currently, the California Masonic Code limits the selection of the name
of a consolidated Lodge to the name of one of the Lodges composing it
(C.M.C. 2104).
Essentially, this Resolution merely seeks to provide in the Code for a
practice which has long been allowed and approved by the Grand Lodge.
A study of the history of consolidated Lodges in this Grand Jurisdiction
reveals:
a. Consolidating Lodges as early as 1961, and as late as 1985, have
adopted a name for the Lodge thus formed which was in some manner a combination of the names of the consolidating Lodges some 62
times.
b. Consolidating Lodges as early as 189 l, and as late as 1985, have
adopted a name for the Lodge thus formed which was an entirely new
name, not related to the names of any of the Lodges forming it some
14 times.
We see no reason why Lodges should not be permitted to continue a
practice so long ago established and so frequently used, and, thus permitted, why our Code should not provide for same.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes"
vote.
•
Adopted.

Respectfully submitted,
VARNUM PAUL, PM No. 169

AVOUCHEMEN T
(86-12)
The proponents of this Resolution seek to have the California Masonic
Code changed so that a Master Mason can vouch for a Brother if they have
sat in a School of Instruction together.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A . M. of California:
WHEREAS, all Lodge Officers are required to attend District Officers'
Association Schools of Instruction; and
WHEREAS, the Master vouches to the Inspector that all his members in
attendance at the School of Instruction are Master Masons; and
WHEREAS, all work and business within a School of Instruction is conducted while said school is tiled; and
WHEREAS, members of different Lodges meeting in these tiled Schools
of Instruction would know all those in attendance to be Master Masons.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 2418 of the California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
"To vouch for a visiting Brother, a Master Mason must have sat with
him in open Lodge, in a School of Instruction or examined him under
proper authority, or, in case a member of one Lodge has sat in open
Lodge with a visiting Brother, such Brother so sitting, can vouch for
such visiting Brother to a member of any other Lodge, all three being
present, and such Brother to whom such avouchment is made, can then
vouch for such visiting Brother to the Master of his Lodge:•
Respectfully submitted,

Secretary to the constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of

This Resolution seeks to amend the Ordinances of Grand Lodge and a
five-sixths (5/6) affirmative vote for adoption is required.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 86-12 proposes to amend the California Masonic Code
to allow avouchment for a visiting Master Mason by a Brother if they have
sat in a School of Instruction together.
Inspectors are required to provide Schools of Instruction for the officers
of the Lodges in a District Officers Association. The Master is required to
vouch to the Inspector that all his members in attendance are members in
good standing. The Schools of Instruction are tiled meetings where all in
attendance are required to be Master Masons in good standing. Thus
attendees at said Schools of Instruction would know all others to be Master
Masons.
The proponents propose to amend Section 2418 of the California
Masonic Code to read as follows:
"To vouch for a visiting Brother a Master Mason must have sat with him
in open Lodge, in a School of Instruction or examined him under proper
authority, or, in case a member of one Lodge has sat in open Lodge with
a visiting Brother, such Brother, so sitting, can vouch for such visiting
Brother to a member of any other Lodge, all three being present, and
such Brother to whom such avouchment is made, can then vouch for
such visiting Brother to the Master of his Lodge:•
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes"
vote.
The Committee on Ritual:
This Committee believes that it is common practice to vouch for any
Mason with whom you have conducted Fraternal Intercourse. All admissions to Schools of Instruction are by avouchment only. It is unnecessary to
spell out all what-ifs in our Code. A change in this Section is not necessary.
We recommend a "No" vote.
Failing the required five-sixths affirmative vote for adoption, but receiving a majority affirmative vote, the Resolution will be held over until the
1987 Annual Communication.

MODERNIZING PHYSICAL REQUIREMENT S
(86-13)
The proponent of this Resolution seeks to have Section 2600 of the California Masonic Code amended to delete from the physical requirements
thereunder the words, "nor eunuch:'

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A . M . of California:
WHEREAS, it appears that Section 2600 of the California Masonic
Code was originally composed to state, briefly, the required moral and
physical qualifications necessary for an applicant for the degrees of
Masonry; and
WHEREAS, it is further acknowledged that this action was undertaken
with the desire to embody the intent of the "old charges;" and
WHEREAS, historically, the reference to a eunuch was never a part of
any known Ancient Landmark or Constitution before the year 1738 when
Dr. Anderson, in his writings, added the words "nor eunuch" to the
English Constitution "for no apparent reason" or "by any known authority" at the time (reference Coils Masonic Encyclopedia, Page 493-4~; and
WHEREAS, in this day and age people generally are more enlightened
and more prone to question; and
WHEREAS, today we are encouraging Masons to open up and talk
more about Masonry; and
WHEREAS, it becomes more and more difficult and embarrassing for
Masons to defend the exclusion of an unfortunate individual, who might
also be a good al)d qualified man, to become a Mason because of a vague
law which became part of our California Masonic Code; and
WHEREAS, there are an increasing number of men who, for medical
reasons, have undergone castration (cancer being one of the reasons); and
WHEREAS, a castrated man is defined in dictionaries as a eunuch; and
WHEREAS, Section 2600 of the California Masonic Code does literally
exclude a eunuch from becoming a Mason; and
WHEREAS, the context in which the words "nor eunuch" are used, following the word "no woman;• tends to classify such person as womanish
and not a man, categorically denying him the opportunity to become a
Mason; and
WHEREAS, there seems no logical reason to retain these words in our
physical requirements .
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 2600 of the California Masonic Code be amended by deleting the words, "nor eunuch" so
that said Section would thus read:
"Section 2600. MORAL AND PHYSICAL QUALIFICATIONS . An
applicant for the degrees of Masonry must be a man; no woman; free
born, being neither a slave nor the son of a bond woman; a believer in
God and a future existence; of moral conduct; capable of reading and
writing; having no maim or defect in his body which cannot be and is

218

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

not corrected by a prosthesis or other artificial substitute for the maim
or defect, such as an artificial leg which will render him capable of
learning the art and thus physically able to conform substantially to
what the several degrees respectively require of him:'
Respectfully submitted,
WILLIAM B. BOONE, SR., PM No. 209
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence and Policy and General Purposes.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Comittee on Jurisprudence to which Resolution No. 86-13 has been
submitted, reports as follows:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to have Section 2600 of the California Masonic Code amended to delete from the physical requirements
thereunder the words, "nor eunuch:'
Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand

This Resolution seeks to amend an Ordinance and a five-sixths (5/6)
affirmative vote for adoption is required.
To place the matter before Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponent of this Resolution seeks to have Section 2600 of the California Masonic Code amended so as to delete from the physical requirements listed therein the words, "nor eunuch:'
Section 2600 of the Masonic Code sets forth the physical requirements
which an Applicant for the Degrees of Freemasonry must possess, one of
which is that he not be eunuch. The dictionary defines a eunuch as a castrated man.
In former and ancient times this limitation was valid and reasonable.
However, in this day and age of modern medicine with its many life saving
operations now being performed, it sometimes becomes necessary, such as
where the area of the body involved is cancerous, to remove a man's testicles in order to save his life, or to slow down the spread of that dread disease. The loss of a man's testicles, however, is in no way a maim or defect
in his body which renders the Applicant for the Degrees of Freemasonry
incapable of learning the art or physically unable to conform to what the
several degrees respectively require of him.
Therefore, we believe that the words "nor eunuch" should be. removed
from Section 2600 of the California Masonic Code, and your Committee
on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote on this Resolution.
Adopted.

USE OF HOLY WRITINGS IN LIEU OF HOLY BIBLE
(86-14)
The proponents of this Resolution seek to replace the words, "Holy
Bible" with the words, "Holy Writings" in degree ritual only and to use the
Holy Writings of a candidate's faith for obligation if he requests such use.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, members of the Fraternity reside in virtually every country
in the world; and
WHEREAS, many of the members of the Fraternity are members of and
practice a variety of religions because "The Kingdom of Heaven is made o f
many Houses;" and
WHEREAS, Section 2600 of the California Masonic Code requires o f an
applicant for the degrees of Masonry to be "a believer in God and a fu t ure
existence;' and our ritual requires such a belief, and Annotation 2600b
states that such a belief is "an indispensable requirement;" and
WHEREAS, non-Christian candidates are required to obligate on the
Christian Holy Bible which is not a part of their religion.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Committee on Ritual
be directed to make word changes in our Masonic degree ritual from "Holy
Bible" to "Holy Writings;" and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that new Section 2689 be added to the
California Masonic Code as follows:
"Section 2689 . USE OF HOLY WRITINGS. A candidate for the
degrees of Masonry may select the Holy Writings of any recognized religion of his choice upon which to be obligated, provided it is a sufficient
size to conform to the requirement of the ritual and is not placed upon
the regular Lodge Bible but is substituted for that Bible during the entire
meeting.
"During Stated Meetings, other special meetings, and installation of
officers the Holy Bible shall be the only Holy Writing to be used:'
Respectfully submitted,

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 86-14 seeks to have the Ritual Committee of this Grand
Lodge make the word changes in our ritual which refer to "Holy Bible" to
"Holy Writings", and it also proposes to add a new section to the California Masonic Code as follows:
"Section 2689. USE OF HOLY WRITINGS. A candidate for the
degrees of Masonry may select the Holy Writings of any recognized religion of his choice upon which to be obligated, provided it is a sufficient
size to conform to the requirement of the ritual and is not placed upon
the regular Lodge Bible but is substituted for that Bible during the entire
meeting.
"During Stated Meetings, other special meetings, and installation of
officers the Holy Bible shall be the only Holy Writing to be used'.'
A similar Resolution was presented in 1984 and in referring back to the
report of this Committee at that time it is noted that extensive research has
been made with regard to this issue. We note that this is the fourth time in
the last nine years that this issue has appeared before this Grand Lodge.
We again point to the report of a Special Committee appointed by Grand
Master John Roberts, in 1976, to investigate and determine the consequences involved in making such changes. That Committee sought advice
from former Grand Chaplains and recognized authorities in the field of
Theology. The Committee reported that besides the substantial changes in
our ritual which would result, this could also lead to requirements that our
Lodges have available a myriad of "Holy Writings" for candidates of different faiths.
This report concluded that "the problems which would be encountered
would far outweigh any possible advantage to the Craft or any individual:'
It ~ecommended that the "Holy Bible continue to be the only book upon
which all candidates are obligated" and that the recommendation be made
bearing fully in mind that the use of the Holy Bible in our degrees does not
imply that "Freemasonry is limited to a Christian belief:•
This recommendation was adopted by this august body at our 1977
Communication.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

221

This position was reaffirmed by this Committee in 1984 in its report to
Grand Lodge, stating "our ritual clearly does not intend the use of the
Holy Bible to demand or even suggest that a candidate compromise his
own religious beliefs" and concluded that the use of the Holy Bible was
absolutely necessary to preserve the unanimity which now exists in our
Lodges.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes hereby reaffirms this
position and recommends a "No" vote.

The Committee on Ritual:
At the Annual Communication cf 1976 this Grand Lodge adopted the
Recommendation of John F. Roberts, Jr. to form a Committee consisting
of the Policy and General Purposes, Jurisprudence and Ritual Committees. The sole purpose of this Committee was to determine what changes
would be required to permit an obligation to be taken on Holy Writings
other than the Holy Bible.
That Committee reported as follows: "In making this study many factors were considered by the Committee, each having a strong bearing upon
the subject. The most important of these considerations, however, is the
great number of changes in our law and ritual, and additional problems for
Lodges which would result from the substitution of another book for the
Holy Bible.
"Because of the complex nature of the study, the Committee deemed it
advisable and necessary to seek additional advice of those more expert in
the field of Theology and Holy Writings . Opinions were therefore solicited
from Brothers Roland A. Bach and Rabbi Edgar Magnin, both former
Grand Chaplains- and recognized authorities in the field of Theology.
"Both of these former Grand Chaplains stated that in their opinion, the
practice of substituting other books for the Holy Bib~e in obl.igati.ng ~ C~n­
didate could lead to a myriad of problems. Both advised against mst1tutmg
such a practice. To substitute another book for the Holy Bible in our
degrees would require substantive changes in our law to permit the necessary revisions to the adopted California ritual. It could also lead to requirements that Lodges have available, not only the Koran, but the Pentateush,
the Veda, the Old Testament without the New Testament, and a myriad of
other Holy Writings. A change such as this could well lead to further, undesirable changes in our present system of ritual. The problems which would
be encountered would far outweigh any possible advantage to the Craft, or
to any individual'.'
It was the recommendation of that Committee that the Holy Bible continue to be the only book upon which all Candidates are obligated, bearing
fully in mind that the use of the Holy Bible in our degrees does not in any
way imply that Freemasonry is limited to a Christian belief. The findings
of that Committee as reported here in 1977 are as valid today as then.
Your Committee on Ritual respectfully recommends a "No" vote.
Not Adopted.

REMISSION OF DUES FOR
GOLDEN VETERAN RECIPIENT
(86-15)
The proponent of this Resolution seeks to relieve fifty year members of
the necessity of paying dues.

To the Most Worship/ul Grand Lodge, F. & A . M. of California:
WHEREAS, any Master Mason should be entitled to free membership
after fifty years as a member in good standing of any Lodge; and
WHEREAS, they are entitled to this honor for the many years of service
and membership in our Lodge; and
WHEREAS, there are only three members in our Lodge who would be
eligible for this honor and this would not be a hardship on any Lodge; and
WHEREAS, if a fifty year member does not want to accept the free
membership he can donate the money to any of our Masonic Charities.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 2804 of the California Masonic Code be amended by adding the following sentence at the
end:
"A member receiving from this Grand Lodge a Golden Veteran Award
shall thereafter be deemed a life member of his Lodge, and forever
exempt from the payments of dues therein, which dues shall be deemed
remitted; but such member shall have no interest in the life membership
fund of such Lodge:'
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Annotation 2810a be deleted.
Respectfully submitted,
ELLIS E. SAXTON, PM No. 460

Referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes, and Finance.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Resolution No. 86-15 has
been submitted, reports as follows:
The proponent of this Resolution seeks to relieve fifty year members of
the necessity of paying dues.
Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand
Secretary to the constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of
the proponent.
This Resolution seeks to amend an Ordinance and a five-sixths affirmative vote for adoption is required.
To place the matter before Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

223

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 86-15 proposes to amend Section 2804 of the California
Masonic Code to remit the dues automatically of all recipients of the
Golden Veterans Award. Resolutions similar to this have been presented in
1969, 1973, 1975, and 1984. Your Committee believes that this Resolution
should be rejected for like reasons as before. It is the privilege and duty of
every Master Mason to help meet the costs of Masonry in general and his
Lodge in particular when he has been given the means to do so by the
Great Architect of the Universe. Every Mason should pay his fair share.
This Grand Lodge has consistently rejected proposals which would create distinctions among Masons. For example, we have rejected proposals
to lower the age of admission for members of the Order of DeMolay. We
should not now create two classes of membership, one for those required
to pay dues and one for fifty-year members not required to pay dues.
Finally, your Committee believes that this Resolution, if adopted, could
have a devastating effect on the financial stability of a number of our
Lodges which have many fifty-year members. Often, these are Lodges with
a declining membership which do not have the revenue base of newer
Lodges with younger members. How would these Lodges compensate for a
precipitous drop in dues income?
We are proud of our Golden Veterans Award recipients. We honor them
with recognition at many Masonic functions, a pin of gold and an impressive ceremony to present that pin. If that Brother is in need, his dues may
be remitted by the Lodge as it may do for a needy Brother who is not a
fifty year Mason. We should remit a member's dues as an act of Masonic
charity rather than as a mark of distinction.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes therefore recommends
a "No" vote.

The Committee on Finance:
The authors of the Resolution have proposed that dues for fifty year
members be remitted. This will reduce the number of members over which
the annual Grand Lodge budget will be spread in the form of per capita
tax.
The financial effect of this Resolution is not known as the Finance Committee is not aware of the number of active fi fty year members on our
rolls. The total number of Golden Veteran awards issued by this Jurisdiction is about 34,000 to date with about 550 awards issued per year. As a
result of the ever increasing per capita tax, the Finance Committee feels we
should not approve actions which would unnecessarily increase this tax and
thereby place an even heavier burden on the constituent Lodges of this
Jurisdiction .
Therefore, the Finance Committee recommends a "No" vote.
Not Adopted.
