RESOLUTION WITHDRAWN

During 1987, a new anniversary brochure will be mailed to all Lodges in
the Fifth Masonic District , inviting them to visit the Temple or plan a meeting night. We are pleased to report that Loyalty Lodge No. 529 has again
made the first reservation for use of the Temple on January 22, 1987. This
is the fourth successive year that Loyalty has requested a meeting night at
the Old Temple.
In the near future, a metal plate will be affixed in the interior of the Temple designating it as State Historical Monument No. 23.
Nine Lodges rented the Temple for degrees during the past year, and two
Youth Organizations reserved the Hall for Saturday morning meetings.
The Los Angeles Recreation and Parks Department, overseeing the
Pueblo area where the Old Temple is located, notified Temple authorities of
an overall renewal program for the $15 million rehabilitation and conversion of the 1880 Pico-Garnier block into a restaurant and shopping complex.
Reservations for use of the Old Temple can be made by contacting the
Custodian, Worshipful Oliver Celaya, at (213) 626- 4933 or (818) 912-0444.
The Temple is open to visitors on Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday from 10:00 A.M. to 3:00 P.M . . Masonic Lodges pay $45.00 rental fee
per night. Youth groups are charged $25.00 for Saturday morning dates.
We have one permanent tenant, Plaza de Los Angeles Lodge No. 814,
which meets every Thursday evening.
We look forward to a great 25th anniversary year during 1986-1987. It is
hoped some type of a Grand Lodge affair could be held at the first Temple
in Los Angeles.

The following Resolutions which had been submitted, titled, numbered
and printed for distribution for consideration at the 1986 Annual Com.
munication were withdrawn by the proponents.
No. 86-2) Professional In-Depth Study.
No. 86-7) Advertising and Sale of Tickets to the Public for Lodge
Events.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
OLD MASONIC HALL AT LOS ANGELES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Silver Anniversary of the rededication of the Old Masonic Hall at
Los Angeles - birthplace of Masonry in Southern California - will occur
during 1987.
A series of City and County programs, involving Lodge visitations to the
historic buidling, are planned by the Committee.
Originally erected in 1858 as the fourth commercial building in Los
Angeles, the site at 416-1 / 2 North Main Street, served as the first Masonic
home of Los Angeles Lodge No. 42 until 1884.
Work by artisans of the State Division of Architecture refurbished the
Old Temple as near like the original as possible to make. Restoration
started in September, 1959 and was finished in early 1962. Grand Lodge,
under the direction of former Grand Master Guy B. Mize, conducted the
symbolic cornerstone laying and rededication on Saturday, August 23,
1962. Worshipful Edward A. Fromsky, Master that year, participated in the
ceremonies. He will again play an important role in the 1987 programs.
There were 1,480 visitors from many states and several foreign countries
who visited the historic Temple in downtown Los Angeles.
This year, several improvements were installed, notably a complete
rewiring of the electrical system. We also reupholstered three of our most
precious possessions in the 24 feet by 36 feet Lodge room - the magnificently fluted Master and Wardens chairs, which were rescued from the Chicago fire of 1871, and shipped around the Cape of Good Hope to San
Francisco.
While cleaning out a closed area, blocked by a fallen timber, we discovered a cache of fraternal records of the Lodge for 1870 to 1882. These will
be cleaned and be exhibited in one of the two illuminated show cases in the
foyer.
Several new gifts to the Temple were received during the year - Past
Master Edward A. Fromsky (1962) presented three framed exhibits of
priceless photographs of the rebuilding and rededication, and Lodge No.
42 presented a graphically designed montage showing the formation of 28
Lodges, attributed to Brethren from the Lodge .

Respectfully submitted,
MORRIS C. Guss. Chairman

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CEMETERIES

MICHIGAN BLUFF CEMETERY

Here we are fortunate to have Brother Carl L. Shearer overseeing this

232

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
COLUMBIA CEMETERY

Two Brothers and I from Ophir Lodge No. 33 cleaned up the weeds and
trimmed the bushes. The picket fence needed two slats repaired. This was
also done. The cemetery seems to be in good condition.
JAMESTOWN CEMETERY

Toulumne Lodge No. 8 in Sonora had Jamestown Cemetery cleaned of
weeds. This was done under the direction of the Worshipful Master,
Clifford E. Walty. I also took a trip to look at the cemetery. I had received
word from the Worshipful William Armstrong, P.M ., Inspector of the
404th District, that some complaints had been expressed about that same
site. I understand that the Grand Master directed Brother William
Armstrong to erect a chain link fence around the cemetery. This will be
expensive. I have the dimensions of the property, which is 500 feet around.
At about $15.00 per running foot, the cost is approximately $8,800.00. In
my opinion, if the old historical front is taken down, we will have more
trouble with the people in the area. My suggestion is that we repair the few
missing posts on the fence. It is a split cedar post and rail fence.
It has been a pleasure for me to have served on this Committee as chairman for the past two years. I am now a Committee member for the Cemeteries of the Grand Lodge.
Respectfully submitted,
LESTER L. SHAW, JR., Chairman

MORNING SESSION - WEDNESDAY, OCTOBER 15, 1986
At 8:45 A.M. the members of Grand Lodge, their wives, families and
friends assembled in the Masonic Auditorium to honor the various Adult
and Youth Leaders of the Concordant and Appendant Bodies of Masonry.
Severino Malajito, Senior Warden of Hawaiian Lodge No. 21, raised this
Session using the gavel presented to the Grand Master on the occasion of a
Third Degree conferred in Honolulu in which he participated.
The Very Reverend G. Maurice Ottsen offered the Morning Prayer, following which all present joined in the singing of our National Anthem.
The Grand Master requested the Grand Marshal to retire and escort into
Grand Lodge the dignitaries representing the Concordant and Appendant
Bodies of Masonry in California. Each was individually introduced by the
Grand Marshal and cordially welcomed by the Grand Master and then
escorted to seats provided for them.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

233

The Grand Marshal once again retired and escorted into Grand Lodge
the Youth Leaders of our Youth Groups . Seven of these lovely young people were placed West of the altar, individually introduced and individually
welcomed by Grand Master Driskell. They were then invited to take seats
in the East.
Each of the seven Youth Group representatives addressed those present,
bringing warm greetings from their respective organizations and thanking
the Masonic Fraternity for its support and their hope for its continued support. At the conclusion of their respective remarks, those present accorded
them a standing ovation . On behalf of the Masonic Foundation, Grand
Master Driskell presented to each group a check indicating this continued
support.
John Hink and Randy Shaffer, members of the DeMolay, offered the
DeMolay Ceremony of Lights and the beautiful Flower Talk, respectively.
A prolonged standing ovation was given to each of these young men.
A history of the American Flag was then presented by representatives of
Job's Daughters, with Miss Sharon Blackwell acting as the narrator.
A beautiful rendition of the Rose Lecture was then presented by Miss
Debbie Davis and Miss Karen Samora, members of the Rainbow for Girls.
As each presentation was concluded, these young people received a standing ovation.
All in attendance were cordially invited to remain to listen to the Grand
Oration delivered by Grand Orator, Ronald A. Sherod.

"MASONS.HAVE AN IMPORTANT STORY TO TELL"
R ONALD A. SHEROD , Grand Orator
Most Worshipful Grand Master and My Brethren of this Grand Lodge:

During the first several months of this Masonic year, I searched for the
appropriate topic for this Grand Oration. I read many of the Grand Orations of my predecessors and I began to fully realize the unique opportunity I had been given to address California and Hawaiian Masonry and,
hopefully to make a contribution to its great future . I carefully listened to
the Masters and Wardens and, above all, I have listened to our members
throughout this great Jurisdiction tell of their special programs, their concerns and their hopes for Masonry. When you carefully review the Orations
and Grand Masters' messages of prior years and read the speeches that
agonize about reduced membership and the lack of attendance, you would
think they were publications of today! Our problems are not new to
Masonry by any means!
While preparing orations for Grand Lodge ceremonies, I have always
been mindful of the importance of telling the audience something of
Masonic history as it related to that particular community or ceremony. I
would tell them of the great Masons of history who forged our great
nation, who signed our Declaration of Independence, o f the Masons who

As a professional , in my business life I have always been required to
search. out the weaknesses in a system and to look for ways to overcome
a_dvers~ty. ~ven though many times I looked upon a problem as an impossible s~tuation,. r. soon _learned that all problems approached intelligently
and with a positive attitude are soon resolved . I became a believer in the
axiom "THERE ARE NO PROBLEMS - JUST OPPORTUN ITIES'.' We
must l<>?k ~pon this _growing pessimism in our great Fraternity regarding
the declme m Masomc membership as our OPPORTUN ITY to show ourselves and our families that we have the will and the skill to match the wisdom, courage and fortitude of our early Masons who built our great nation
~nd a_t the same time built Masonry on a strong foundation. We must stop
hstenmg to the "doomsday" story and start believing that we can and will
develop a growing interest in Masonry, not only within our exis;ing mem~

w;

235

bership but from within the communities in which we Jive. The natural tendency of man is to take for granted that which is serving him reasonably
well: his Country, his politics, his religion and his Masonry. We cannot take
for granted any of these great cornerstones of freedom. If we do, we will
one day find that we have lost one or all of them.
If we demonstrate to our DeMolay Brothers that we are interested in
them and that they are the future of Masonry, we will have them joining
our Fraternity as soon as they turn twenty-one. We don't want them to join
just to become a Mason. We want them to first learn the great teachings of
our Fraternity and then contribute to the future of Masonry. We must look
upon our youth as exactly what they are . .. the leaders of tomorrow's
America! Past Grand Master Ingalls, in his "Masonic Social Responsibilities" report to Grand Lodge in 1984, said, "It is a Masonic responsibility
to strive with all our strength and intelligence to make certain these young
people have the chance to be wiser than we are, better than we are, and
stronger in mind and character than we are. They are the ones who must
build a new society, plumb the depths of the oceans, and follow the trackless paths of the comets into tomorrow. They are the ones who must take
man's final steps toward the fountainhea d of all wisdom, all power and all
glorY.' Our young adults of today are intelligent, sensitive, questioning,
willing and energetic and those are exactly the "credentials " we need in
Masonry today! Those were our credentials when we were their age!
Our Grand Master in his message to our membership throughout this
year, has repeatedly said that our youth organizations continually ask for
our help, not for money, but for adult guidance. They only ask us to teach
them how to run their respective organization s. For the most part, we continue to ignore tbeir plea. We take for granted that someone else will step
forward and help them to learn and to grow into responsible citizens . If we
demonstrate our willingness to help, and in so doing demonstrate what
Masonry is really about, they will join our Fraternity at their earliest
opportunity!
The Executive Director of the Southern California DeMolay, Tom Boles,
made the sta tement that has to be a shock to all real Masons. He said,
" They have never had to close a DeMolay Chapter for the lack of money
or interest on the part of the youth . .. they have only closed Chapters due
to the lack of adult leadership from within the Chapter.• We cannot take
for granted that someone else will fulfill our responsibilities as Masons and
as parents . The youth of today are different from the youth of just ten
years ago. Today, they have the attitude that education is the central path
to a quality life and they are now taking the college courses that lead to
their goals. I sat in a dinner meeting between the DeMolay Order and the
several Bodies of Masonry, where it was obvious that the youth were less
than impressed with what they observed of Masons, and for good reason.
If we cannot provide a quality image of ourselves as individuals, or as
Masons, then why do we think they will take their time to join the Masonic
Lodge?
The Rainbow and Job's Daughters Orders display great adult support.

236

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Like DeMolay, they are enthusiastic and skilled in their ritual work. They
demonstrate love and true compassion for one another and they go out of
their way to help each other become better members of their Order. The
DeMolay will become our Masons of tomorrow, ... if we set a good example. The Job's Daughters and Rainbow Girls will want their husbands to
become Masons and their children to join the Youth Orders if they see us
setting a good example today. Yes, the youth of today are the Masons of
tomorrow but, ... we Masons of today have to give them good reason to
belong. We cannot assume they will follow in our steps in Masonry. We
cannot take them for granted!
Masonry is the oldest known fraternal order in the world. Our teachings
are of historical significance, found within the Books of the Holy Bible.
What Masonry teaches the candidate is the cornerstone of our society brotherly love, respect, to aid a Brother in distress and to be truthful in all
you do and say. These tenets of Freemasonry will never die nor will they
ever lose their luster.
Earlier, I aJiuded to our decline in membership as an "opportunity" and
that we must overcome those well meaning members that can only predict a
continuing membership decline. If we allow ourselves to despair, and if we
cannot meet this test of our times, then we deserve whatever fate is in store
for us. Masonry, like America, was built on the confidence of its people
that "if it is worth having it is worth fighting for.' I have listened to prior
Grand Orators and I have listened to Grand Masters. I have listened to the
members throughout our great States of California and Hawaii and, I have
listened to our youth and their leaders, and, I must tell you the key to
growth in membership, rather than decline, is for the Masonic Fraternity
to accept change and then go about making those necessary and orderly
changes to meet the needs of our modern day membership. In an article
written by our own Deputy Grand Master, Jack R. Levitt, for the California Freemason titled "AFFIRMATIVE FREEMASONRY'', he speaks of
optimism; and I quote: "Not only is there reason for optimism, but we will
be better off thinking of solutions than of the problems. We should realize
that what we are and how we exist depends to a large extent upon how we
think. As a poet put it, 'two men look out through the same bars; one sees
the mud and the other the stars: The optimist sees order being brought out
of chaos and does not allow apathy or negativism to interfere with his
endeavors to improve!' He goes on to say that, "change is inevitable and
our Fraternity must change with the times . .. we must have long range
goals'.' end of quote.
I would like to offer a modern day Masonic example of how times force
change in order to accommodate need. When our Fraternity in California
founded our Masonic Widows and Orphans Home in Decato in 1891, it
was to serve members and widows without financial means and orphans.
Neither of these original requirements for admission to our great Homes
are of paramount importance to us today as the justification for admission. If we held fast to our admission requirements of 1891 and said these
were our requirements of today, we would not be serving our membership

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

properly. Today, the primary need f.or a~missi~n to Union City is for the

Masonry and to not accept the premise that Masonry 1s gomg to contmue
its decline.
There is no "quick- fix" for our loss of membership and the .solut~on is
certainly complex. Better ritual performances by our Lodge Officers m the
Degree work will certainly enhance attendance, bu~ it ~ii~ not bring in ne~
members. Ritual alone is not Masonry. No one demes its importance, but 1t
is only a means to an end. The foundation of Masonry is the fa~ily a~ a
unit. Observe the Lodge that invites the wives to the Stated Meetmg dmners and provides entertainment for them while the husband is attending
his meeting and you will see a Lodge that flourishes in both attendance a~d
leadership. Look at the Lodge that supports a Youth Group and you will
see a progressive and dynamic Ldoge. Look at the Master th~t kn~ws ho-:V
to be an administrator; that can lead his Officers; that can guide his candidates and members, and you will find a Lodge with great vitality and above

Holy Bible has been modernized to meet the needs of ~oday'~ societ~. The
simple fact remains that to interest a person you must first be mterestmg to
him.
Our Masters must not continue to take for granted that by holding
twelve Stated Meetings everything else will fall into place for the year. Each
Lodge is a business that will either grow or die. Nothing stands still. In all
my discussions with Lodge Officers this year, I never once heard the subject of Long Range goals. How will the Master and W~rdens know where
they are going? How are they to get there? And how will they know when

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

they have arrived if they have not set goals?
You cannot blame a Mason for not going out at night to attend Lodge if
the ritual is of questionable quality. You cannot expect that Mason to
attend Lodge if it is poorly organized administratively and the Master and
Officers do not extend a feeling of friendship. You cannot expect a Mason
to attend his Lodge just to see the degrees. You must look to your social
programs as the foundation to build interest, support and membership
growth. You must always include the family as a unit. If you don't, your
Lodge is in direct competition with the member's wife and children for his
free time and you will surely lose. A very positive example of what I say is
displayed in the attendance at Scottish Rite meetings where the wife is a
central consideration in the many social activities.
Ritual alone is not Masonry. It is not being an Officer and it is not
totally the degree. I submit that Masonry is applying the tenets of our
Craft outside the Lodge room ... brotherly love, relief and truth. Masonry
is really caring about each other. When we do not take the time to inquire
of a Brother why he is asking for a dimit or why he has not paid his dues,
but simply violate the Code and issue him a dimit without a proper investigation, or suspend him for non-payment of dues without proper inquiry,
we are not deserving to be called Masons.
Our Grand Master, on several occasions this year, has told his audience
of the fact that our decline in membership can be reversed simply by remitting dues when a Brother has a genuine economic problem and finding out
why a Brother is asking for a dimit. .. he will probably tell you, as many
have already said to him when he asked, ... "nobody seems to care about
me". Let me tell you ... every Mason counts! How can a Master of his
Lodge be too busy to ask his Brother if he can be of help? When we leave
Lodge of an evening, do we remember the degree work or, do we remember
the fellowship of the evening? We remember mostly the Brother that we
hadn't seen for quite awhile. This summer I was asked by a member of my
own Lodge if I would go with him to our Lodge as he was afraid to go
alone after not attending for several years. I think he was afraid of being
ignored! After that meeting, he turned to me, with tears in his eyes, and
said, "Thank you. Now I can attend regularlf.' That is a memory I will
have for ever and a friend for life, simply because I took the time. The
reward was more mine than his!
Masonry is not how many candidates we can raise in a year and it is not
how perfect the delivery of the ritual. We assume once the Brother has
received his T hird Degree that he can make it on his own. It is at this specific moment that he is the most vulnerable and needs our assistance for a
better grasp of the symbolic meaning of the ritual. It is at this moment that
he needs direction in how he can best serve his Lodge on a committee or by
becoming a coach or an officer. It is at this moment the new Master Mason
is the least prepared and the most willing to participate. We must not continue to waste this talent!
I submit that the solution to the decline in membership has little to do
with television and it has little to do with our busy daily lives. The solution

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

239

is that we must realize that Masonry is like a business and unless we are diligent in our efforts to provide a quality product we will lose our customers
in Masonry as we certainly will lose them in business. Through the Leadership Workshop programs, we are informing our Lodge officers of their
administrative responsibilities and informing them of the valuable tools
available to them as Masters and Wardens of their Lodge through the
Grand Lodge. Through the Layman's Night program, we are informing
those we believe to be interested in what we represent. Through the Ritual
Committee, we continue to strive for excellence in the degree work. All o f
these are required to make your Lodge a viable entity. If you do not demonstrate a real interest in your individual Lodge member by calling upon
him to see why he has not attended Lodge, if you allow him to drop from
sight, then it will not matter, for your Lodge is surely headed for a steady
decline in membership and finally will cease as a Lodge.
We have a Masonic heritage in America that includes fourteen Presidents, eighteen Vice Presidents, many Governors, Senators, Congressmen,
thirty-five Supreme Court Justices (including our own Past Grand Master
Earl Warren) and twenty-three of the thirty-nine signers of the Declaration
of Independence. Every step in the opening of the great and mighty West
was prominently pioneered by Masons. Astronauts are the pioneers of
today's frontier and many of them are Masons. We do not take this heritage lightly. The few major accomplishments of individual Masons that are
herein recorded are but a small representation of Freemasonry's contribution to a growing America. The record is extensive, the cast too numerous,
and the scope too broad to trace in more than general outline in this oration, but the point is clear: Freemasons helped to conceive, build and shape
this great America! As you already know, Masons of California and
Hawaii have contributed over $900,000.00 to the refurbishment of the
Statue of Liberty, America's most tangible reminder to the rest of the
world that we are a free Nation, made up of all races, colors and creeds;
willing and able to live in harmony and freedom. As you see, Masons continue to contribute in the building and shaping of America!
As Masons, we give our time and money to the care of our elderly at our
Union City Home and the care of our children at our Covina Horne. Our
operating budgets for these Homes alone exceed $1,000,000.00 per month
and are supported by California and Hawaii Masons. Masons, through
their memberships in the Concordant Bodies, fully support the Burn Centers, the Orthopedic Hospitals and the Aphasia Clines, to name just a few.
Through the Scholarship Program the Masons of California support many
deserving young people in obtaining a higher education.
One of the great tragedies of today's California Masonry is the Mason
that moves out of State and affiliates with another Jurisdiction and then
<limits. Consequently he loses his right to petition our Masonic Hornes for
residency. Beyond that is the tragedy of thousands of Masons that live in
California but do not affiliate with a California Lodge and therefore cannot petition the Horne for residency, or assistance, when they need it most.
Therein exists a great source of membership that we have not attracted. It

might be of great benefit to that sojourning member once he fulfilled the
minimum requirements of California membership.
Yes, we have an important story to tell our neighbors and friends, our
own sons and daughters; of the magnificent heritage we Masons possess
and of the "good works" we do by way of philanthropy. We have something to be very proud of and it is time we tell our story to the world.
This oration is reaching the membership that attends Lodge and that is
interested in its progress. Usually, this is the wrong audience, but not this
time. YOU , in this audience, are the ones on which depends the future of
Masonry. Let's wear our Masonic pins with pride and be prepared to tell
our story of Masonry and what it represents when we are asked. Let's quit
tel.ling people that Masonry is a secret organization when in fact it is anythmg but secret. Let's promote a family environment in our Lodge. Let's
take the time to meet with our Brother that is asking for a dimit and see
what we can do to change his mind. Above all, let's visit the Brother that is
not paying his dues to see why and if necessary what we can do to relieve
his distress.
I had several opportunities to address the school children during cornerstone ceremonies this year and would leave them with an important
thought that they could carry with them. I believe we can apply this
thought to our daily living and, more particularly, to resolving the problem
of our membership decline.
"If you think you are beaten .... You are.
"If you think you dare not. .. . You don't.
"If you'd like to win, but think you
can't. .. It's almost a cinch you won't.
"If you think you 'II lose ... You 're lost.
"Life's battles don't always go to
the stronger or faster man;
"But sooner or later the man who wins
is the one who thinks he can . . . . .. "
Yes, we have a great story to tell about Masonry, how Masons contributed extensively to the forming of this great Nation and at great personal
risk; how Masons forged the great Plains and opened the West to new
growth; how Masons became great leaders of our Nation as Presidents,
Statesmen and as Justices; how Masons have contributed to our space program and have given their lives in exchange; how Masons have been great
military leaders. No part of our great American history is without Masonic
influence. There is, in fact, no area of American life that Freemasons have
not bettered through their devotion to God, Country and Humanity.
If these great Masons of history, while serving their country, found time
to be Masters of their Lodges or Grand Masters of their Jurisdictions, isn't
it logical to assume we of today can give an equal measure of devotion to
maintain such a magnificent heritage? Our forefathers in Masonry did not
take their obligations to Masonry and America lightly and they did not
take for granted that someone else would do their job for them. Let us go

forth and tell the world the truth about Masonry. We have an important
story to tell of our heritage and of what we stand for and above all what we
are doing to make this a better place to Jive as Americans, as parents and as
Masons! It is time for all Masons to take upon their shoulders the responsibility to tell their friends, children and neighbors what Masonry is all about
and that we are not a secret organization. It is time for all Masons to r:ne_w
their pride in Masonry. It is time for all Masons to pull together w1thm
their own Lodge. It is time for Lodge Officers to realize that the manner in
which they conduct their Lodge business and the quality of their delivery of
the ritual is in direct relation to the interest of their membership in attending Lodge and participating in the Lodge operations. It is time for Grand
Lodge to carefully consider constructive changes to the approach and
broad administration of Masonry in order to meet the challenges of modern day America. We must take seriously our responsibilities and duties as
the Master or Warden of our Lodge, to insure the quality of the ritual, the
proper administration of our Lodge business and to attend to the needs of
the individual member and to make certain that each member is fully aware
that he is indeed important to Masonry. Masonry is not the individual ...
Masonry is the family as a unit. MASONRY IS A FAMILY
EXPERIENCE.
As Masons of California we have a golden opportunity to prove that to
reverse the decline in membership is a simple task of telling, and re-telling
the important story of Masonry to our friends, neighbors and children.
Telling them of what we do for our charities; how we make good men better; how we believe in the founding principles of our Grovernment and
how our early Masons helped to found this great country of ours. Yes, we
have a great story to tell and one that we can be most proud of. We must
tell them we are not a secret organization and that everything we stand for
is printed within the Holy Bible and the Constitution of our great United
States. We are Masons that believe strongly in the tenets of brotherly love,
relief and truth and in God and country! Our people are once again demonstrating their love for our Country, they are returning to the Church .
The moral fibre of this Country has once again been tested and proven
strong. Mason are strong.
Masons are America!

MASONIC WIDOWS PROGRAM
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
To achieve one's goal is a truly rewarding experience, and this feeling is
shared by each member of the Committee. The objectives of the Masonic
Widows Program are to let the wives of departed Brothers know that they
have not been forgotten , that they are remembered, and that we care.
Thanks to the cooperation of officers and members throughout the
Jurisdiction, seventy-six percent of our California Lodges are inviting these
wives to attend various social activities as part of our Masonic family. It is
our hope that the number of participants will continue to increase as it has
since the introduction of this Grand Lodge activity, and that their enjoyment will reflect our gratification in making this possible.

REPORT OF COMMITTE E ON TAXATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A . M. of Calif ornia:
The G rand Lodge Committee on Taxation renders advice on matters o f
taxation when requested b y the Grand Lodge, subordinate Lo dges, and

248

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

other organizations under their jurisdiction. Our assistance has been
requested with respect to matters of income, property, sales and employ.
ment taxes . An annual report to the Grand Master is a part of the work of
the Committee.
Last year's report was effectually a manual and treatise on practical tax.
ation Jaw for Masonic Lodges. It is available as a part of the 1985 Proceed.
ings of the Grand Lodge of California, of which the Secretary of every
Lodge receives a copy. Repeating a part, or all, of it herein would serve little purpose.
Section 2304 of the Masonic Code has been amended so that a Lodge
(after consent by the Temple Properties Committee) may invest in memberships or shares in a Masonic Temple Association to hold or acquire land to
be occupied by a Masonic Lodge.
Section 2305 was added to the Masonic Code to provide:
(a) A Masonic Temple Association may be organized to own or acquire
land or a building;
(b) The exclusive purpose for which these Associations may be organized is to hold title to property, collect income from it, and turn
over the net income to its member or members;
(c) All of the members must be organizations described in Section 50l(c)
of the Internal Revenue Code;
(d) Uniform Articles and By-Laws are to be promulgated by the Temple
Properties Committee.
During this Grand Lodge year, this Committee has given assistance to
Lodges and Temple Associations on the following matters: Employment
taxes, property taxes, income tax exemptions, tax forms, Internal Revenue
Service audits, manner of making donations.
Lodges are warned not to permit commercial advertising in their trestleboards. If discovered in a tax audit, amounts received would be treated as
taxable income.
Although the Grand Lodge has a blanket exemption from Federal
income tax that covers individual Lodges, the State of California has never
issued such a blanket exemption. If a Lodge has exemption difficulties, it
should contact this Committee for help.
Several Thmple Associations may share ownership of one property without incurring Federal or State tax difficulties. However, when the Temple
Properties Committee issues its new model Articles and By-Laws, secure a
copy of these. The approval of the Temple Properties Committee must be
finally received for au changes.
If real property is purchased for cash, and there is no purchase debt, no
income from unrelated business is generated by rents from the property.
Respectfully submitted,
VINSON BRICE, Chairman
ALBERT f. SIMMONS

WILLIAM J. MOIR

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON YOUTH ORDERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M . of California:
The Committee on Youth Orders has applied its greatest effort this year
in endeavoring to get acquainted with the officers of the Lodges in this
Jurisdiction and to encourage them to initiate and expand their activities in
support of our Masonic Youth Groups. With 38 members on the Committee this past year it has been possible to increase our visibility, both with the
Lodges and with the Youth Groups and their leaders.
We Masons recognize that we each have received a great many solid
character building lessons and personal growth opportunities through our
association with Masonry. The question then arises, what are we to do with
all these marvelous ideas and qualities with which we have been blessed?
Well, Brethren, each and every member of your Youth Orders Committee
would strongly urge you to PASS IT ON! - and to whom better than our
young people. Ways and means of accomplishing this is one of the primary
goals of this Committee.
Enthusiasm and good fellowship are strongly evident throughout California in all of the Youth Groups. They have during this past year, however, continued to lose Chapters, Bethels and A ssemblies at the same time
that our Lodges are diminishing in number. The causes are, of course, varied but certainly include: 1) Lack of Time (possibly due to increased
demands and activities at school and elsewhere); 2) Insufficient numbers of
adult leaders who are willing to spend their time working with the young
people; and 3) Too few parents who really understand and appreciate the
benefits of having their children involved in these activities. These parents,
therefore, fail to encourage their youngsters' participation. This last item is
one that Masons can influence through an increased visibility and participation in Community and School affairs.
The accomplishments of the Committee during the past year include :
A . Completion of the computerization of information on: l) All of the
Masonic Youth Groups in California, including when and where they
meet and the adult contact person for each; 2) All of the Lodges and
Inspectors for each Inspectoral District; and 3) The Youth Orders
Committeeman and the Districts assigned to him. This data can be
retrieved and printed out in a variety of ways and will be made available to all interested parties.
B. Written reports have been received from most of the Committeemen
which indicates that approximately 160 visits, representing the Grand
Lodge, have been made by them to Lodges, Schools of Instruction,
Youth Groups and Youth functions.
C. The Committee has made a presentation as a part of the program at
each of the Masonic Leadership Workshops scheduled this year and
has provided and staffed a booth which supplied all kinds of literature and brochures promoting the Masonic Youth Groups.
D. A thirty page booklet describing Masonically oriented scholastic

250

PROCEEDING S OF THE

assistance programs available to young people in California has been
pr~pared for distri?ution. Copies will be available for each Lodge at
this 1986 Communicatio n.
E. The Youth Group Membership Referral Flyer project has been continued from last year. The remaining 25,000 flyers have been distributed to Lodges asking for them.
F. A "Youth Extravaganza" was planned and carried out by this Committee. This was really a large "prospect party" for all of the youth
groups. This event was initiated for the first time this year was
enthusiastically received, well attended, resulted in a good number of
new members for the various youth groups involved and, we intend
will b.e rep7ated in several parts of the State next year. 1Welve Lodg;
and five High Twelve Clubs participated financially in this most successful event.
G. In August the (now, I think) annual meeting between the Executive
Committee of the Grand Lodge and the Adult Heads of the various
Masonic Youth Groups was held under the auspices of this Committee. These meetings serve as a forum for the discussion of ideas of
mutual concern and for the interchange of information and seem to
be beneficial to all.
H . The Committee continues to staff an information booth on "G"
Floor during the Grand Lodge Communicatio n for the benefit of the
Lo?g~s in general and for Senior Wardens in particular regarding
theu mcluding youth activities in the Lodge calendar for the coming
year.
Respectfully Submitted,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON FINANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Finance has reviewed the audited financial statements presented by the Grand Treasurer for the fiscal year ended June 30,
1986, as required by our Code.
The necessary supplemental appropriations for those items where budgets were exceeded totaled $111,866, which were duly approved by the
Grand Master. Three items represent more than half of the total overruns:
Appointed Officer Expense - $31,852; Grand Master's Travel - $10,128;
and Liability Insurance - $17 ,502. Very few committees exceeded their
budgets and we congratulate the committee chairmen for their diligent control.
Estimates on the publication and distribution costs for our California
Freemason Magazine indicate that our present per capita assessment of
$1.10 will be adequate for the coming year and no increase will be
required.
New capital additions have been budgeted in the amount of $33,000 as
shown below:
Computer System Upgrade (Phase II) ..... . ............ $ 25,000
Membership Address Conversion . . .............. . .. . . .. $ 8,000
Total . . ......... .... .. .. ....... . ........... . ... . ...$ 33,000
This represents a continuation of our program to upgrade our membership and accounting computer systems.
The rate of reimbursement for the use of personal vehicles on Grand
Lodge business shall remain at $.18 per mile until this time again in 1987.
Although your Committee considered the decline in the cost of oil and gas,
this trend may not continue and a reduction would have only a nominal
effect on the per capita as opposed to other major cost items on the
budget.
Your Committee on Finance continues to be very concerned about the
increase in per capita tax and the various items of expense in the Grand
Lodge budget. We note that the per capita tax has increased from $5 .84 in
the 1984-1985 fiscal year to a proposed assessment of $7. 70 in the 19861987 fiscal year. This is an increase of 32 percent over a two year period, all
of this at a time when inflation has been greatly reduced. While many of
the items which affect the per capita tax are beyond our control, such as
insurance premiums which will double this year, and our continuing decline
in membership, as graphically represented in the Grand Treasurer's Report,
Exhibit D, there are several items that can be controlled and reduced.
It is our recommendatio n to the incoming Grand Master that serious
consideration be given to reducing expenses in the area of Annual Communication costs, particularly for Inspectors' travel and expenses which
accounts for $.27 of the per capita tax, and the area of Grand Lodge Elective and Appointive Officers' expense which accounts for $1.27 of the per

252

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

capita tax. We would like to commend the current Grand Master for help.
ing to hold down this year's Annual Communication expense by continuing
to limit it to three days.
Again this year we have provided all Lodge Secretaries with advanced
notice of the proposed per capita assessment following our August budget
meeting with the Grand Lodge Elective Line.
Once again we wish to thank Very Worshipful John A. Sickenberaer.
Grand Treasurer, for his wise counsel concerning the management of 0 ~
financial affairs; and our Accounting Manager, Brother Hugo Delfin, and
his staff for their continued assistance.
As always, our Grand Secretary, Very Worshipful Robert A. Klinger, and
his staff have been most helpful during the year and deserve our sincere
appreciation.
The proposed 1986-1987 budget is presented here in summary form.
Details are also published in the Proceedings as part of this report.

AFTERNOON SESSION
WEDNESDAY, OCTOBER 15, 1986
At 3:00 P.M. the retiring Grand Lodge Officers were escorted into the
Auditorium and conducted to seats which had been previously provided
for them. As they were escorted to their seats they were greeted with a very
warm round of applause. The newly Elected and Appointive Officers to
serve for the ensuing year then entered the Auditorium led by the newly
appointed Grand Marshal and assumed their stations and places for the
purpose of being formally installed.

258

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

INSTALLATION 01'~ OFFICERS
With Past Grand Master Donald G. Ingalls acting as the Installing Offi.
cer and Past Grand Master Kermit A . Jacobson acting as Master of Ceremonies, the Appointive Officers were individually introduced and duly
installed. Donald Nielsen as soloist, accompanied by Grand Organist
Harold Hand, rendered the song "Accentuate the Positive:' the theme of
incoming Grand Master, Jack R. Levitt. The Grand Lecturer, the Grand
Secretary and the Grand Treasurer were then individually introduced and
installed, following which the Junior Grand Warden and Senior Grand
Warden were introduced and installed. The next officer to be installed was
the Deputy Grand Master, and the Installation Ceremony was concluded
with the installation of the Grand Master who was saluted with Public
Grand Honors.
Eleanor Driskell, wife of retiring Grand Master John W. Driskell, was
escorted to the East, and the newly installed Grand Master made a presentation to her on behalf of the members of Grand Lodge. The now Junior
Past Grand Master John W. Driskell was then escorted to the East for the
customary presentations. The Past Master's Lapel Pin was presented to
him by Past Grand Master Robert 0. West, the Past Grand Master's
Apron by Past Grand Master Raymond A . Ebbage, and the Past Grand
Master's Certificate by Past Grand Master Edward H. Siems.
Past Grand Master Chester R. MacPhee then presented to Eleanor
Driskell a token of appreciation also on behalf of the members of Grand
Lodge, following which the Arthur S. Crites Lapel Pins were exchanged
between the Grand Wardens, the Deputy Grand Master and the Grand
Master.
Grand Master Levitt was then pleased to introduce various groups which
had come to see him installed. He also introduced certain individuals and
then asked each Officer to introduce members of their respective families
who were in attendance. At the conclusion of these introductions Grand
Master Levitt spoke to the programs he wished to continue during the
ensuing Grand Lodge year. He also commented on several new programs
which he wished to institute, concluding his remarks by stating that it is his
intention to continually dwell on the positive and not the negative in
accordance with his theme, "Accentuate the Positive:• These most positive
remarks along with his positive attitude were received with a very warm
and generous standing ovation.
Following the newly installed Grand Master's remarks, all in attendance
were invited to a reception to be held in the Exhibit Hall of the Memorial
Temple. Adjournment was at 4:20 P.M. with Grand Lodge to be formally
closed at 9:00 A.M. on Thursday, October 16, 1986.

ANNOUNCEMENT
Reviews of the Proceedings of other Grand
Lodges have appeared quarterly in the "California Freemason," copies of which have been
sent to each Grand Lodge. This program will
be continued.
The " California Freemason" is issued quarterly and each copy carries additional reviews.
Hence, they do not appear in these Proceedings.
